At $q=257$, we introduce zero-selector encoding: zero payload bytes locate ambiguous coefficients, and selector bits resolve their values. We analyze selector capacity, overflow, and key-generation retries. For $n=1024$, a 1033-byte configuration has overflow probability at most $2^{-128}$ under independent uniform coefficients. Checked AVX2 decoding takes 213 cycles, compared with 2203 cycles for BAT's 1040-byte format. At $q=769$, we lower conversion costs using an existing compact radix format at the same encoded length as BAT. We specialize rejection sampling to simplify coefficient extraction at $q=257$ and reduce random-bit demand at $q=769$. At $(q,n)=(769,1024)$, expected candidate-bit demand decreases by 24.39\% relative to direct 10-bit rejection. Four-polynomial generation uses 7.14-13.21\% fewer AVX2 cycles. For residual multiplication, proven range bounds justify omitting strict input-centering corrections, while register scheduling reduces stack accesses. We integrate the public-key codecs and multiplication components into BAT and END. Across the tested C and AVX2 implementations, encapsulation costs decrease by $39.93-55.25\%$ in BAT and $41.36-48.84\%$ in END. The corresponding decapsulation reductions are $5.42-8.55\%$ in BAT and, for END, $23.99-45.89\%$ in C and $6.98-8.04\%$ in AVX2. END AVX2 gains mainly come from the public key codec. These results quantify the effect of modulus-specific optimizations on complete component and KEM costs.
papers.authors: Ying Liu, Yu Zhang, Xianhui Lu

papers.title: Averaging Collusion Breaks Traceability in Personalized Neural Audio Watermarking
papers.abstract: Personalized neural audio watermarking systems embed user-specific payloads into audio to trace the user associated with a leaked or misused copy. Existing evaluations mainly assume access to a single personalized copy, but real-world distribution may expose multiple copies of the same recording. We find that simple sample-wise averaging breaks traceability: averaging only two copies produces tracing-failure rates of 87.7-99.7% across the five systems while largely preserving audio quality. Decoder outputs show distinct responses to coalition payload composition across systems, with high majority agreement in TimbreWM but substantially lower agreement in WMCodec. In a more sophisticated payload-aware setting, mixture weighting can further steer the decoder toward a selected nonmember, achieving a target success rate of 92.3% in TimbreWM. Preliminary confidence screening rejects many collusion-induced assignments while retaining most valid single-copy outputs. Code and results are available at https://github.com/Silwan5z/neural-audio-watermark-collusion-attack. This work highlights multi-copy traceability as an additional evaluation dimension for personalized neural audio watermarking alongside conventional single-copy robustness.
papers.authors: Yangming Liu, Haiyun Li, Dongfu Song, Ziang Xu, Jiehui Luo, Yining Zhang, Zhiyong Wu

papers.title: Gaussian Difference Dynamics: Breaking the $2^{n/2}$ Barrier for the Shortest Vector Problem and Discrete Gaussian Sampling
papers.abstract: We give classical randomized algorithms in a word RAM model that break the $2^{n/2}$ barrier for both discrete Gaussian sampling (DGS) and the Shortest Vector Problem (SVP). For every fixed $α>1$, shifted DGS on arbitrary lattices at width $σ\geαη_{1/2}(L)$ takes $$ (3/2)^{n/2+o(n)}\text{ time} \qquad\text{and}\qquad (4/3)^{n/2+o(n)}\text{ space}. $$ These bounds match the Becker--Ducas--Gama--Laarhoven (BDGL) heuristic sieving exponents. At widths at least $3η_{1/2}(L)/2$, the same total cost suffices for an entire batch of $\lfloor(4/3)^{n/2}\rfloor$ samples jointly close to independent target Gaussians. For SVP on arbitrary lattices, our algorithm returns a shortest nonzero vector with high probability in $$ 2^{0.4130n+o(n)}\text{ time} \qquad\text{and}\qquad 2^{0.3138n+o(n)}\text{ space}. $$ As a corollary, we obtain centered DGS at every width with the same exponents, answering a question of Stephens-Davidowitz (SODA 2016). We introduce Gaussian difference dynamics (GDD), a framework for tracking expected counts and pairwise clustering of vectors through repeated differencing. A closed recursion for the first two counting moments controls these quantities relative to a Gaussian reference, without requiring independence within intermediate lists. Accurate moment bounds let us extract a Gaussian sample by weighted selection, while the weaker bounds needed to establish a shortest vector representation allow us to retain more differences. We perform these transitions on thin spherical shells, where the Gaussian rejection weights can be renormalized at subexponential cost. For batch sampling, we combine this geometry with the double rejection technique of Doulgerakis and Laarhoven to control the joint distribution of outputs while reusing vectors.
papers.authors: Yiming Gao, Xuyuan Han, Honggang Hu

papers.title: VerfGraph: Efficient Zero-Knowledge Verifiable Graph Query Evaluation System
papers.abstract: Graph databases are often used to manage relationship-rich data, whose graph structure and attributes may be sensitive. In many applications, a database owner or a service provider evaluates queries over a private graph for a client. Because the graph cannot be fully disclosed and independently re-executing the query may be impractical, the client cannot directly verify the returned result. This creates a need for verifiable graph query evaluation that preserves data confidentiality. We present VerfGraph, a zero-knowledge system for verifiable graph query evaluation, which enables a client to verify that the query result was correctly computed over a committed graph data, without revealing private graph records or intermediate query values beyond the public inputs and what is implied by the query result. Building on the expansion-centric model introduced by the state-of-the-art zero-knowledge verifiable graph query evaluation system ZKGraph (ICDE'26), VerfGraph achieves more efficient and expressive zero-knowledge verifiable graph query evaluation by advancing design in two key ways. First, we propose novel operator-proof methods for core expansion and shortest-path operations that reduce costly sorting and comparison checks and eliminate edge canonicalization for bidirectional expansion. Furthermore, we introduce correctness proofs for count and weighted shortest-path operators, broadening the class of graph queries that can be verified. We evaluate VerfGraph using the LDBC Social Network Benchmark. Compared with ZKGraph on complex IC queries, VerfGraph achieves $33.9\times$-$59.7\times$ speedups in proof generation and reduces peak prover memory by factors of $4.5\times$-$6.6\times$, while maintaining millisecond-level verification and producing sub-MB proofs.
papers.authors: Tianyi Ma, Yuncong Zhang, Yuanzhuo Yu, Boshi Yuan, Shi-Feng Sun

papers.title: Distill and Conquer: Cryptanalytic Extraction of Local Rules in the Hard-Label Setting
papers.abstract: Cryptanalytic extraction can expose proprietary neural network parameters, but unknown architectures and large parameter counts complicate recovery under hard-label access. Local class-pair rules offer a narrower target by making class-switching conditions explicit and predicting nearby labels under a specified sampling law. Distillation methods mainly return substitute models rather than explicit rules whose local agreement has been tested against the victim. We propose Distill–Probe–Extract to produce such rules without first identifying the victim architecture. Verified boundary events guide student training, and student gradients propose directions at boundary anchors refined through victim queries. Fresh hard-label queries then test the proposed rules, retaining validation inputs and victim labels for each accepted rule. On a digits multilayer perceptron and pooling convolutional networks, fixed-candidate comparisons isolate the savings from replacing victim-normal estimation with student gradients. For the multilayer perceptron, median recorded online cost decreases from 246 to 118 queries per attempt after student preparation. With preparation and failures counted, full Fashion-MNIST sessions produce 2.03–2.23 times Direct's accepted-rule count under the original validation gate at 320,000-call caps. At 320,000 calls, a separate student-level test on trained Blended watermarks yields 99.99% trigger agreement and 91.79% clean agreement, with all three seeds passing joint verification.
papers.authors: Chun Li, Di Li, Liping Zhuang, Siqi Zhu, Yufeng Tang, Xingfu Yan, Zheng Gong

papers.title: Construction and Classification of Minimum-Latency 5-Bit APN S-Boxes
papers.abstract: S-boxes serve as essential nonlinear building blocks in symmetric-key cryptography, where their cryptographic properties and hardware implementation costs jointly dictate the security and efficiency of lightweight primitives. This paper studies the construction and classification of minimum-latency 5-bit APN (Almost Perfect Nonlinear) permutations under a prescribed gate-delay model, using exact minimum latencies of Boolean component functions. Under the fixed gate-delay model of the NanGate 45nm standard cell library, we partition the search space into input-variable permutation (IP) equivalence classes to establish a comprehensive minimum-latency database covering all 5-input balanced nonlinear Boolean functions. This database delivers exact minimum latencies and gate-level implementations for all equivalence classes up to a latency of 150ps, while guaranteeing strict lower bounds on latency for classes exceeding that threshold, combining property filtering with circuit synthesis. We search the five affine equivalence classes of 5-bit APN permutations. For each affine transformation of the input, we use exact component-function latencies to select components with linearly independent masks and choose their polarities, obtaining S-box circuits without repeating gate-level synthesis for each candidate. Exhaustive search with latency-preserving input-variable permutation reduction establishes a minimum latency of 126.745ps over all 5-bit APN permutations under the prescribed gate-delay model, with explicit constructions attaining this minimum in every class.The classification results give the optimized latency distributions and numbers of optimal IP classes of input-affine transformations within each affine class. Comparisons with selected 5-bit S-box implementations under the same model show simultaneous reductions in some cases: latency decreases by $10.20\%$--$29.18\%$ and normalized gate area by $5.37\%$--$27.69\%$, while preserving the original S-box mappings.
papers.authors: Yaqi Qu, Xiutao Feng, Ruanyiyang Sun

papers.title: Polynomial Batch Accumulators for Onboarding-Dominant Zero-Knowledge Membership Proofs
papers.abstract: Zero-knowledge membership accumulators are conventionally tailored for slowly growing sets with frequent proof generation, creating severe efficiency bottlenecks for modern compliance architectures. Governance-driven applications like FATF customer due diligence, eIDAS 2.0 wallet issuance, and MiCA VASP authorization invert this structure. In this regime, rosters are ingested at an enterprise scale, while proofs are requested selectively. To resolve this mismatch, we introduce Polynomial Equation Batching (PEB), a membership accumulator for onboarding heavy workloads. PEB represents up to 128 members per batch as a characteristic polynomial and hashes its coefficients via Poseidon, seamlessly scaling to arbitrarily large populations through parallel batching. We present two variants: PEB-A, which maps member secrets directly to polynomial roots for maximum performance, and PEB-B, which hashes secrets in-circuit for hardened security. Implemented in Noir and Barretenberg on BN254, and evaluated for up to 1,048,576 members, PEB provides significant performance improvements. Compared to incremental Merkle trees, PEB-A achieves up to a 149.07x mean speedup in per-user initialization while incurring a modest 33.87% proof-generation overhead. Additionally, against static Merkle trees, PEB-A delivers a 15.71x speedup during setup. By shifting off-circuit overhead from hash evaluations to field multiplications, PEB provides a highly efficient, scalable solution for real-world zero-knowledge compliance systems.
papers.authors: Samanta Karmaker, Sampad Sikder, Md Ariful Islam, Md Sadek Ferdous

papers.title: Quantum Time-Space Tradeoffs for Short Merkle-Damgård Collisions
papers.abstract: We study time-space tradeoffs for finding short collisions in Merkle-Damg{\aa}rd~(MD) hashing in the quantum auxiliary-input quantum random-oracle model~(QAI-QROM). An adversary may preprocess the compression function into $S$ qubits of arbitrary oracle-dependent quantum advice and, after receiving a fresh salt, make $T$ superposition queries to find a collision consisting of at most $B$ blocks. Previous quantum analyses gave an $\widetilde{O}(ST^3/N)$ security bound for MD collisions with classical advice. Unlike the classical theory of short MD collisions, however, this bound is insensitive to the collision length $B$: existing quantum techniques did not exploit the combinatorial structure forced by a short collision. We develop a structure-sensitive compressed-oracle analysis that overcomes this obstacle. For two-block collisions, we prove an upper bound \[ \widetilde{O}\left(\min\left\{1, \frac{ST^2+T^3}{N}\right\}\right), \] even against arbitrary quantum advice. For $M=N$, together with the known attack, this gives a tight characterization up to logarithmic factors, closes the previous factor-$T$ gap in the preprocessing term, and resolves an open problem of Akshima, Guo, and Liu~(CRYPTO '22, JoC '24). For general $B\le T$, we show in the regime $(2S+1)(T+2B)^3\le N$ that the success probability is at most \[ \widetilde{O}\!\left(\min\left\{1, \frac{ST^2B+T^3}{N}\right\}\right). \] Thus, when $B\ll T$, the preprocessing term improves over the previous $ST^3/N$ bound by a factor of roughly $T/B$. Motivated by the tight two-block result, we propose the $ST^2B$ conjecture, asserting that $ST^2B=\widetilde{\Theta}(N)$ is the correct constant-success tradeoff for short MD collisions in the regime $T^3=o(N)$.
papers.authors: Shashwat Agrawal, Ashrujit Ghoshal, Venkata Koppula

papers.title: Gaussian Difference Dynamics: Breaking the $2^{n/2}$ Barrier for the Shortest Vector Problem and Discrete Gaussian Sampling
papers.abstract: We give classical randomized algorithms in a word-RAM model that break the $2^{n/2}$ barrier for both discrete Gaussian sampling (DGS) and the Shortest Vector Problem (SVP). For every fixed $\alpha>1$, shifted DGS on arbitrary lattices at width $\sigma\ge\alpha\eta_{1/2}(L)$ takes $$ (3/2)^{n/2+o(n)}\text{ time} \qquad\text{and}\qquad (4/3)^{n/2+o(n)}\text{ space}. $$ These bounds match the Becker--Ducas--Gama--Laarhoven (BDGL) heuristic sieving exponents. At widths at least $3\eta_{1/2}(L)/2$, the same total cost suffices for an entire batch of $\lfloor(4/3)^{n/2}\rfloor$ samples jointly close to independent target Gaussians. For SVP on arbitrary lattices, our algorithm returns a shortest nonzero vector with high probability in $$ 2^{0.4130n+o(n)}\text{ time} \qquad\text{and}\qquad 2^{0.3138n+o(n)}\text{ space}. $$ As a corollary, we obtain centered DGS at every width with the same exponents, answering a question of Stephens-Davidowitz (SODA 2016). We introduce Gaussian difference dynamics (GDD), a framework for tracking expected counts and pairwise clustering of vectors through repeated differencing. A closed recursion for the first two counting moments controls these quantities relative to a Gaussian reference, without requiring independence within intermediate lists. Accurate moment bounds let us extract a Gaussian sample by weighted selection, while the weaker bounds needed to establish a shortest vector representation allow us to retain more differences. We perform these transitions on thin spherical shells, where the Gaussian rejection weights can be renormalized at subexponential cost. For batch sampling, we combine this geometry with the double rejection technique of Doulgerakis and Laarhoven to control the joint distribution of outputs while reusing vectors.
papers.authors: Yiming Gao, Xuyuan Han, Honggang Hu

papers.title: Elliptic Curve Arithmetic for Quantum Cryptanalysis: A Study of Curve25519
papers.abstract: Recent quantum resource estimates over prime fields have largely focused on prime order elliptic curves. We implement modern affine circuit techniques on the widely deployed composite order curve, Curve25519, and obtain a scalar circuit using 47,199,530 CCX gates and 1,189 peak logical qubits. This uses approximately 35% and 18% fewer gates than Schrottenloher's published space- and gate-optimized secp256k1 circuits, respectively. We separate three contributions. First, we apply established arithmetic and signed table techniques to Curve25519. In a comparison using the same arithmetic framework and signed half tables, its field and subgroup parameters, together with the chosen GCD iteration budgets, save 2,218,944 CCX gates relative to secp256k1. Second, we adapt odd signed digit recoding to quantum windows using fixed output translations. This saves a further 15,204 CCX gates and also applies to prime order curves. Third, we combine nonzero digits with a fixed 8-torsion offset point to keep the accumulator outside the lookup points' subgroup. With zero slope support and exact field arithmetic, this yields an exception-free addition schedule and nonzero denominators during slope uncomputation, without additional quantum point additions. Our counts include the full scalar schedule, lookup and cleanup. The corresponding implementation uses truncated arithmetic and heuristic GCD budgets, and excludes Fourier rotation synthesis and classical recovery.
papers.authors: Yintong Luo, Craig Costello

papers.title: Penalty Deposits For Discrete Logarithms
papers.abstract: We propose a technique that allows a trusted party in some protocol to attach deposits to their own secrets, without impacting security, and convincing other parties using zero-knowledge proofs. The rationale is that, should this party compromise the protocol by blundering or revealing its secrets, they lose the attached deposit to attackers. As a result, stakeholders gain confidence on how this trusted party operates, and breaches become public as soon as deposits are claimed. We formalize this technique and related security notions, provide two practical constructions in generic discrete logarithm groups, and analyze its application to ECDLP-based protocols.
papers.authors: Francisco Vial-Prado, Louis Goubin

papers.title: Extracting System Prompt of LLM Services in Complex (Agentic) Settings: Hierarchical Optimization and Reliable Evaluation Metrics
papers.abstract: System prompt is a critical intellectual property of large language model (LLM) services. To analyze its leakage, prompt extraction attacks have been extensively studied. However, we validate that existing attacks substantially degrade on recent LLM services, whose complexity has evolved in both the prompt itself and system-level constraints. Specifically, (1) system prompts become longer and more structured to contain pre-defined tool schemas, execution logic, safety guardrails, etc., and (2) only the final post-processed outputs (e.g., agent's actions) but not the raw textual response can be observed. In this paper, we address the above increased complexity by proposing Extraction with Hierarchical Optimization (ExtraHerO), which (1) decomposes the prompt extraction into a hierarchical reconstruction process with a pre-defined structural prompt template, and (2) iteratively updates the adversarial query with guidance of feedback-template differences to observe diverse outputs. In particular, we monitor the information gain of attack optimization to early stop or reset it for a good trade-off between effectiveness and efficiency. We also find that existing evaluation metrics for prompt fidelity can be misleading because they do not account for structural information. Therefore, we rely on global textual similarity and prioritize structural keywords. Moreover, we introduce a system-level metric, adversarial utility, to measure the help of prompt extraction for real-world downstream attacks. Experimental results demonstrate the consistent superiority of ExtraHerO, with average improvements of 12.5\% (fidelity), 2.3\% (functionality), and 6.0\% (adversarial utility) on chatbots, and 12.2\%, 34.3\%, and 30.5\% on agents.
papers.authors: Shuaidong Li, Chenhao Lin, Xinshan Yang, Chao Shen, Yufei Chen, Zhengyu Zhao

papers.title: Weir: Bounded-Memory Indexing and Proving with Sequential Storage
papers.abstract: A low-memory prover must control sumcheck tables, sparse accesses, commitments and proof assembly. We present Weir, a Shockwave-derived protocol with a complete read-write (RW) index-and-prove schedule. The schedule restores sparse request order, retains commitment state through later openings and assembles the proof externally. These steps preserve the direct RAM prover's canonical bytes across buffer choices, with a common verifier. Under an external-query-tape model, the schedule uses $O(B+\log T)$ field RAM, constant digest RAM and polylogarithmic auxiliary RAM. Algebraic work and record traffic are quasilinear; oracle-query byte work is charged separately. A classical random-oracle analysis bounds knowledge error. Fused Split-Butterfly-Merge removes $n-1$ materialized transform passes at length $2^n$. Its ordered routing contract extends to multiplicative-coset Reed-Solomon (RS) and recursive foldable encoders; component checks match reference codewords, traffic counts and RS fold states. In a fixed 64 MiB worker-cap grid, RW completes all tested matrix and Poseidon inputs; RAM completes matrix dimension 8. Within the matrix grid, the largest RW point has 64 times as many padded constraints as that RAM point, using 3.33 MB prover RSS and 9.51 minutes index+prove. We report latency, external payload, query bytes, proof size and verification time for this offline operating range.
papers.authors: Kyeongtae Lee, Jihye Kim, Hyunok Oh

papers.title: VeriSpoof: Beyond Real or Fake with One Audio LLM
papers.abstract: A speech deepfake detector estimates whether a recording is synthetic, but a forensic analyst also asks which system produced it, whether recordings share a source, and what evidence supports each conclusion. We present VeriSpoof, an audio language model that unifies five tasks with shared weights: deepfake detection, generator attribution (generator, acoustic model and vocoder), recording-condition analysis, synthesized-span localisation, and source verification. Each decision is supported by grounded rationales whose statements can be independently verified. Answers are scored by sentence likelihood, allowing detection and source verification to be thresholded without separate heads. Rationale statements can be checked against waveform measurements, span labels, or generator metadata. Counterfactual examples train decisions to follow the stated evidence. Across the 14 Speech-DF-Arena test sets, VeriSpoof-Plus achieves 2.14% pooled EER, ranking third of 28 systems and first among open-weight systems. VeriSpoof-Base, trained only on official training splits of eight corpora, achieves 4.43% EER, less than half that of the next open-weight detector. With the same weights, VeriSpoof-Plus verifies whether recordings from generators unseen in training share a source at 6.2% EER. Controlled studies show that the audio representation governs detection, the LLM governs recording comparison, and source supervision is necessary for neural-codec fakes. Statement-checkable rationales catch partial fakes missed by one-step answers (99.6% vs. 78.4% on PartialEdit) and determine decisions under edits unseen in training (99.5%). Training updates only 29.7M of 2.85B parameters, fitting a single 24 GB GPU with gradient checkpointing. We release both models, inference code, a demo, and VeriSpoof-Bench, the evaluation suite covering these questions.
papers.authors: Yang Xiao, Ting Dang

papers.title: Voluntary Servitude: Weaponized Safety Warning Mechanisms for Controlling AI Agents
papers.abstract: LLM agents increasingly act on information retrieved from public sources they treat as credible, which turns a manipulated recommendation into a transaction, a dependency, or a decision with physical consequences. The security literature models this threat as instruction injection, in which an adversary writes a command into retrieved content and deployed defenses learn to recognize command syntax. We show that an attacker can instead steer an agent through the agent's own harm-avoidance. A single fabricated hazard, written as an ordinary review, leads the agent to disqualify the legitimate options and select the attacker's target by its own reasoning, with no command for a detector to recognize. We call this voluntary servitude. These payloads steer agents about as often as instruction injection (60.4% vs. 66.0%), and deployed injection detectors score them as benign, so behind a filter they are 1.7-4.4x more effective. We measure this at the generation stage across six models and ten consumer-service domains, for three attack families, and show that it transfers to production browser agents, outperforming instruction injection, and to a retrieval pipeline (1.0-57.0% end-to-end success, depending on the retriever). We then show that a corroboration requirement added to the agent's instructions removes roughly 95% of the exposure against a non-adaptive attacker without retraining. With the requirement in place, the agent still reads the planted hazard and no longer acts on it.
papers.authors: Ilan Zendel, Matan Levy, Stav Cohen, Avi Mendelson, Amit LeVi

papers.title: CloakFEM: Agentic FEM Code Generation for Red-Teaming Computational Resource Exhaustion
papers.abstract: Finite element method (FEM) solvers are foundational to scientific and engineering simulation, yet their susceptibility to \emph{efficiency attacks} remains largely unexplored. An adversary can craft syntactically valid and runnable FEM programs that complete successfully while forcing excessive computational work, enabling computational denial-of-service (DoS) attacks. Finding such inputs is challenging because FEM programs occupy a vast, structured space constrained by numerical, geometric, and constitutive requirements. We introduce CloakFEM, a domain-guided LLM-agent framework for automatically generating runnable adversarial FEM programs that amplify solver computation. CloakFEM combines LLM-guided search with an FEM-specific intermediate representation and a deterministic validity gate that enforces runnable constraints. Across three FEM stacks, 17 problem classes, and 1,068 seeds, CloakFEM discovers adversarial inputs that substantially amplify solver work while remaining valid and solvable. In the most extreme case, solver iterations increase from 43 to 247,367, a \(5{,}752.72\times\) amplification. CloakFEM outperforms five generic black-box baselines and retains an advantage over evolutionary search under a controlled bounded action space. Cross-solver analysis further reveals both problem-intrinsic and solver-specific sources of vulnerability. Our results uncover an underexplored efficiency-attack surface in FEM solvers and show that runnable FEM programs can serve as adversarial inputs.
papers.authors: Li Zheng, Simin Chen

papers.title: Permitted but Unauthorized: Affordance-Induced Delegated-Scope Violations in Multi-Agent LLM Systems
papers.abstract: Multi-agent LLM systems place several agents on shared infrastructure, where each agent holds permissions far broader than the task it is delegated -- so every agent is routinely permitted to act on a peer's resources it was never assigned. We ask: under competitive pressure, what determines whether an agent crosses from its delegated scope into a peer's resources, and can such crossings be enforced away? We study this across eight LLMs in two simulated environments -- a CI/CD release pipeline and a security-operations incident queue -- using a deterministic, no-model-in-the-loop detector over hash-chained, replay-verified logs. In a controlled 2x2x2 factorial over competitive incentive, candidate visibility, and payoff information (three models, n=52 per cell), we find that action representation, not permission, governs the behavior: no agent crosses when the peer action is unlisted, whereas listing it under competitive pressure with a stated payoff raises crossings sharply -- up to 52 of 52 episodes for Claude Sonnet 4.5. We also observe a model-dependent split: two newer models (Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Opus 5.5) refuse the identical attack in 0 of 100 episodes, where prior-generation models cross in 9 of 10. We then evaluate two defenses -- a deterministic reference monitor and a model-based pre-execution judge -- both block every crossing and, when the task is winnable, cut avoidable peer deadline misses from 15/40 and 14/40 to at most 1/40. But scope enforcement is not harm prevention: an agent can still set a peer back through an authorized action on its own resources -- misreporting its incident's severity -- which neither defense detects. Our results establish action representation, not permission alone, as a controllable driver of inter-agent scope violations, and show that enforcing delegated scope is distinct from preventing harm, motivating effect-aware authorization.
papers.authors: Shravya Kanchi

papers.title: Gather or Act? Belief-Level Counterfactual Labels for Deadline-Aware Incident Response in Cyber-Physical Systems
papers.abstract: When an industrial control system misbehaves, the defender often must choose between acting now on the most likely cause and first gathering evidence that separates two look-alike causes, while the process drifts toward a shutdown. Learning or evaluating such decisions requires the cost of every candidate action from the same situation, which no public cyber-physical security dataset provides. We present TE-GvA, a counterfactual decision dataset for fault-driven incident response on the revised Tennessee Eastman process, with 9,908 decision points from 1,990 simulated incidents, each with 4 to 35 candidate actions labelled by branched rollouts with common random numbers. Labels computed under the true hidden cause (hindsight labels) make gathering the best choice in only 1.1-1.3% of decisions. For the dominant look-alike pair, a failed network link versus a frozen I/O module, we add pair-conditioned belief labels from twin episodes that replay the defender's history under the other cause, weighted by the exact posterior. With them, gathering is best in 15.5% of ambiguous natural decisions and in 33.1% of ambiguous stress decisions without a backup channel. When the posterior is correct and the twin is faithful, belief labels have the same regression target as hindsight labels and lower variance. In a pre-specified, single-look test evaluation, a gradient-boosted rule trained on belief labels has 11% lower regret on the stress set than the same rule trained on hindsight labels, and 27% lower regret on ambiguous stress decisions without a backup channel, which remains significant after Holm correction. With a backup channel and in the natural distribution, the two label sets perform about the same. Soft labels tolerate moderate posterior errors, whereas hard labels that commit to one cause do worse than hindsight labels.
papers.authors: Ali Mohammadi Ruzbahani

papers.title: Verifiable Data on Bitcoin: FlatMerkle Commitments, Refutable Proofs, and FlatChecks
papers.abstract: We give a method to publish data on Bitcoin and to verify properties of that data on Bitcoin itself, against a publisher who may lie. The data is a FlatMerkle file – a structured byte string whose ordinary SHA-256 supports logarithmic inclusion proofs and logarithmic proofs of malformation – placed in a transaction's annex or, at four times the cost but relayable by Bitcoin Core, in an output. We show that the publisher's ordinary Taproot signature, with a suitably chosen signature-hash type, binds the publisher to the published data in a form that a dispute can authenticate with a single SHA-256 compression plus the signature check, or with three compressions when no annex is used. Claims about the data, and claims about such claims, are published as proof messages in two formats: a plain encoding, refuted by revealing it whole, and a traced encoding that stores the verifier's output after each level, so that any false message is refuted by revealing at most five of its elements. The format, chosen by a cost model that weighs challenge bytes against published bytes, is fixed by public context so that no message can be read in two formats; chains of claims about claims settle at four logical elements. A dispute thus reduces to a few dozen SHA-256 compressions and one Schnorr verification per commitment – too large for Bitcoin Script, but small enough to adjudicate with an interactive bisection game, a chunked script in the manner of BitVM2, or a garbled circuit. The same technique verifies any locally refutable verifier, one whose every rejection is witnessed by a single check over a few words of a canonical trace. In a FlatCheck, the prover publishes only the proof; the trace, the verifier's intermediate values, is published only if a challenger asks for it, and the dispute then examines the single check he names. When the verifier splits into groups that each read a few parts of the proof, a challenge forces the trace of one group only. We give two examples: a toy L2 of signed transfers, whose 512-transfer batches cost 12,200 vbytes to claim, and a Bitcoin header-chain light client verified on Bitcoin itself, which claims a retarget period of 2,016 headers in 45,200 vbytes; a dispute over a local check costs about 37,500 and 49,200 vbytes, and one over a malformed trace about 77,100 and 99,800, independently of the number of groups. Verifying STARK proofs is another application. We also remove FlatMerkle's restriction to power-of-two sizes without padding.
papers.authors: Sergio Demian Lerner

papers.title: Hidden Curves and Short Duals: Cubic Jets, Dual Leaks, and the Limits of Masked-Code Encryption
papers.abstract: Masked-code encryption hides a decodable code behind a transformation meant to make it look random. We study the two masks proposed as compact alternatives to Goppa codes---Wang's RLCE and the $(U\,|\,U{+}V)$ construction of UVW-KEM---over the decodable hidden codes they have been or could be applied to, and find that, among the families examined, none yields a compact trapdoor. Over Reed--Solomon and algebraic-geometry codes the mask hides a \emph{curve}, and curves are not hidden from jets. We explain the October 2026 key recovery of UVW-KEM (NGCC) and show it is not specific to UVW: for \emph{hidden-pairing codes} we bound from below the dependencies among order-$r$ jets of degree-$d$ forms at the columns of any shortening---for cubics $2k_1-k_2-k_l+2$ (UVW) and $2(n{-}k)-w-k_l+2$ (RLCE), attained in every regime tested, and we prove that the structured part of the dependency space carries the pairing and the secret ratios in closed form. Every proposed UVW parameter set has the predicted cubic deficiency (key recovery has been demonstrated at UVW-KEM-128). RLCE's long-key regime $w\ge n-k$, out of reach of the square-code attack for eight years, falls at degree three: on a full-size Level-1 parameter set we recover an equivalent key from the public key alone and decrypt fresh ciphertexts. HermitianRLCE is distinguished the same way. A forcing law, a master count and a redundancy law make the \emph{jet degree} an invariant of hidden-pairing codes: within that model, each unit of structural depth costs a unit of redundancy. Without a curve the masks fail differently: both \emph{preserve the dual} of the hidden code, at most doubling the weight of every dual word. polarRLCE at rate $\le2/3$ leaks dual words found in $47$--$94$ bits; at higher rates no certified decoding radius supports $143$-bit security up to length $16384$, and at $32768$ the key is $58$\,MiB, $234\times$ Classic McEliece. LDPC codes leak their sparse checks, MDPC codes are better left unmasked, and UVW carries a matched-pair subspace for every hidden code. Reed--Muller-heavy codes under RLCE resist every attack here at $4$\,MiB keys, but only if a decoder at $3.4\times$ the bounded-distance radius exists.
papers.authors: Yongge Wang

papers.title: Poly Versus Polyval
papers.abstract: We revisit the basic construction of polynomial evaluation based hash function, which we call Poly, over binary extension fields $GF(2^n)$, where $n=64k$ and $k\geq 2$. Unlike GHASH, the NIST standard polynomial evaluation based hash function for $n=128$, Poly does not perform the unnecessary bit reversals of each $n$-bit block, and consequently is faster than GHASH. Further, Poly differs from Polyval, -- a faster alternative to GHASH, -- in that Poly performs usual reduction, while Polyval performs Montgomery reduction. We identify suitable choices of the field representing irreducible polynomials which make usual and Montgomery reductions efficient. We provide detailed algorithms, and associated proofs of correctness for both kinds of reductions. Based on the algorithms, we report carefully optimised assembly implementation of both Poly and Polyval for $n=128,256$ and $512$. Our theoretical analysis and experimental timing results show that for $n=128$, Polyval is faster than Poly, while for $n=256$ and $512$ (as well as for higher values of $n$), Poly is faster than Polyval. The cases $n=128$ and $n=256$ are of current relevance due to the ongoing NIST process for developing cryptographic accordions.
papers.authors: Kaushik Nath, Palash Sarkar

papers.title: Anamorphic Proofs of Knowledge from Prover Randomness
papers.abstract: Anamorphic encryption and signatures deliver a hidden message through a normal-looking ciphertext or signature. We move from hidden messages to hidden knowledge claims and introduce anamorphic proofs of knowledge, in which a single proof certifies its normal statement publicly while convincing a designated checker that the prover knows a witness for a separately registered anamorphic statement, such as a long-term credential. Our construction reuses a commitment the normal prover already makes to its own randomness. The prover adds a secret mask to the anamorphic witness and uses the sum as those coins, so the existing commitment carries the anamorphic statement while the public statement, proof format and length, and normal verifier remain unchanged. Two properties of the normal proof system suffice: its randomness commitment must be extractable, and the complete proof must be simulatable at a commitment that the checking key fixes in advance, which normal zero knowledge does not provide. The resulting normal and anamorphic modes are indistinguishable to an external observer, even given both witnesses and the normal prover's actual random coins. The same opening extractor gives anamorphic knowledge soundness and two guarantees against the checker: it cannot produce an accepting proof for a statement registered independently of its key, and it cannot produce a proof and witness for a statement of its own choice, in both cases at an unused label and after obtaining honest proofs at other labels. The checker learns neither witness. We instantiate the construction in random-base Compressed $\Sigma$ and in Bulletproofs with range aggregation in the random-oracle model. Finally, we show that three-move protocols with witness-assisted challenge transfer, including Schnorr and uncompressed representation protocols, cannot support the primitive in a local-checking model.
papers.authors: Zhi Lu, Songfeng Lu, Jiaheng Zhang

papers.title: Card-Based Protocols with Mixed Encoding: Computable Functions and the Minimum Number of Cards
papers.abstract: Card-based cryptography performs secure computation with physical cards, where a bit is usually encoded by two cards but can also be encoded by a single card. We study mixed encoding, in which one player gives a single-card commitment and the other a two-card commitment, for perfectly secure protocols with finite runtime and public actions. Mizuki (Theoretical Computer Science, vol.~622, 2016) proposed an AND protocol with mixed encoding as a building block for the conjunction of many variables. To give a single-card commitment, a player chooses one of two cards of different types and must keep the other card hidden. We call this card a frozen card and include it in the number of cards. We show that a secure protocol in committed format never turns over a single-card input, and use this to determine the functions that can be computed when all inputs are single-card commitments and to characterize those that can be computed with mixed encoding, which include AND but not XOR. We prove that Mizuki's five-card protocol is card-minimal. No AND protocol with mixed encoding uses four cards, including the frozen card, even with arbitrary shuffles and a non-committed output. For formal verification, we express the existence of a protocol as a quantified Boolean formula (QBF) in which security is a quantifier alternation, and confirm this lower bound with QBF solvers for a class of protocols. We discuss the number and type of shuffles, and analyze Mizuki's protocol under injection attacks that change only the input.
papers.authors: Saeki Koizumi, Xiao-Nan Lu, Hidetomo Nabeshima

papers.title: Efficient Scalable Oversight via Rewinding
papers.abstract: Scalable oversight asks how a weak verifier can check the outputs of computations performed by more powerful AI systems. One proposed approach uses relativizing interactive proofs, in which a weak verifier checks the output of a complex oracle-aided computation by interacting with one or more powerful provers. A prominent example is debate, which is highly efficient but assumes that one of two powerful AI models, or provers, is truthful. For certain classes of oracle-aided computations, this assumption can be removed, but at substantially greater computational cost. In this work, we introduce \emph{rewindable interactive proofs} (RIPs), a new model of relativizing interactive proofs for scalable oversight. In an RIP, the verifier may rewind the prover to an earlier state of the interaction and continue from there. This is possible when the prover is an AI model, since the verifier can save a snapshot of the model's state and later restore it. We construct a relativizing RIP for computations whose outputs are robust to changing a small fraction of oracle answers. Our construction is more efficient than prior relativizing proofs that do not assume a truthful prover, and it uses no cryptography. In our construction the honest prover runs in time linear in that of the original computation, and the verifier, after a one-time preprocessing step, runs in time nearly linear in the input length (which can be much smaller than the computation itself). We implement our protocol, report a preliminary MNIST experiment, and show that an RIP can be faster than a state-of-the-art deployed proof system. RIPs may be of independent interest. Rewinding is possible whenever the verifier controls the prover's machine, for example when the prover runs on trusted hardware or in a virtual machine whose state can be checkpointed.
papers.authors: Ziyi Guan, Yael Tauman Kalai, Ron Rothblum, Zoe Xi

papers.title: Practical Collision Attacks on 22- and 23-Step SM3 (Preliminary Version)
papers.abstract: SM3 is a 256-bit cryptographic hash function specified in the Chinese national standard GB/T 32905-2016 and the international standard ISO/IEC 10118-3:2018. In this paper, we present practical collisions for 22- and 23-step SM3 with the standard initial value. Compared with the 20-step collision result of Mendel et al. (2013), our constructions cover two and three additional steps, respectively. The time complexities are approximately \(2^{52.4}\) and \(2^{54.5}\) evaluations of 22- and 23-step SM3, respectively. We also present a semi-free-start collision for 24-step SM3.
papers.authors: Sitong Yuan, Haorui Cui, Hongbo Yu

papers.title: Registered Functional Encryption with Certified Everlasting Security
papers.abstract: Registered functional encryption removes the trusted authority bottleneck of standard functional encryption by allowing users to register their own public keys, with a transparent aggregation procedure producing a compact master public key. On the other hand, certified everlasting deletion enables a recipient to produce a classical certificate guaranteeing that a ciphertext has been information-theoretically destroyed, even against computationally unbounded adversaries. In this work, we initiate the study of registered functional encryption with certified everlasting deletion (RFE-CED), combining both properties for the first time. We define the syntax and security of RFE-CED, capturing two complementary guarantees: everlasting privacy, which bounds the trace distance between residual adversarial states after certified deletion, and post-verification indistinguishability, which ensures the adversary cannot distinguish the encrypted message even after the deletion certificate is verified. To construct RFE-CED, we also introduce public-slot registered functional encryption (PS-RFE) as a building block, in which each registered function takes both a secret and an arbitrary public input. Combining PS-RFE with a pseudorandom and authenticated BB84 encodings, we obtain a secure slotted RFE-CED scheme with the help of an interactive version of certified everlasting lemma.
papers.authors: Shayeef Murshid, Ramprasad Sarkar, Mriganka Mandal

papers.title: The Power of Interaction in Locally Edge-Private Subgraph Counting
papers.abstract: We study (non-induced) subgraph counting under interactive local edge differential privacy (LEDP). Given a fixed pattern graph $H$ with $k$ vertices, $\ell\ge1$ edges, and $q$ connected components, our goal is to approximately count its copies in an arbitrary $n$-vertex undirected graph while preserving edge privacy. We give two complementary accuracy guarantees. First, for every $H$, we give Linear Noise Cancellation (LNC), a two-round $\varepsilon$-LEDP algorithm with additive error and root mean square error both $O(n^{k-3/2}/\varepsilon^\ell)$ on every $n$-vertex graph. For fixed sufficiently small $\varepsilon$, this improves the optimal noninteractive additive error for triangles by a factor of $\sqrt n$ and gives the same improvement in worst-case root mean square error for all cliques on at least three vertices. To our knowledge, this is the first separation between interactive and noninteractive LEDP subgraph counting, showing that a single additional round can improve worst-case accuracy polynomially. Second, we determine how accuracy improves when the graph has maximum degree at most a public bound $d$. Our Predict and Correct (PC) framework gives an $(\ell+2)$-round $\varepsilon$-LEDP algorithm with additive error $O(n^{q-1/2}d^{k-q-1}\log^{3\ell-2}n/\varepsilon^\ell)$. For connected patterns, its polynomial factor is $\sqrt n\,d^{k-2}$, giving sublinear error on constant-degree graphs at fixed privacy. We prove matching lower bounds in $n$ and $d$, up to logarithmic factors at fixed privacy, even under arbitrary interaction and approximate privacy with sufficiently small $δ$. At $d=Θ(n)$, the lower bound also establishes the optimality of LNC's dependence on $n$.
papers.authors: Xian Chen, Pan Peng

papers.title: Residual Attribute Leakage Is an Interface: Auditing Privacy Evaluation After Text De-identification
papers.abstract: A privacy evaluation of de-identified text asks a language model (the adversary) to guess a person's protected attribute. We introduce a prior-normalised clipped leakage score of its confidence gain on the true value and audit the conclusions drawn from it. Each verdict depends on an evaluation interface (the queried person, answer options, prior, adversary model and scoring rule), which we vary on fixed releases of three corpora. In a stress test, an editor that writes the opposite-sex form at the same spans a redaction editor would redact misleads the adversary about most people, yet ranks first among editors scored on the same MedQA entries under this score, as under attack accuracy and proper scoring rules read as privacy. A relabelling-invariant reading of AUC ranks that editor sixth of eight, and a rule-aware adversary recovers the attribute from the same text. On ordinary releases most verdict changes are gains or losses of separability; of six choices varied over all pairs, only the adversary reverses comparisons (5 of its 124 changes), and the query can target the wrong person. SACC, a traceable editor we build as the instrument, lets us ablate two editing principles and show where its advantage does not hold.
papers.authors: Tuan Thanh Duong, Joongmin Shin, Jeongho Yoon, Junyoung Son, Heuiseok Lim

papers.title: A Security Analysis of Verifiable Credential Verification Pipelines: Attack Surface Arising from JSON-LD/RDFC Canonicalization Compared with SD-JWT VC and mdoc
papers.abstract: We evaluate, at implementation level and under an explicit threat model, the verification pipelines of three Verifiable Credential (VC) formats: SD-JWT VC; the W3C Verifiable Credentials Data Model 2.0 with the Data Integrity cryptosuite eddsa-rdfc-2022 (W3C VCDM); and mdoc (ISO/IEC 18013-5). For W3C VCDM we identify and exercise three structural attack surfaces from remote context resolution and RDFC-1.0 canonicalization: denial of service (DoS) via poison graphs, context injection through @context, and server-side request forgery (SSRF) reachable via malicious URLs, all at default settings. A poison graph, whose blank-node references are symmetric enough to force RDFC-1.0 into deep recursion, raises it to 278x the baseline from five blank nodes in 527 bytes, and to 13.5 s from eight. Every experiment ran in four environments sharing runtime and library versions; the multiple moves with the machine (251--424x for one input), not with its speed. Cost tracks that symmetry rather than the node count: an acyclic input with 1,500 blank nodes stays at 462--714x. A call limit separates the two: every attack family aborts at 16 or below, every legitimate credential completes at 1, but a shallow, wide recursion, such as the acyclic control, passes whatever the bound. DoS does not presuppose adversarial input: with production education schemas, canonicalization costs 23--34x a simple credential in one environment, 16--49x across four. Effective mitigations are a static document loader, which removes the retrieval latency and both remote-context surfaces; a context allowlist; and a call limit with a size bound. SD-JWT VC and mdoc need neither canonicalization nor external references, and our verifiers resisted every vector evaluated. These are not format-specific defects but properties of the pipeline and its configuration.
papers.authors: Naohiro Fujie, Shigeya Suzuki

papers.title: TxBench: A Benchmark of Attack Transactions and Evidence-Backed Negatives on Seven EVM Chains
papers.abstract: Researchers evaluate detectors of malicious smart-contract transactions on datasets that each paper assembles anew. Their positives come from incident trackers, whose citations mix attacks with setup steps and transactions that never ran, or from a detector's own output, which makes the evaluation circular; their negatives are ordinary transactions. A shared benchmark needs positives whose own execution shows the attack and negatives that use the attacks' mechanisms, with no detector deciding either label. We present TxBench, a benchmark of attack transactions and evidence-backed negatives on seven EVM chains, with the five-step pipeline that builds it. The pipeline collects every transaction that BlockSec's incident library or the EVM Hack Registry cites, maps its weakness to OWASP's SCWE taxonomy, and rebuilds its execution from free data sources. A cited transaction qualifies as a valid TxBench attack only if it extracts value from others during execution, is consistent with all verified source claims, and is independently linked to the reported incident by corroborating evidence. Negative examples are sampled from each chain's traffic near the attacks and retained only when positive evidence confirms their legitimacy. Of 1,850 cited transactions, TxBench accepts 1,012 attacks from 602 incidents, worth USD 868.1 million: 846 contract exploits and 166 key compromises. A blind review under rules fixed in advance confirms 98 of 100 sampled attacks (97.7% weighted) and all 100 sampled negatives. As baselines, four zero-shot LLMs reading anonymized traces are precise but find at most 0.43 of the attacks and no key compromise, leaving ample room for better detectors.
papers.authors: Tamer Abdelaziz, karim Ali

papers.title: Bilateral Protection for Private LoRA Inference with Intel TDX
papers.abstract: Cloud services using private low-rank adaptation (LoRA) must protect client inputs and outputs alongside owners' proprietary parameters and execute the approved adaptation. We design and implement a system for bilateral protection of private LoRA inference using Intel Trust Domain Extensions (TDX), connecting approved application identity to actual artifact consumption and adapter activation. The client and LoRA owner independently verify remote attestation, application identity, and binding to the actual Transport Layer Security (TLS) public key before releasing inputs and the weight-decryption key. A fixed read-only image and verified-byte consumption connect approved identities to inference objects, with all inference inside a trust domain. Experiments on real TDX hardware reject controlled application and boot-parameter modifications before secret release. Across 400 fixed dialogues, protected and native CPU inference in the same trust domain produce identical token sequences for all 400 pairs. Across 12 independent trust-domain boots, the steady-state service-to-native time ratio is 1.0094, with a 95% interval of [1.0064, 1.0126]. The system connects bilateral secret release, approved model use, and task-capability preservation, providing verifiable implementation and cost evidence for confidential inference with a public base and private adapter.
papers.authors: Xiaodong Li, Mingyuan Ma, Dongbo Yan

papers.title: Can Benign Skills Induce Misaligned Behavior in LLM Agents?
papers.abstract: LLM agents increasingly rely on reusable skills to plan tasks, invoke tools, recover from errors, and complete workflows without modifying model parameters. Although these skills are typically developed to enhance benign tasks, they may also make an agent more capable of executing procedures for harmful purposes. We study this risk, which we call skill-induced behavioral misalignment: adding benign skills may cause an agent to execute external actions that violate safety requirements. We first conduct a systematic study to validate the existence of this phenomenon. It compares agents with and without benign skills across five LLM backbones and three benchmarks under matched requests. On average, skill augmentation improves benign task accuracy by 10.3 percentage points (pp), but also increases unsafe action rate (UAR) by 10.3 pp. The regression also occurs with skills curated by experts. A paired trajectory analysis shows that 24 of 50 newly unsafe trajectories fail to complete the harmful objective, revealing violations that task completion alone would miss. We further disclose multiple factors and scenarios that could exacerbate this risk. (1) Evolving skills with benign feedback can amplify unsafe execution; (2) This regression is more pronounced when retrieved skills are matched to task and contain procedural guidance; (3) Distilling benign experience into reusable skills yield higher UAR compared with their source trajectories. (4) A guard that checks proposed tool actions before execution reduces violations while retaining gains on benign tasks. All these findings confirm the significance of skill-induced behavioral misalignment, and the urgent need for new mitigation solutions.
papers.authors: Xuanye Zhang, Yongsen Zheng, Kaiyu Zhou, Bowen Shen, Haoran Ou, Zhuqin Xu, Tianwei Zhang, Kwok-Yan Lam

papers.title: The Native Menace: Host-to-Browser Cross-Boundary Attacks via Native Messaging
papers.abstract: Modern browsers are complex software platforms that users can customize through browser extensions to further expand their functionality. Extensions derive their functionality from privileged browser APIs that expose powerful capabilities. Prior work has extensively studied how malicious webpages or extensions can target those capabilities. However, prior research has overlooked the NativeMessaging API, which allows extensions to create a communication channel that bridges the gap between web content rendered in the browser and native apps running on the user's machine. This API enables workflows that cross the browser's boundary to perform critical operations (e.g., digital signing) or exchange sensitive data (e.g., credentials). In this paper, we conduct the first, to our knowledge, empirical security analysis of NativeMessaging, and present a novel attack that allows a non-privileged malicious native app to misuse browsers' native messaging capabilities to stealthily intercept sensitive communications or launch confused deputy attacks against other native apps. To demonstrate the significant risk introduced by native messaging, we present a series of concrete attacks against popular and critical apps (e.g., 1Password, the European Union's eID system, Google Drive), whose browser extensions have more than 532 million cumulative downloads. Our attacks have severe ramifications, including full password vault leakage, and arbitrary document signing in governmental workflows. Fundamentally, these attacks are possible due to native messaging being built on top of an untrusted communication channel without providing a root of trust or enforcing some form of client attestation. Accordingly, we propose a straightforward mitigation technique of message encryption with out-of-band secret sharing, to prevent our attacks.
papers.authors: Jyotirmay Chauhan, Rownak Islam, Jason Polakis

papers.title: Say the Same, Act Differently: Diagnosing and Steering Text-Action Divergence in Reasoning VLAs
papers.abstract: Reasoning vision-language-action (VLA) models pair physical control with natural-language rationales that supervisors can read to monitor embodied safety. Prior attacks on VLA reasoning corrupt the rationale itself and leave visible evidence in the text. We show that visual perturbations can instead alter the physical action while keeping the generated rationale word-for-word identical. At the shared text/action interface of Alpamayo for driving and InstructVLA for manipulation, our text-neutral action-subspace (TNAS) diagnostic shows that the locally most action-sensitive direction is nearly orthogonal to the active text-loss gradients, with 1.87% and 5.28% norm overlap. At equal hidden-state perturbation norms across both models, interventions along this text-neutral residual shift actions 4.64x to 47.8x more than text-gradient perturbations, whereas text-gradient perturbations induce 21.2x to 277x more text drift. Steering visual perturbations along this direction reaches the same decoupling from the image. Across 154 obstacle-annotated driving scenes in Alpamayo, TNAS-guided attacks induce a new collision under a word-for-word identical rationale in 52.6% of scenes under full-image perturbations and 35.1% under a localized forward-camera patch, compared with 4.55% for unguided action attacks. Relative to a text-preserving baseline, TNAS guidance raises exact rationale preservation from 83.0% to 89.5% and cuts teacher-forced text drift by 68.4% at a comparable collision rate. In InstructVLA, TNAS guidance cuts text drift by 40.5% and preserves the exact response on 85.0% of examples alongside a 1.73-unit action-chunk shift. An unchanged rationale therefore cannot certify a safe action, so monitors for reasoning VLAs must verify the predicted action channel directly.
papers.authors: Zihao Feng, Qingzhao Zhang, Chunyu Xia, Bo Yu, Z. Morley Mao, Ramesh Govindan

papers.title: Revisiting Elliptic++ for Bitcoin Forensics: Feature Reconstruction and Leakage-Resistant Evaluation
papers.abstract: Elliptic and its address-level extension Elliptic++ are widely used benchmark datasets in Bitcoin forensics, cited by more than 1300 academic studies according to Google Scholar. We identify future information leakage in Elliptic++. Its positional data split does not respect temporal order, and the exact definitions of its address-level features remain undocumented. We revisit how the 55 Elliptic++ address-level features are computed and propose a leakage-resistant pipeline. First, the exact feature definitions are recovered by linking Elliptic transactions to public ledger data. Second, we compute the features with a temporal split based on each address's first appearance, using only information available at the time of prediction. Once temporal ordering is enforced, the random forest (RF)'s strong predictive performance largely disappears: its F1 score on the illicit class falls from $0.846$ under the original leaky evaluation to just $0.291$ under our leakage-resistant pipeline. Furthermore, RF no longer outperforms a simple logistic regression baseline. We provide the exact feature definitions and executable code to reproduce the leakage-resistant features, so that future Bitcoin forensic models can be evaluated based on genuine predictive capability rather than temporal data leakage.
papers.authors: Runlin Liang, Simon Trimborn, Noud van Giersbergen

papers.title: RuntimeTickets: Source-Grounded Security Obligations for Agent Skills
papers.abstract: Third-party Agent Skills extend what an autonomous agent can do, but a malicious Skill can hide data exposure or output manipulation inside a legitimate workflow. Neither reading a Skill's description nor granting it tool permissions tells whether its execution meets the user's security requirements. We introduce RuntimeTickets, a protocol that enforces and audits these requirements while a Skill runs. From released malicious-Skill datasets we derive a risk model and build adversarial-benign Skill pairs. From the task's delivery contract, a language model proposes security obligations for that task. Each obligation cites the Skill lines it answers, and the ticket tightens the host's approvals into fine-grained allowed actions but never loosens them. A runtime gate checks the recipient, object and amount of every outbound send before forwarding it, and trusted monitors record the effects within their observation scope. The ticket links these checks and observations to the approved obligations of each Skill run, and a deterministic decoder turns the ticket's status into governable data flows and verifies each obligation. Neither enforcement nor decoding involves a language model, so text injected by a Skill can change the proposal but never the rule that decides a send. We evaluate RuntimeTickets at the network egress boundary of three unmodified agent frameworks against production Skill scanners and runtime baselines, among them an AgentBound-derived allow-list and SkillGuard. RuntimeTickets eliminated both failure modes of current Skill defenses, overlook (malicious Skills let through) and overkill (benign Skills blocked): its overlook rate was 0.0% and its overkill rate 0.0%, while the scanners erred on both sides. RuntimeTickets ties approved requirements to verifiable execution evidence and offers a common foundation for the safe and auditable deployment of third-party Skills.
papers.authors: Kuiyi Gao, Xue Liu, Bowei He

papers.title: JevBreak: Your Model, Their Decision
papers.abstract: Restricting what a model can say is often mistaken for restricting an attacker's influence over its decision. An attacker can add text to the evidence and steer the model toward a wrong answer that still belongs to the allowed set. We evaluate seven decision models spanning hosted APIs, open-weight models and an encoder on 16 tasks in seven domains from Decision Bench, targeting every wrong option across 240 text examples (990 targets per model). We present Slot Attack, a black-box attack designed for decision models that appends text assembled from named components to steer predictions toward an attacker-selected incorrect option. The method relies solely on returned label probabilities, achieves success rates of 32--99\% on initially correct decisions, and identifies the effective component combinations with a median of 17--72 queries per successful attack. Accuracy and confidence do not reliably reveal this vulnerability. Models with near-identical accuracy on the sampled tasks differ by about 20\%age points in attack success. We demonstrate that an attacker can force not just one wrong answer but every available one: on about 20\% of correct decisions for the JEV models, 77\% for gpt-6-luna and 98\% for GLiNER2.5; a confidence threshold does not reliably screen the attack out. A fixed answer set constrains a decision's form, not its source; robustness must be measured per model, per task and per version rather than assumed from output format.
papers.authors: Nitin Aravind Birur, Divyanshu Kumar, Sahil Agarwal, Prashanth Harshangi

papers.title: Normal-Jet Masking: A Retraining-Free Defense Against Cryptanalytic Extraction of Neural Networks
papers.abstract: Cryptanalytic extraction (CEA) of piecewise-linear neural networks recovers hidden signatures and parameters by locating critical points or hard-label dual points that expose off-manifold geometry. Proposed mitigation methods include query monitoring, output perturbation, ownership verification, and extraction-aware training. Train to Defend (TTD) directly addresses CEA through extraction-aware training, but cannot protect an already-trained checkpoint without retraining. We propose Normal-Jet Masking (NJM), a post-training wrapper that leaves the source model unchanged. NJM calibrates a tangent–normal tube around protected data, keeps private normal-direction mask channels inactive inside the tube, and mixes their piecewise-linear activations into served outputs outside it. NJM targets the shared evidence-acquisition stage rather than one attack implementation: mask events enter both raw-logit (soft-label) critical finding and hard-label dual finding before downstream signature and parameter recovery. Across seven MLPs, NJM reduces raw-logit evidence F1 by 53.8–93.1%, raises query cost by 1.4–9.3×, and eliminates pure hard-label duals. On CNNs, it preserves at least 0.9993 agreement while lowering source precision. These results show that post-training geometric masking complements training-time hardening across soft- and hard-label CEA.
papers.authors: Chun Li, Liping Zhuang, Di Li, Yufeng Tang, Ming Duan, Zheng Gong

papers.title: LoRA-Patch: Defending Against Backdoored LoRA Adapters via Directional Steering
papers.abstract: Third-party LoRA adapters introduce serious backdoor risks: malicious adapters can maintain normal task performance while embedding hidden, trigger-activated behaviors, making them difficult to detect through standard utility evaluations. Existing removal-based defenses typically sanitize backdoored models by updating, pruning, distilling, or mixing model parameters. However, these approaches are misaligned with adapter-based deployment, where the trusted base model is expected to remain frozen. In this work, we propose LoRA-Patch, a lightweight backdoor defense tailored to LoRA adapters. Our key insight is that backdoor injection distorts the directional geometry of a poisoned adapter relative to its trusted base model. Building on this insight, LoRA-Patch suppresses trigger-activated behaviors by realigning adapter directions through layer-wise steering, without modifying the base model weights. Extensive experiments across five backdoor attacks and three models show that LoRA-Patch effectively mitigates trigger-activated backdoors, outperforming existing baselines while preserving benign task performance. Moreover, LoRA-Patch is computationally efficient, constructing patches within 20 seconds across all evaluated models and adapters. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/FOXVEDA/LoRA-Patch.
papers.authors: Shengyan Huo, Peihai Jiang, Xixiang Lyu, Yige Li

papers.title: Key Recovery Against RLCE via the GIJS Distinguisher
papers.abstract: We present an experimental cryptanalysis of the RLCE cryptosystem at the heretofore secure $w=n-k$ parameter regime. Our attack relies crucially on the recent Ghoshal--Ishai--Jain--Sun (GIJS) distinguisher The attack shortens the public key at random positions, runs the GIJS distinguisher with \emph{every} column as hold-out, and uses this distinguisher to identify twin pairs based on how they appear across trials. Three pairs so identified are unmixed by a root-finding cascade, and Sidelnikov--Shestakov on the resulting $k \times (k+3)$ pure matrix recovers the key. We experimentally verify our attack by breaking the ID-0 (128-bit) in 30.5 core-hours (about 3 hours of wall time) on a standard higher-end laptop.
papers.authors: Jacob Alperin-Sheriff

papers.title: CHAMPing at the Bit: Short Square-Root Collisions for Two-Generator Cayley Hashes
papers.abstract: For $A,B\in\text{GL}(\mathbb{F}_p)$, a Cayley hash $\text{HM}(w)$ maps a bit string $w \in \{0,1\}$ to the corresponding product of $A$ and $B$. We construct collisions by finding two palindromes whose matrix products commute. A symmetric form shared by the two generators places the hash of every palindrome in a three-dimensional subspace containing the identity. Two such hashes commute when their traceless parts are proportional, which defines a class map with $p+2$ values, so the pigeonhole principle gives collisions of $4\lceil\log_2(p+3)\rceil$ bits. Under a uniformity heuristic, a dictionary search finds such a pair after about $\sqrt{\pi p/2}$ class evaluations. Adding one bit to each half-message gives an expected bound of $O(\sqrt p)$ evaluations, with no assumption on how the classes are distributed. When the common form is singular, the generators are simultaneously triangular and the same argument applies to ordinary words. For CHAMP-512 and CHAMP-1024, the heuristic search finds collisions of $512$ and $1024$ bits after about $2^{64}$ and $2^{128}$ class evaluations, and the one-bit-longer, distribution-independent variant finds collisions of $516$ and $1028$ bits at the same leading cost. This matches the asymptotic cost of an earlier commuting-product search for CHAMP, whose messages have $O(\log^2(p))$ bits, and improves on the bound of about $p$ given by an earlier palindrome restriction. For every pair over an odd prime field, this also shortens the collisions of the general algorithm of Mullan and Tsaban from $O(\log^2(p)/\log(\log(p)))$ to $4 \lceil \log_2(p+3) \rceil$ bits. Since the argument applies to every pair $A,B$, no pair of generators gives a $2\times2$ Cayley hash over $\mathbb{F}_p$ with collision resistance greater than $O(\sqrt p)$. We give an explicit proof-of-concept collision for the CHAMP matrices at a $36$-bit prime, and prove that every sufficiently short message can be recovered from its digest for the main CHAMP pair. To close, we demonstrate that since reversal and symbol exchange act as sign changes on quaternion coordinates, the alternative CHAMP pair possesses a much greater degree of symmetry, but do not yet see how to utilize this to find collisions below the square-root bound.
papers.authors: Freeman Slaughter

papers.title: Concrete Minimum Distance Bounds of Accumulate Codes over any Fixed Finite Field
papers.abstract: We present a new concrete unified distance analysis of three accumulate-type error-correcting codes over any finite field, specifically the Repeat-Accumulate (RA), Repeat-Accumulate-Accumulate (RAA), and Expand-Accumulate (EA) codes. For message length $k$, codeword length $n$, finite field size $q>2$, and target relative minimum distance $\delta$, we give new upper bounds on the probability that each of the above codes do not have minimum distance at least $\delta$. Our bounds are concrete and explicit: they do not rely on $n$ or $q$ being sufficiently large. We present (multiple) closed-form upper bounds on the failure probability for each code, and complement these bounds with asymptotic analyses that (nearly) match prior-known asymptotic bounds. Our technical core is a new fine-grained union bound for accumulate codes, which may be of independent interest, that examines inputs to the accumulator from a purely distributional perspective, deriving properties that are necessary for an input vector to accumulate to a targeted output weight, and analyzing the probability the input distribution achieves these properties. This fine-grained union bound generalizes the input-output weight enumerator approach used by many prior works. Our concrete analysis shows that (1) the RA code has concretely small distance (a maximum of $\delta\leq 2.4979\times10^{-8}$ for $k=2^{40}$ and $q=2^{32}$, except with probability $2^{-60}$), and (2) the RAA and EA codes achieve somewhat large concrete distance for smaller field sizes $q \leq 2^{32}$. Concretely, for rate $k/n = 1/4$, $k\in\{2^{40},2^{50}\}$, and $q=2^{8}$, the RAA code has distance $\delta=1/8$ except with $2^{-60}$ probability, whereas the rate $1/2$ and $1/4$ EA code for the same $k$ and $q=2^{4}$, respectively, has distance $\delta\leq 0.0689756$ and $\delta \leq0.232955$ except with probability $2^{-60}$. For fields of size $q\geq 2^{32}$, under our concrete bounds, all codes experience a sharp drop-off in attainable minimum distance, as our analysis targets (small) fixed $q$.
papers.authors: Alexander R. Block, Himanshu Dongre, Hendrik Waldner

papers.title: Private Accounts Without $O(N)$ Work Through a Hybrid State Model
papers.abstract: Privacy-preserving smart contracts face a scalability problem. In account-balance-vector designs, hiding which accounts changed requires that every transaction perform an indistinguishable update over the global state, so validators pay work linear in the number of accounts for every private transfer. UTXO systems avoid this by validating local spends, but do not provide the same account-style programming model. We argue that the usual "account vs.~UTXO" framing conflates state representation and execution model, two choices that can be made separately. Miden, an Ethereum Layer 2, separates them. It uses persistent accounts for programmability, asynchronous notes for value transfer, and client-side proving for execution. Validators verify proofs and update commitments without re-executing transactions or accessing uninvolved state. The result is an account-based platform with private transfers and private computation, while keeping validator work per transaction logarithmic in the number of accounts.
papers.authors: Philipp Gackstatter, François Garillot, Marti Górny, Adrian Hamelink, Al Kindi, Philippe Laferrière, Robin Salen, Brian Seong, Bobbin Threadbare

papers.title: SPIDER: A Faster and Smaller Identity-Based Signature From Isogenies
papers.abstract: PRISM is an isogeny-based digital signature whose security relies on the problem of computing large prime degree isogenies from a supersingular elliptic curve of unknown endomorphism ring. In this paper, we design SPIDER, a digital signature that builds on a sigma protocol which when given a supersingular elliptic curve $E$, proves the knowledge of an isogeny $\phi: E\rightarrow E'$ of prime (or non smooth) degree $d$. SPIDER can hence be seen as a proof of knowledge of a PRISM signature. The latter observation allows us to combine SPIDER and PRISM to obtain an Identity-Based Signature (IBS) which we denote by SPIDER-IBS. SPIDER-IBS is the most efficient and the most compact isogeny-based IBS scheme, as all its predecessors are based on isogeny group actions.
papers.authors: Tako Boris Fouotsa, Gustave Tchoffo Saah

papers.title: Ratio-Based Ring Oscillator PUF Statistical Model
papers.abstract: A ratio-based ring oscillator physical unclonable function (ROPUF) provides high reliability and is capable of extracting multiple bits from a single ring oscillator pair. However, the derivation of the response bits from such PUFs and the assessment of their randomness have relied only on empirical statistical tests. This paper introduces a novel, mathematically derived closed-form statistical model that characterizes the counter value distribution of the ratio-based ROPUF and formally describes the behavior of this PUF design. We empirically validate the model's assumptions using a large-scale real-world ring oscillator measurement dataset of 218 Xilinx Artix-7 FPGAs. We demonstrate that this statistical framework enables theoretical quantification of response entropy of the ratio-based ROPUF. Furthermore, the model unlocks the use of advanced bit derivation methods, such as Equiprobable Quantization and Two-Metric Helper Data schemes. These were previously inapplicable to this PUF architecture, and we empirically show on the real-world dataset that they achieve better combinations of PUF reliability, randomness, and bit yield than the original counter-based derivation.
papers.authors: Ondřej Staníček, Jiří Buček, Róbert Lórencz

papers.title: Short Collisions Separate Sponge from Merkle-Damgård
papers.abstract: We study short collisions in salted Merkle-Damg{\aa}rd (MD) and Sponge under the query-bounded preprocessing model introduced by Ghoshal and Tessaro (CRYPTO '23). The adversary makes at most $T_1$ oracle queries before a random salt is revealed and at most $T_2$ queries afterwards, and must output two colliding messages of at most $B$ blocks. Our main result is a separation between the two constructions. Let $N=2^n$, give MD and Sponge matching $n$-bit salts, message blocks, and outputs, and set $T_1=\Theta(N/T_2)$ with $T_2=o(\sqrt N)$. For Sponge, there is an attack that finds a collision with constant probability using only three-block messages. In contrast, every MD adversary restricted to $B=o(T_2)$ blocks succeeds with probability at most \[ O\left(\frac{B}{T_2}+\frac{T_2^2}{N}\right)=o(1). \] Thus, under the same query budgets, three blocks suffice for Sponge, while every MD adversary with $B=o(T_2)$ blocks has success probability $o(1)$. On the MD side, we prove an upper bound for arbitrary block bounds $B$. The proof uses a simple graph argument that distinguishes collisions already present in the preprocessing transcript from those that can actually be reached by a short computation starting from the subsequently sampled salt. This extends query-bounded preprocessing analysis beyond the previously understood one- and two-block cases. On the Sponge side, we give a three-block attack that uses inverse permutation queries to make one precomputed collision useful from many different capacities.
