Moving beyond textual analysis, we uncover structural memorization: a novel vulnerability where a fine-tuned model memorizes not only its training data but also the internal pathway used to process it, creating a characteristic routing fingerprint unique to the training process. We provide comprehensive empirical evidence that structural memorization emerges consistently even from a few samples, and that its intensity is directly influenced by the choice of trainable modules. We show that these memorized expert pathways can be stealthily recovered through the model's unconditional generation, using only routing and output logits, with no knowledge of the fine-tuning data or procedure. In distributed deployments, this vulnerability is amplified as routing information is exposed at multiple trust boundaries, including federated aggregation points, edge-cloud interfaces, and multi-tenant monitoring systems. Recovery exposes a critical blind spot: traditional membership inference metrics, viewed through the lens of expert routing, fail to identify memorized data corresponding to these structural pathways. To close this gap, we devise composite metrics combining reference model tail likelihood with complexity-aware normalization, significantly improving detection of memorized routing structures. This enables adversaries to pinpoint critical experts shaped by fine-tuning, whether dominant or dormant, and execute targeted attacks such as router manipulation or backdoor injection in realistic distributed settings where attackers lack training data but can observe routing patterns across system components.
papers.authors: Fei Wang, Baochun Li, Bo Li

papers.title: CLIC: Closed-Loop Intent Consistency for Securing LLM-Driven Control in Open RAN
papers.abstract: With the progressive capabilities of large language models (LLMs), researchers are finding ways to integrate them into the control loops of Open Radio Access Network (O-RAN) to enable slicing and resource management through user intents. However, integration of LLMs in the O-RAN control loop via the RAN Intelligent Controller (RIC) makes the system vulnerable to \textit{runtime prompt injection threats}, which manipulate control decisions without violating interface authentication, and \textit{residual virtual prompt injection (VPI)} attacks that plant trigger mechanisms to silently steer the behaviour during fine-tuning. Existing studies address only the runtime threat and do not enforce consistency across the full control path, i.e. from the certified A1 intent, through the multi-step LLM trajectory, to the final E2 action. We propose a closed-loop intent-consistency layer (CLIC) that jointly mitigates both threats. The proposed CLIC defines a formal consistency score using a small quantized language model, which is deployed as a Non-RT rApp for model-integrity certification along with a Near-RT xApp for runtime enforcement. We implement CLIC on the OpenAI Cellular (OAIC) platform and evaluate it under domain-adapted JailbreakBench, AdvBench, and VPI workloads. The experimental results show that the proposed CLIC reduces the attack success rate from 0.92 to 0.29 and residual VPI attacks from 0.37 to 0.04, while improving isolation and fairness at slightly higher latency costs, i.e. approximately 27 ms.
papers.authors: Sunder Ali Khowaja, Kapal Dev, Joongheon Kim, Angelos Antonopoulos, Nikolaos Bartzoudis

papers.title: Nenya: Efficient zkSNARKs for Integer Rings Z/2kZ via Reverse Multiplication-Friendly Embeddings
papers.abstract: Zero-knowledge succinct non-interactive arguments of knowledge (zkSNARKs) are powerful cryptographic tools for certifying the correctness of computations with short proofs, fast verification, and zero-knowledge privacy guarantees. However, most existing zkSNARK schemes support arithmetic only over finite fields defined by large primes or their extensions. This creates substantial overhead when proving computations written in high-level programming languages, which typically operate on fixed-width integer types such as 32-bit and 64-bit integers. In this paper, we introduce Nenya, the first practical SNARK scheme that supports native arithmetic over the integer ring $\mathbb{Z}/2^k\mathbb{Z}$. At the core of Nenya are new reductions from rank-1 constraint systems (R1CS) over $\mathbb{Z}/2^k\mathbb{Z}$ to constraints over Galois rings via reverse multiplication-friendly embeddings (RMFEs). We also design a polynomial commitment scheme based on suitable classes of error-correcting codes, which supports well-formedness checks and packing rotations on committed witnesses essentially for free, resulting in sublinear verifier time. Experimental results demonstrate that Nenya achieves strong concrete performance. For a rank-1 constraint system of size $2^{25}$ for data-parallel computations over 32-bit integers, Nenya achieves a prover time of only 4.8 seconds. This is four orders of magnitude faster than the state-of-the-art SNARK scheme over $\mathbb{Z}/2^k\mathbb{Z}$, and only 1.06$\times$ slower than a SNARK over a field with the same number of constraints. For general computation, the prover time of Nenya is 34.6 seconds. Moreover, for proving pixel-level image transformations that arise in media-provenance workflows, such as filtering that operates natively modulo $2^8$, Nenya proves the same computation 12$\times$ faster than a field-based SNARK.
papers.authors: Tianyu Zhang, Nikita Borisov, Yupeng Zhang

papers.title: High Precision Noise Cleaning for CKKS with Application to Asynchronous Threshold CKKS
papers.abstract: Noise cleaning in discrete CKKS uses Hermite interpolation to reduce the input error while preserving the encrypted discrete message. Cryptographic applications based on noise flooding require the error after cleaning to be sufficiently small for the added noise to provide statistical hiding without preventing exact recovery. This requirement is more stringent than decryption correctness alone, but the achievable noise reduction is limited by errors introduced during homomorphic evaluation. In particular, key switching and rescaling can dominate the output error even when a higher interpolation order substantially reduces the polynomial residual. We propose a high precision noise cleaning method for CKKS that preserves encrypted integer messages while attaining a prescribed bound on normalized output noise. We jointly select the cleaning polynomials and evaluation parameters according to a complete error bound that accounts for the input noise and the errors introduced during homomorphic evaluation. By composing Hermite polynomials of lower degree, we can achieve the same output noise bound with a smaller ciphertext modulus and lower evaluation cost than a single higher degree polynomial. In addition, to reduce the ciphertext tensor degree, we construct polynomial representations with noisy auxiliary powers that cancel selected auxiliary error terms. For integer messages, we extract the bits through multi-value functional bootstrapping, then clean and recombine them into a single ciphertext. Finally, we apply high precision noise cleaning to construct an asynchronous threshold CKKS scheme that achieves strong simulation security in the random oracle model. We implement binary and integer noise cleaning in OpenFHE. For binary messages and a normalized output noise target of $2^{-300}$, the selected composition reduces cleaning time from $9.63$ to $1.54$ seconds compared with a single Hermite evaluation under the same input error bound and security requirements. The composition also requires a smaller input ciphertext modulus and less evaluation key storage. We also evaluate the complete construction on 8 bit integers packed into all $32{,}768$ slots. The maximum measured normalized output noise is below $2^{-300}$ with either leveled digit extraction or functional bootstrapping.
papers.authors: Zhihao Li, Cheng Hong, Tao Wei

papers.title: Optimality and Efficiency of Higher-Order Rank-Based Side-Channel Attacks against Inner Product Masking Schemes
papers.abstract: Higher-Order Spearman Coefficient Analysis (HO-SPA) is of particular interest in non-profiling Side-Channel Attacks (SCA) due to its effectiveness against monotonic nonlinear leakage. However, the optimal form, effective order combinations, and performance of HO-SPA (or its variants) remain underexplored. This work systematically revisits HO-SPA in the presence of Boolean Masking (BM) and Inner Product Masking (IPM). Specifically, we propose a new variant of HO-SPA, called HO-ASPA (Higher-Order Adjusted Spearman Coefficient Analysis), and derive the optimal form of HO-ASPA for two-share BM and IPM across a wide range of order combinations under the Hamming weight (HW) leakage model. We first derive the optimal form of HO-ASPA by extending the Spearman Coefficient Analysis to higher-order moments, while preserving the centered-product combination of the share leakages. We then establish an upper bound on the maximal correlation induced by the rank transformation and characterize the relationship between the signal-to-noise ratio and the optimal correlation coefficient in the rank-domain, and extend these analyses to IPM. To enable a fair comparison, we also derive the optimal forms of Higher-Order Correlation Power Analysis (HO-CPA) and HO-ASPA for both BM and IPM under the Least-Significant-Bit (LSB) leakage model. Our analysis highlights a key distinction: unlike HO-CPA, where higher orders often outperform the lowest feasible order, HO-ASPA shows no significant performance gap between higher-order and lower-order attacks. Moreover, under the HW leakage model, our HO-ASPA not only aligns with existing results and succeeds in counteracting the security order amplification, but also significantly outperforms Kruskal-Wallis Analysis (KWA)-based attacks at various order combinations. We further validate the effectiveness of the proposed HO-ASPA through simulated and real-world experimental evaluations.
papers.authors: Haitao Zhan, Wei Cheng, Yuejun Liu, Jingdian Ming, Sylvain Guilley, Yongbin Zhou

papers.title: From Quantum Mechanics to the Hidden Subgroup Problem: an Overview from Finite to Infinite Groups
papers.abstract: The Hidden Subgroup Problem (HSP for short) is an important problem in quantum computing and computational group theory, which has connections with several quantum algorithms, including Shor's algorithm for integer factorization and the discrete logarithm problem. The HSP can be stated as follows: given a function on a group that is constant and distinct on cosets of a hidden subgroup, determine the hidden subgroup efficiently. The problem captures the essence of exploiting group structures for computational advantage and provides insights into the power of quantum algorithms over classical approaches. While abelian instances of HSP are well-understood and efficiently solvable using the quantum Fourier transform, non-abelian cases remain challenging and are active areas of research. The goal of this survey is to put together all the basic background needed to understand well the Hidden Subgroup Problem in groups, reviewing recent results and discussing open problems.
papers.authors: Federico Di Concilio, Ramón Flores, Delaram Kahrobaei, Marialaura Noce

papers.title: Sybil-Proofness of Generalized Adaptive Clinching and Implications for Blockchain Mechanism Design
papers.abstract: The adaptive clinching auction of Dobzinski, Lavi, and Nisan (FOCS'08) is a cornerstone of mechanism design with budget-constrained bidders, and it has since inspired a broad range of extensions to substantially richer market settings. Adaptive clinching enjoys compelling guarantees: it is Pareto optimal, and truthful bidding is a dominant strategy whenever budgets cannot be overreported. In many real-world environments, however, identities are cheap to create, making resilience to Sybil attacks an additional requirement. Whether the guarantees of adaptive clinching survive when a bidder can split its budget across fake identities has remained open. We introduce a generalized framework for adaptive clinching and prove that it satisfies Sybil-robust incentive compatibility: a bidder cannot benefit from splitting into any finite number of identities with arbitrary value reports, provided their aggregate reported budget does not exceed the bidder's enforceable true budget. Sybil resilience thus joins the list of ideal properties of adaptive clinching. Our work is motivated by practical mechanism-design problems in blockchain-based decentralized finance, where two-asset automated market makers (AMMs) are among the most widely used applications. We design a new AMM adaptive clinching mechanism that extends classical adaptive clinching in two ways: it supports a two-sided market and protects against two-sided strategies, and it allows the supply function to depend on the auction state. Its one-sided special case is captured by our generalized adaptive clinching framework, and we further extend our proof techniques to show that the full two-sided mechanism simultaneously satisfies Sybil-robust incentive compatibility and a relaxed notion of Pareto optimality. In light of known impossibility results, together with a new impossibility proved in this paper, we argue that these guarantees are essentially the best possible. More broadly, our work reveals new connections between classical algorithmic game theory and modern decentralized blockchains.
papers.authors: Chengkai Zhang, Yuhao Li, Elaine Shi, Mengqian Zhang, Lirong Xia, Qishen Han

papers.title: Quasi-polynomial time algorithms for block basis reduction of linear codes
papers.abstract: The block code basis reduction algorithm (BKZ) proposed by Ghentiyala and Stephens-Davidowitz requires an exponential number of calls to the minimum weight codeword (MWC) oracle according to the weak complexity bounds established in the original paper. In almost all cases these bounds are worse than plain enumeration of codewords, despite the fact that in practice the algorithm works much better. In this work we propose block code basis reduction algorithms with polynomial and quasi-polynomial complexity for fixed $\beta$. Our algorithms are relaxations and modifications of the original algorithm. First, we show that the truncated version of the BKZ algorithm requires heuristic quasi-polynomial time of calls to MWC-oracle with the same basis quality as in the full BKZ algorithm. Second, we add some weak restrictions on the code basis that enables the algorithm to run in polynomial number of calls to the oracle. Third, we introduce the DeepBKZ algorithm which is adapted from lattice reduction. Under some relaxations (analogs of PotBKZ from the lattices) it also runs in quasi-polynomial number of calls to the MWC-oracle. We provide an implementation of proposed algorithms which is capable to process block sizes $2-24$ and more. Based on this implementation, we provide concrete complexity estimates and an analysis of the approximation factors achieved for the low-weight codeword problem on random linear codes.
papers.authors: Kolesnikov N.S., Novoselov S.A.

papers.title: Improving Code Rate and Query Complexity for the Ligero-IOP System
papers.abstract: This work presents two main contributions to the analysis and design of Ligero-style zero-knowledge proof systems. First, we analyze the original Ligero IOP in the list-decoding regime and show that mutual correlated agreement suffices to obtain improved soundness guarantees and lower query complexity, without modifying the protocol. Second, we propose a new variant of Ligero that incorporates out-of-domain sampling, leading to further soundness improvements and enabling Reed--Solomon code rates above $1/2$. The new protocol preserves the constant-round structure of the Ligero IOP and its compatibility with memory-efficient proving, while achieving perfect honest-verifier zero knowledge.
papers.authors: Ignacio Cascudo, Carmit Hazay, Muthu Venkitasubramaniam

papers.title: A Quantitative Evaluation of Constant-Time Analysis Tools
papers.abstract: The constant-time programming policy protects cryptographic code from timing side-channels. However, writing constant-time code remains challenging even for experienced developers. Therefore, over 50 CT analysis tools have been published to help them identify constant-time violations. While several studies have examined those tools, they predominantly rely on qualitative observations and case studies, rather than quantitative assessments. Therefore, we present AutoBench-CT, a modular benchmark that manually verified per-violation ground truths across 64 cryptographic tasks and the first unified quantitative metrics to quantify the Operational Performance, Detection Quality, and Usability for seven such tools. With the results, we quantitatively show why CT-grind, the first tool published in 2010, is still the most popular tool in the wild. Based on the quantitative findings, we further provide new insights into recurring limitations across tools and propose a composite pipeline to maximize the security guarantees of constant-timeness in practice.
papers.authors: Zhenzhi Lai, Zhiyuan Zhang, Tian Qiu, Van-Thuan Pham, Udaya Parampalli

papers.title: Cryptanalysis and Enhancement of VTBSAE: Provably Secure Verifier-Based PAKE Protocols for the Industrial Internet of Things
papers.abstract: Verifier‑based password‑authenticated key exchange (PAKE) enables a client and a server to establish high‑entropy session keys from low‑entropy passwords without requiring the server to store plaintext passwords. This asymmetric design reduces the risk that leakage of server‑side credentials directly leads to client impersonation, making verifier‑based PAKE well suited to authentication and session‑key establishment for Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT) devices. In this paper, we analyze the recently proposed VTBSAE, a verifier‑based PAKE protocol, and reveal that it fails to provide the claimed resistance against server‑compromise client‑impersonation attacks. To fix this vulnerability, we propose E‑VTBSAEv1. While preserving the lightweight structure of VTBSAE, E‑VTBSAEv1 binds the client‑generated point \(E_{1}\) to fresh server‑side randomness. We also briefly discuss E‑VTBSAEv2 as a challenge‑based variant. We provide a formal security proof for E‑VTBSAEv1 in the random‑oracle model under the CDH assumption, covering AKE security, forward secrecy, and resistance to server‑compromise client‑impersonation attacks after server‑side verifier‑file leakage. We evaluate E‑VTBSAEv1 under two practical deployment settings: a Raspberry Pi 4B server with an AutoDL client, and a Raspberry Pi 4B server with a Raspberry Pi 4B client. The experimental results show that E‑VTBSAEv1 preserves the communication and storage overheads of VTBSAE and achieves runtime performance comparable to that of VTBSAE.
papers.authors: Jiahui Gao, Zhiqiang Zhao, Xuexian Hu

papers.title: SoK: Multiple Concurrent Proposer Blockchains
papers.abstract: Multiple concurrent proposer (MCP) protocols let several parties contribute transactions to the same ledger update. They can distribute communication and reduce one proposer's control over inclusion and order, but these benefits depend on how the contributions are combined. We describe a common architecture from transaction receipt through proposal formation, agreement, data recovery, ordering, execution, and state finality. Within it, we identify four direct MCP families: fixed proposal vectors, selected proposal collections, persistent proposal streams, and causal proposal DAGs. We compare them with constrained assembly, where several parties restrict a block assembled by one party. Across 39 configurations, we distinguish agreement and progress from service for a particular transaction, and compare hiding, ordering, communication, throughput, and latency at explicitly named endpoints. The comparison shows why additional proposers alone do not guarantee inclusion, why hiding does not settle who can react last, and why parallel disseminations need not improve useful execution. It also identifies the recovery, payment, and organizational assumptions needed to turn independent proposal rights into reliable transaction service.
papers.authors: Benjamin Marsh, Alejandro Ranchal-Pedrosa, Max Resnick

papers.title: Stop Calling Them Provers: The Case for Calling ProVerif and Tamarin Symbolic Protocol Analyzers
papers.abstract: A claim that a cryptographic protocol has been proved secure depends on the theory, the analysis software, the protocol model, and the security property being checked. I examine each of these for ProVerif and Tamarin. An audit of their published soundness arguments finds false statements, missing proofs, and gaps between the procedures justified on paper and those the tools run. I also reproduce previously reported bugs that cause Tamarin to accept false claims about the submitted models. ProVerif supplies no certificate for its full analysis, while Tamarin replays its proof tree with its own solver, leaving the correctness of that code to be trusted. A correct symbolic result can still fall short of the security claim made for a protocol. Models can omit behavior in parsers and state machines; secrecy queries can allow information to leak; and equations for cryptographic primitives need justification before they support computational guarantees. Better models, stronger queries and computational soundness arguments can address these problems, but someone must establish that they apply to the protocol at hand. For these reasons and more, I argue that calling ProVerif and Tamarin "provers" is misleading: we should call them symbolic protocol analyzers and report their results with the models, assumptions and evidence that support them. They remain useful for finding attacks and establishing symbolic properties, including for unbounded sessions.
papers.authors: Nadim Kobeissi

papers.title: (Balanced) Boolean Functions on 375 Variables with Nonlinearity Exceeding the Patterson-Wiedemann Direct-Sum Bound
papers.abstract: Patterson and Wiedemann [IEEE-IT 1983] constructed Boolean functions on 15 variables with nonlinearity 16276, which is strictly greater than the bent concatenation bound. Taking their direct sum with a bent function gives nonlinearity $2^{n-1}-27\cdot2^{(n-11)/2}$ for every odd $n\ge15$. Much later, Schmidt [JCT-A 2019] proved that the asymptotic maximum nonlinearity is $2^{n-1}-(1+o(1))2^{n/2-1}$ as $n\to\infty$. In this work, we construct Boolean functions $f$ on 375 variables such that the nonlinearity is greater than $2^{374}-442367\cdot2^{168}=2^{374}-2^{187}+81921\cdot2^{168}$, which exceeds the direct sum of a 15-variable Patterson-Wiedemann function and a bent function on 360 variables. To be specific, the direct sum of a 15-variable Patterson-Wiedemann function and a 360-variable bent function has nonlinearity $2^{374}-2^{187}+20\cdot2^{180}=2^{374} 2^{187}+81920\cdot2^{168}$. Thus our construction improves on this direct-sum value by more than $2^{168}$. Our construction idea is as follows. Let $H$ be the multiplicative subgroup of order $(2^{375}-1)/751$ in $\mathbb F_{2^{375}}^*$. The support of $f$ is the disjoint union of 375 prescribed cosets and a subset $B\subseteq H$. The evaluation of Gauss sums reduces the contribution of the prescribed cosets to a computation of 751 integers. The conditions on $B$ form a $0$-$1$ linear feasibility problem. Using a potential criterion for simultaneous linear constraints, we prove the existence of a single subset $B\subseteq H$ satisfying the constraints at all frequencies. Taking direct sums with bent functions extends the result to every odd $n\ge375$. The support construction does not require balancedness. As a natural follow-up, we also obtain balanced functions with the same strict lower bound by changing the minimum possible number of values, using sampling without replacement. The subsets $B$ and the sets of modified points are obtained by existence proofs.
papers.authors: Deng Tang, Subhamoy Maitra

papers.title: Beyond the Scope of This Paper: Practical Flash-Accelerator and Cache-Collision Timing Attacks on Microcontrollers
papers.abstract: Cache and cache-collision attacks against AES are well-known since 2005, but their application to small (Cortex-M sized) microcontrollers has been limited in prior work, and in many cases the devices are assumed to be immune when they do not have a cache. However, the flash architecture of almost all microcontrollers introduces the same timing collision required for the well-known attacks and as a greatly underestimated channel. Recovery of AES keys using as little as 750 traces will be demonstrated on six popular cryptographic libraries across eight architectures and over twenty devices. Practical recovery on high-level applications is demonstrated against SPI bootloaders, Ethernet applications, CTAP2 over USB, and 802.15.4. wireless protocols. In addition, a new open-source tool called FlashWhisperer is introduced to assist with evaluation of microcontrollers, cryptographic libraries, and applications. Countermeasures already exist in the form of bitsliced implementations, and this work also discusses other countermeasures that existing libraries offer.
papers.authors: Colin O'Flynn

papers.title: Smoothness of Shortest Isogenies to Frobenius Conjugatess
papers.abstract: Let \(E\) be chosen uniformly from the geometric isomorphism classes of supersingular elliptic curves over \(\overline{\mathbb{F}}_p\) and \(\delta_E\) be the minimum degree of isogenies from \(E\) to its Frobenius conjugate \(E^{(p)}\). We establish bounds for the smoothness probability of $\delta_E$ and hence affirm Wesolowski's \(p^{1/3+o(1)}\) attack on the supersingular endomorphism ring problem is unconditional. We also establish a uniform asymptotic formula, with a main term expressed in terms of Dirichlet \(L\)-values, for the probability that a connection isogeny of degree $n$ exists between $E$ and $E^{(p)}$.
papers.authors: Yi Ouyang, Wei Wei, Zheng Xu

papers.title: Trustworthy Distributed Machine Learning in Cloud-Edge-IoT Systems: A Heterogeneity-Aware Survey of Security, Privacy, and Robustness
papers.abstract: Distributed machine learning (DML), including conventional distributed training and federated learning (FL), enables collaborative model development across cloud-edge-IoT systems without fully centralizing raw data. However, distributing data, computation, updates, and orchestration increases the attack surface and introduces coupled challenges across privacy, robustness, reliability, fairness, and governance. This survey presents a security-centered, heterogeneity-aware roadmap for trustworthy DML, with FL treated as a prominent high-risk case. We first characterize the assets, adversaries, trust assumptions, and coordination patterns that define DML/FL security boundaries. We then analyze how statistical, system, and trust heterogeneity, including non-IID data, resource asymmetry, intermittent participation, and cross-silo/cross-device trust differences, affect convergence, fairness, attack detectability, and defense reliability. Next, we synthesize attack-defense interactions across poisoning, backdoors, Byzantine manipulation, privacy leakage, model extraction, network/orchestration attacks, Sybil behavior, and strategic participation. We further compare layered defenses, including robust aggregation, drift-aware optimization, differential privacy, secure aggregation, homomorphic encryption, secure multiparty computation, trusted execution environments, watermarking, provenance, authenticated communication, and monitoring. Finally, we discuss deployment, evaluation, governance, and open research guidelines, emphasizing reproducible, non-independent and identically distributed (non-IID) partitions, attack-aware benchmarks, privacy budgets, attack success rate, client-level disparity, latency, communication, memory, energy/carbon overhead, and auditable lifecycle artifacts.
papers.authors: Long Dang, Ali Alfatemi, Kaiqi Xiong, Mohammed Aledhari, Abdellah Chehri, Shawqi Al-Maliki, Mohamed Rahouti

papers.title: Rosemary: Efficient and Adaptable In-Storage Acceleration for Fully Homomorphic Encryption
papers.abstract: Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) enables computation on encrypted data and is promising for privacy-preserving computing. However, FHE deployment remains constrained due to massive computational, memory, and data-movement overheads. Existing acceleration strategies often overlook the storage I/O bottleneck caused by the enormous size of FHE data in large-scale applications, as most prior works focus on small benchmarks that fit in main memory. Our studies show that state-of-the-art FHE systems spend 71\% to 85\% of their execution time moving data between storage and compute units rather than performing useful computation. To address the I/O bottleneck, we present Rosemary, a heterogeneous FHE acceleration system that incorporates a novel in-storage processing (ISP) architecture with compiler-level and algorithmic optimizations. Our key innovations include 1) an adaptable hardware-aware FHE engine inside a NAND flash-based solid-state drive (SSD) for efficient and cost-effective in-storage FHE processing, 2) a Throughput-Data-Aware Program Allocator (TDAP) that partitions FHE workloads into heterogeneous programs, and 3) a Compiler-Level Ciphertext-Aware Optimizer (CLCAO) that exploits ISP-friendly FHE kernels for low-cost ISP execution. Across a diverse set of FHE workloads, including encrypted deep learning inference and cloud database queries, Rosemary achieves geometric-mean speedups of $185.7\times$ over state-of-the-art CPU/GPU implementations and $3.7\times$ over prior FHE accelerators, while improving energy efficiency by up to $3.9\times$ and Energy-Delay-Area-Product (EDAP) by up to $16.5\times$.
papers.authors: Xuan Wang, Tianqi Zhang, Gabrielle De Micheli, Yujin Nam, Keming Fan, Augusto Vega, Minxuan Zhou, Tajana Rosing

papers.title: RecHash: Segmented Hash-Entangled Chains for Stateful Sequential Authentication
papers.abstract: RecHash is a stateful sequential authentication construction based on paired hash-chain openings and an authenticated record history. It develops the decreasing position relation of the 2019 hash-entangled construction, whose exact integer normalization yields a two-coordinate constant-sum antichain. Direct proportional reuse is constrained by integer capacity and multiplicative contraction. The main construction instead assigns each record to a predetermined chain segment, with complementary positions encoding each digest block. All digests fit every scheduled slot, independently of preceding messages. For an $\ell$-bit digest distributed over $k$ equal-length chain pairs, balanced allocation gives $\lfloor L/(2^{\lceil\ell/k\rceil}+1)\rfloor$ slots. A 256-bit digest, 32 pairs, and length 65535 provide 254 application records followed by a renewal certificate, with 2048 bytes of openings per record for 256-bit chain outputs. We give a complete segmented state transition, a worked trace, exact allocation and resource results, and a renewal-free security-composition theorem conditional on authenticated history and an adaptive one-step guarantee. The analysis relates the construction to constant-sum encodings and standardized hash-based signatures; a concrete post-quantum reduction and security across renewal remain open.
papers.authors: Luis Adrián Lizama-Pérez

papers.title: Syndrome Trellis Decryption in Post-Quantum Cryptography
papers.abstract: We present a novel post-quantum cryptographic framework based on masked high-memory convolutional codes in the Niederreiter paradigm. The public key is derived from a high-memory polynomial parity-check matrix augmented by dense random masking and additional invertible linear transformations. The resulting matrix exhibits strong random-like properties, effectively concealing its algebraic structure and resisting known structural and algebraic attacks. Legitimate recipients retain polynomial-time decoding capability, whereas adversaries appear to be limited to generic information-set decoding with exponential complexity. Under standard cryptanalytic estimates, the proposed construction achieves security margins exceeding those of classical McEliece- and Niederreiter-based systems by factors greater than 2^200. Beyond its enhanced security profile, the construction offers considerable design flexibility, supporting arbitrary plaintext lengths, linear-time decryption, and a uniform per-bit computational cost, enabling efficient scalability to very long messages. Practical implementation is facilitated by a parallel array of syndrome-trellis decoders, dynamically instantiated according to candidate syndrome values, enabling efficient hardware and software implementations with high throughput. Overall, the proposed scheme is a promising candidate for robust, scalable, quantum-resistant public-key cryptography.
papers.authors: Meir Ariel

papers.title: Provably Secure Diffusion Watermarking Against Removal Adversaries with Batched Detector Access
papers.abstract: Recent latent-based watermarking methods can embed undetectable watermarks into AI-generated content. However, these approaches are vulnerable to removal attacks as their watermark detection boundaries are exposed, prompting the use of secret long-term transformations to hide these boundaries. We show that such defenses are insecure under a stronger threat model motivated by publicly reachable detectors: an adversary with batched detector access can reconstruct the transformations, permanently re-exposing the decision boundary. To address this, we propose a watermarking scheme based on a hybrid of long-term and one-time secret transformations, which prevents the reuse of structure across samples and keeps the long-term secret hidden. Besides undetectability, we show that this scheme is provably secure against removal adversaries with batched detector access, in the sense that no probabilistic polynomial-time adversary can achieve a non-negligible advantage over an adversary restricted to adding isotropic white-noise with a $\sqrt{2}\times$ larger perturbation budget, and we show this $\sqrt{2}$ factor to be tight. Evaluations on Stable Diffusion 2.1 and XL demonstrate the attack against the existing defense, and show that our scheme preserves generation quality and withstands common perturbations and targeted removal attacks.
papers.authors: De Zhang Lee, Ee-Chien Chang

papers.title: CLaW: Codec-Guided Adaptive Latent Watermarking for Traceable Diffusion Image Generation
papers.abstract: With the rapid advancement of text-to-image diffusion models, increasingly realistic AI-generated content has raised serious concerns about misuse and copyright infringement. Digital watermarking offers a promising solution by enabling user-level traceability, yet existing methods remain difficult to deploy at scale, hindered by costly model retraining or detection, poor effectiveness-fidelity trade-offs, and limited robustness to image transformations. To address these challenges, we propose CLaW (Codec-guided Latent Watermarking), a robust and efficient watermarking framework for traceable diffusion image generation with frozen diffusion backbones and inversion-free detection. Specifically, CLaW first uses a pretrained watermark codec to map each watermark message to a latent residual, enabling low-cost sampling-time injection. Then, the residual is injected within a late denoising window, where image semantics are better preserved and the watermark signal is less perturbed by subsequent denoising updates, yielding a better balance between watermark effectiveness and image fidelity. Furthermore, we introduce a decoder-guided adaptive injection mechanism that uses decoding confidence as feedback to dynamically calibrate watermark strength, reinforcing weak watermark signals and improving robustness under image transformations. Extensive experiments show that CLaW preserves high visual fidelity and achieves state-of-the-art robustness under image transformations, enabling reliable user-level traceability.
papers.authors: Huangchao Song, Lingyun Yu, Cong Li, Peiqi Jiang, Mingqi Fang, Hongtao Xie

papers.title: Improved LCL Equivalences and Curve Decoding Alphabet Sizes
papers.abstract: Local Coordinate-wise Linear (LCL) properties, introduced by Levi, Mosheiff, and Shagrithaya (2025), capture coding-theoretic properties such as list decoding and list recovery. They showed that every LCL property has the same rate threshold for random linear codes (RLC) and random Reed--Solomon codes (RRS). Brakensiek, Chen, Dhar, and Zhang (2025) extended this to random additive codes. Thus any property of all subspace design codes holds for RLCs and RRS at the same rate. In this work, we improve the probabilistic guarantees in the RRS local equivalence theorem and extend the equivalence to all known subspace design constructions individually. Each such construction, including folded Reed--Solomon codes, has the same LCL threshold as RLC and RRS codes. We apply these results to alphabet-size bounds for curve decoding. Curve decoding, introduced by Goyal and Guruswami (2025) and Carmon et al. (2026), is a row-span-constrained LCL property implying proximity gaps (PG), correlated agreement (CA), and mutual correlated agreement (MCA), relevant to IOPs and SNARKs. Informally, a rate-$R$ code $C \subset \mathbb{F}^n$ is $(\ell,δ,a,b)$-curve decodable if any degree-$\ell$ curve $u:\mathbb{F}\to\mathbb{F}^n$ that is $δ$-close to $C$ on at least $a$ points has at least $b\leq a$ nearby codewords lying on a degree-$\ell$ curve in $C$. Goyal and Guruswami (2025) and Goyal, Guruswami, Sun, and Wootters (2026) established curve decodability for RLC and RRS codes at radius $δ$ approaching $1-R$, but with large alphabets in $\ell$ and $η:=1-R-δ$. Using our improved LCL equivalence and rank-sensitive counting inspired by Goyal and Guruswami (2026), we exponentially improve alphabet requirements while matching the best known values of $(a,b)$. For $\ell=O(1)$, our alphabet-size bounds match the best known for list decoding, and improves results for PG, CA, and MCA.
papers.authors: Rohan Goyal, Venkatesan Guruswami, Yihang Sun, Mary Wootters

papers.title: The use of post-quantum cryptography in the automotive context
papers.abstract: This study comparatively evaluates post-quantum cryptography (PQC) in automotive communication scenarios, considering the threat posed by quantum algorithms such as Shor's and Grover's algorithms. The simulations use OMNeT++, Veins, INET, and SUMO on two hardware platforms and examine ML-KEM/CRYSTALS-Kyber, ML-DSA/CRYSTALS-Dilithium, and FALCON. ML-KEM and ML-DSA are finalized NIST standards, whereas FALCON is a NIST-selected candidate pending final standardization. The evaluation considers a rural V2V scenario and an urban V2X scenario supported by a roadside unit. Kyber exhibits low {key encapsulation mechanism (KEM)}\color{black} operation latency, Dilithium provides balanced signature performance, and FALCON has high key-generation and signing costs but efficient verification. The results are interpreted as a comparative assessment among the evaluated PQC schemes under the reported simulation conditions; {a conventional ECDSA/ECDH baseline measured in the same simulation setup is also reported for reference.}\color{black} The resulting dataset can support future studies of cryptographic selection in automotive systems.
papers.authors: Mariana do Carmo Barata Gonçalves, Valderi Reis Quietinho Leithardt

papers.title: Understanding Post-Quantum Cryptography Adoption: Practices, Challenges, and Evolution in Open-Source Software
papers.abstract: Post-quantum cryptography (PQC) standards establish algorithms for quantum-safe systems, but empirical evidence about how software projects implement and maintain PQC support remains limited. We investigate this implementation and maintenance work by mining 114,361 commits and 5,713 issues across 179 open-source repositories. We use human annotation and validated LLM classification to identify PQC algorithms in commits, classify their adoption status and deployment mode, and identify technical challenges in issue discussions. The commit classification for PQC algorithms reveals that 90% of commits concern maintenance of existing support. From the issue discussions, we construct an 11-category taxonomy of recurring technical challenges. Build, packaging, and dependency failures, along with functional defects, account for approximately half of categorized issues. To examine how PQC support evolves, we use time-series analysis and first implementations of individual algorithms within repositories around NIST standardization milestones. After the 2024 finalization, standardized algorithm names appeared in more than 80% of the PQC development changes analyzed, although earlier names such as Kyber continued to appear. Development activity increased over the observation period. Our milestone analysis, however, did not find a significant increase in first implementations. Migration plans should therefore account for sustained maintenance, prioritize build reliability and integration testing, and track both standardized and predecessor algorithm names. We make the dataset, taxonomy, annotations, and analysis pipeline publicly available.
papers.authors: Souhardya Saha Dip, Moshood A. Fakorede, Krishna Upadhyay, Umar Farooq

papers.title: TextSeal2: Distortion-Free LLM Watermarking with Copula Mixing and Memoryless Races
papers.abstract: We present TextSeal2, a distortion-free watermark for large language models that keeps its signal under speculative decoding: tokens that replace rejected drafts remain watermarked with the same keys, and the acceptance rate is unchanged. It also preserves output diversity and adds no measurable inference latency. Its predecessor, TextSeal, restores diversity in the Gumbel-max scheme by routing each token to one of two keys via a coin flip. This is suboptimal because the detector averages the scores from both keys without knowing which key was used. TextSeal2 instead merges two or more keys into a single virtual key and couples it to fresh noise through AutoMark's Gaussian copula. Any number of keys, including publicly shared keys, can be merged this way without diluting detection. Under speculative decoding, TextSeal2 verifies keyed drafts with one more exponential race, run on the leftovers of the draft races. By memorylessness, this race reproduces block verification, so the output follows the target model exactly. We evaluate TextSeal2 on three LLMs. At equal output token diversity, TextSeal2 detects 8 to 22 percentage points more 100-token answers than TextSeal at a false-positive rate of $10^{-3}$, and is comparable to textGrain while requiring no post-logits optimization. Under speculative decoding, it detects 18 and 22 percentage points more 200-token answers than TextSeal and textGrain, respectively, at the same acceptance rate.
papers.authors: Tom Sander, Pierre Fernandez, Itai Gat, Haiming Bao, Jiaxin Shi, Jason Park, Valeriu Lacatusu, Sylvestre-Alvise Rebuffi, Hongyan Chang, Hady Elsahar, Tomáš Souček, Tuan Tran, Surya Parimi, Alexandre Mourachko

papers.title: Power Adjusting Games Under Block-Dependent Pool Payout Schemes
papers.abstract: Advanced power adjusting block withholding attacks such as PAW and T-PAW have been analyzed so far under a global-reset version of the proportional scheme (GRP), which is rarely used in practice. In this paper, we analyze T-PAW, which contains FAW and PAW as special cases, under the block-dependent payout schemes deployed in practice: Pay-Per-Last-N-Shares (PPLNS), round-based Proportional (PROP) and exponential-decay (EXP). We derive the revenue ratios analytically, by renewal arguments for PPLNS and through the stationary carry process of an open round for PROP and EXP. We further introduce Power Adjusting Hopping (PAH), where an adversary of any size adjusts its power allocation towards the pool according to the blockwork age of the round without withholding any block, and derive its revenue ratios under PROP and EXP. We show that GRP misestimates the T-PAW gain in a scheme-dependent direction: it overstates the gain under PROP up to an order of magnitude and understates it under EXP for the original slush decay rate. PROP is highly vulnerable to PAH, while EXP faces a trade-off: a slow decay invites PAH and a fast decay invites T-PAW. PPLNS is the least vulnerable scheme: it is immune to PAH and it mitigates, but does not eliminate, T-PAW. All analytical results are verified by Monte Carlo simulations.
papers.authors: Mustafa Doger, Sennur Ulukus

papers.title: Attack-Resilient Multi-Bit Image Watermarking Framework via Latent Coordinate Sign Clamping
papers.abstract: Watermarking is essential for image copyright protection and attribution, yet existing methods suffer from fundamental trade-offs among post-hoc applicability to pre-existing images, multi-bit capacity, training-free deployment, and adversarial resilience. To address these limitations, we propose a training-free watermarking framework that exploits the overcompleteness of diffusion latent spaces to embed multi-bit payloads into arbitrary images while preserving high visual quality. Additionally, we develop a three-layer decoding pipeline that combines magnitude-weighted majority voting, BCH, and Chase decoding to maximize message-extraction accuracy in the presence of channel noise. To counter active adversaries, our framework integrates a steganalysis-resistant noise camouflage layer and a dual-layer forgery defense that combines perceptual hashing with a Reed-Solomon fuzzy commitment scheme over CLIP features. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that our method applies to both natural and AI-generated images with a scalable $32\text{--}128$-bit capacity. Furthermore, it effectively mitigates advanced removal vectors ($94.6\%$ decode rate against CtrlRegen+ regeneration attacks) and secures robust forgery detection ($98.8\%$ accuracy via joint CLIP and RS fuzzy commitment mechanism).
papers.authors: Marjan Beheshti, Ronghua Xu

papers.title: Hardware-Aware Model Inversion in Memristive Spiking Neural Networks
papers.abstract: Hardware-accelerated spiking neural networks (SNNs) implemented on memristive crossbar arrays offer significant gains in energy efficiency, while device variability and analog noise are sometimes assumed to hinder information extraction. However, whether these hardware effects improve, preserve, or degrade privacy after deployment remains largely unexplored. Therefore, we ask whether model-inversion leakage characterized on an SNN remains representative after the same model is mapped to a non-ideal memristive substrate, and how hardware non-idealities and reliability faults affecting synapses, neuron thresholds, and spike processing reshape that leakage. To study this problem, we introduce Spiking Domain Model Inversion (SDMI), an inversion method that combines Expectation over Transformation (EOT) with surrogate gradients to optimize inputs through stochastic analog behavior and non-differentiable spiking dynamics. We use SDMI consistently across the SNN model, its memristive SNN, and the same memristive SNN under additional hardware perturbations. Across four datasets, reconstruction leakage does not vary monotonically with model accuracy or hardware variability. At comparable accuracy levels, neuron-threshold perturbations increase reconstruction fidelity, measured by SSIM, by up to 51.8%, whereas spike-level perturbations primarily degrade utility without consistently improving reconstruction. Weight noise, in contrast, reduces leakage under the same inversion procedure. These results show that hardware variability is not inherently privacy-preserving: model inversion leakage in memristive SNNs depends on the hardware state and cannot be inferred from model accuracy alone.
papers.authors: Pablo Sorrentino, Fernando M. Quintana, Erika Covi, Fatih Turkmen

papers.title: Session-Bound Behavioral Watermarking for Autonomous LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) agents are increasingly acting through Web interfaces and external tools. They produce trajectories. Those trajectories may pass through several intermediaries. They can store, modify, or dispute those trajectories. In Web-based agent deployments, trajectories may pass through APIs, marketplaces, and tool servers. As such, a copied or disputed log may not by itself reveal which agent owner produced it. Behavioral watermarking can embed ownership evidence in agent action choices. However, existing methods mainly address detection, removal, rewriting, or imitation. They do not directly test whether repeated observation of watermarked trajectories enables cross-session forgery by exploiting learned action preferences. We formulate this learned-forgery threat and propose AgentAnchor, a session-keyed behavioral watermark for owner attribution from trajectory logs. We derive each step key from a secret key, a fresh public session identifier, and semantic states of recent observations, while a guarded digest of the action-policy state diversifies linear coding rows. It embeds parity evidence through a KL-bounded exponential tilt, and a trusted verifier checks a disputed log without rerunning the agent, using wrong-key calibration and abstention.
papers.authors: Md Facklasur Rahaman, Yong Xiang, Md Palash Uddin, Shang Gao, Guang Hua, Leo Yu Zhang

papers.title: Progressive-Observation Physical-Layer Fingerprinting for Efficient Open-Set Ethernet Authentication
papers.abstract: Physical-layer fingerprinting (PLF) has emerged as a promising authentication approach for Internet of Things devices. However, most PLF systems acquire and process a fixed-length waveform for every authentication query, burdening resource-constrained edge nodes. To address this issue, we propose a progressive-observation PLF method that adapts the waveform length to each query. Specifically, a lightweight convolutional neural network (CNN) first rejects clearly unknown devices from a short observation. Spectral matching then accepts clearly registered devices from a slightly longer observation. Only ambiguous queries proceed to the same matching on the full-length waveform, reducing both data acquisition and computation. Because fingerprints drift across days, we also design an adaptive calibration algorithm to avoid retraining the CNN. The algorithm realigns the features and decision thresholds using a few current-day references from registered devices. We evaluate the method with 100BASE-TX Ethernet devices of two controller types on held-out days. Compared with fixed-length processing, it keeps the false rejection and false acceptance rates equal or lower for both controller types on both days. It also reduces the waveform data per query by 75.1% and the CPU processing time on a Raspberry Pi 5 by 73.7% on average. With the same monitoring bandwidth, an edge node can therefore serve about four times as many authentication queries.
papers.authors: Chenming Zhang, Jiaxiang Geng, Aiqun Hu, Azzedine Boukerche, Peng Sun

papers.title: From if to Oops: Turning a conditional into a key-recovery oracle
papers.abstract: Deterministic variants of CSIDH remove randomness from the group action, either through implementation techniques or, as in Houben's deterministic CSIDH and OSIDH-LD, by design. Since earlier fault attacks on CSIDH mostly target random point sampling, determinism seems to close that avenue. We show that it opens another: every secret-dependent step occurs at a fixed, public point of every execution, so an attacker can fault the same step repeatedly. Our attack forces the mask that selects which of two lanes computes the next isogeny to zero, for example by skipping one instruction. Whether the output changes reveals whether a secret exponent reaches a chosen threshold, and a binary search over these thresholds recovers the full key with one fault per execution: at most 297 oracle queries for OSIDH-LD and 222 for deterministic CSIDH with CSIDH-512-sized keys. We recover full OSIDH-LD keys in a software fault simulation of the reference implementation, and show on a ChipWhisperer-Lite that the targeted instruction is skipped with probability at least 0.94 at an isolated fault position. Finally, we argue that fault resistance requires giving up determinism, and propose countermeasures relying on randomization.
papers.authors: Gustavo Banegas, Nia Dimitrova, Monika Trimoska

papers.title: PairWatch: Pair-Aware Anomaly Transformer for Detecting Adversarial Rendezvous in Public Satellite Catalogs
papers.abstract: Documented adversarial rendezvous and proximity operations (RPO) appear in the public TLE catalog, yet existing TLE-based maneuver detectors treat each satellite in isolation - mistaking routine station-keeping for adversarial behavior and missing RPO entirely when the target stays passive. We argue that the right unit is the satellite pair and the right inductive bias is the kinematic symmetry between approach and recede. We instantiate both with PairWatch, a pair-aware AnomalyTransformer whose attention prior is augmented with a sign-symmetric geometric similarity over relative-motion features, and release an open benchmark of 359 windows from public Space-Track data spanning 11 documented RPO events, 100 Clohessy-Wiltshire synthetic adversarial windows, and a five-class hard-negative set culminating in the TerraSAR-X / TanDEM-X helix formation. Under the deployment-relevant criterion of a single threshold separating real RPO from operational negatives - a necessary property for catalog-scale screening - PairWatch is the only model that succeeds, with the property holding in 100% of bootstrap resamples versus 0-19.5% for three neural baselines and under 0.1% for four physics-informed detectors. A per-source analysis exposes a shortcut-learning failure mode of single-number AUROC: simpler baselines attain higher overall AUROC by shortcutting a synthetic-vs-formation contrast with no operational meaning; removing this single cell flips the test ranking entirely (LSTM-AD), and these baselines fail the security-relevant task the benchmark was built to measure.
papers.authors: Young Eun Kwon, Ji Won Yoon

papers.title: Adversarial Process Disturbances at a Deployable Alarm Budget: Detector Evaluation on a Simulator and a Real Plant
papers.abstract: Industrial anomaly detection is evaluated largely on simulators, and recent work reports large drops, with unstable rankings, on real plant data. We ask whether that extends to the security case. We evaluate eleven detectors across classical, neural, dependency and causal families on a simulated chemical process and a sodium thermal-hydraulic facility: different processes sharing no equipment, but both continuous, at steady state, and perturbed only through temperature, pressure, flow and valve, never composition. Three conditions prior work does not cover: disturbances authored against a threat model rather than native faults; one construction applied to both processes; and detection read at a declared false-alarm budget. The drop persists throughout. The simulator panel looks deployable, neural matching classical; on plant telemetry detection collapses and the neural family trails, a gap that in-sample thresholds likely understate. Which detector wins transfers between the two processes; how often it fires does not. Two results hold on both. Sequential valve manipulation defeats the whole panel: at tier 2 no detector flags more than 0.17 of its perturbed samples, against 0.89 or better for most disturbances. And the plant's collapse is not merely that its disturbances are weaker, though they are by about twelvefold; matched on measured strength, the plant is never the better detected.
papers.authors: Benjamin Blakely

papers.title: Recurrent Bipartite Graph Neural Networks for QC-MDPC Error Decoding in McEliece Cryptosystems
papers.abstract: As the advent of large-scale quantum computing threatens classical encryption, Quasi-Cyclic Moderate Density Parity-Check (QC-MDPC) codes have emerged as a foundational element of Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC). However, decoding these relatively dense codes using classical Belief Propagation algorithms often leads to failures caused by short graph cycles that stall the decoder. In cryptographic applications, these failures are severe security vulnerabilities that leak secret key information. To address this, this paper proposes a Recurrent Bipartite Graph Neural Network (R-BGNN) as proof of concept. By integrating Gated Recurrent Units (GRUs) into the message-passing framework and employing a multi-topology curriculum training strategy, the R-BGNN actively learns to break limit-cycle oscillations. Evaluated across 20 unseen matrix topologies, the proposed architecture significantly outperforms classical Bit-Flipping and Min-Sum baselines, reducing the Decoding Failure Rate (DFR) by 63.7\% at moderate noise levels ($t=10$) while converging in fewer iterations.
papers.authors: Parth Rajeshkumar Tandel, Elisabeth Fink

papers.title: Zero Trust-Enabled Adaptive Incident Response using Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Modern enterprises increasingly operate through complex information systems (IS) enabled by cloud computing, remote and hybrid work practices, and digitally integrated supply chains. These structural shifts have expanded organizational attack surfaces and weakened traditional perimeter-based trust assumptions, giving rise to new and persistent forms of cyber threats. In response, adversaries have shifted toward identity-centric, trust-based intrusion techniques that exploit legitimate access within organizational systems. This evolution has created a pronounced speed asymmetry, whereby attackers can adapt and act at machine speed while defenders remain constrained by reactive or rule-based incident response (IR) processes. Drawing on design science research, we propose ZT-AIR, an adaptive IR artifact that uses zero trust architecture as its design theory and hierarchical reinforcement learning as its kernel theory. ZT-AIR learns context-aware trust decisions, separates strategic prioritization from tactical execution, encodes zero-trust controls as actions, and jointly optimizes security effectiveness and operational continuity. Experimental results across diverse adversarial strategies, network scales, and defense environments show that ZT-AIR achieves a strong balance between security and continuity through frequent, minimally disruptive interventions. Practitioner validation further confirms the design's practical viability. This study contributes to IS research by extending computational design science from threat identification to response execution, theorizing zero trust architecture for adaptive IR, and deriving reusable design principles for adaptive decision support artifacts.
papers.authors: Jisoo Lee, Bhagath Singh Bondili, Harshith Doppalapudi, Gwynith Godin, Nathaniel D. Bastian, Ankit Shah

papers.title: Revision-Bound Evidence Cuts: Authenticated Queries and Contextual Witness Capacity
papers.abstract: Authentic records can support unauthorized narratives when their qualifications, query scope, or counterevidence are silently dropped. We present revision-bound evidence cuts, a framework for authenticating both supporting and opposing inference obligations across changing source versions. Signed complete-update frontiers permit transport of unaffected certificates, alternative-cut recovery, and an exact certified-reuse radius given by a frontier-hypergraph transversal number. Their source obligations induce an integral model of context-bound authorization. To secure database-derived claims, we introduce an authenticated relational query contract that binds original source records, complete selected bags, counting units, parameters, and aggregates independently of execution strategy. A full-source verifier checks 16,824 Chogha Mish records across SQLite scans, indexes, and materialized views; three valid strategies agree and eight contract/view mutations are rejected. A separate 340-row NISP cohort shows that changing the admitted weighting rule can reverse a comparison while preserving every source record. A frozen English text-to-frame compiler produces qualified evidence receipts, with linguistic accuracy evaluated separately from cryptographic integrity. We also separate logical-source from transport commitments so lossless re-encoding need not invalidate unchanged scientific evidence. The SCENE prototype evaluates signed revisions, authenticated queries, scoped disclosures, and adversarial mutations at scales reaching one million source records. These guarantees rely on declared policies and independently pinned trust roots; they authenticate specified computations and obligations, not historical truth, complete counterevidence, or institutional endorsement.
papers.authors: Faruk Alpay, Taylan Alpay

papers.title: The Privacy and Security Risks of Edge LLM Optimization
papers.abstract: Edge deployment of Large Language Models requires optimization techniques that reduce memory, computation, and energy costs. However, preserving task performance does not necessarily preserve security. We argue that optimization is an information transformation that can alter representations, decision pathways, and trust boundaries, creating security drift and optimization-induced attack surfaces.
papers.authors: Mingchen Li, Ren-Yi Huang, Dumindu Samaraweera, Prashant Shekhar, J. Morris Chang

papers.title: Efficient Scalable Oversight via Rewinding
papers.abstract: Scalable oversight asks how a weak verifier can check the outputs of computations performed by more powerful AI systems. One proposed approach uses relativizing interactive proofs, in which a weak verifier checks the output of a complex oracle-aided computation by interacting with one or more powerful provers. A prominent example is debate, which is highly efficient but assumes that one of two powerful AI models, or provers, is truthful. For certain classes of oracle-aided computations, this assumption can be removed, but at substantially greater computational cost. In this work, we introduce \emph{rewindable interactive proofs} (RIPs), a new model of relativizing interactive proofs for scalable oversight. In an RIP, the verifier may rewind the prover to an earlier state of the interaction and continue from there. This is possible when the prover is an AI model, since the verifier can save a snapshot of the model's state and later restore it. We construct a relativizing RIP for computations whose outputs are robust to changing a small fraction of oracle answers. Our construction is more efficient than prior relativizing proofs that do not assume a truthful prover, and it uses no cryptography. In our construction the honest prover runs in time linear in that of the original computation, and the verifier, after a one-time preprocessing step, runs in time nearly linear in the input length (which can be much smaller than the computation itself). We implement our protocol, report a preliminary MNIST experiment, and show that an RIP can be faster than a state-of-the-art deployed proof system. RIPs may be of independent interest. Rewinding is possible whenever the verifier controls the prover's machine, for example when the prover runs on trusted hardware or in a virtual machine whose state can be checkpointed.
papers.authors: Ziyi Guan, Yael Tauman Kalai, Ron Rothblum, Zoe Xi

papers.title: Investigating Data Flows from Android Games
papers.abstract: Online applications can share data with arbitrary parties, without users noticing. In practice, these data flows could constitute privacy violations to individual users, with the lack of transparency leaving users unaware of the unwanted data flows. To understand the spread and scale of this privacy threat, we investigate what data is collected and where it is sent in popular free-to-play Android games. As part of our investigation, we conduct a measurement study where we collect and analyze over 16 GB of network traffic from 50 puzzle games. Additionally, we explore the effectiveness of user-side countermeasures for a selection of the apps. We find that while most countermeasures, such as ad-blocking DNS services, decrease data flows, withholding consent and opting out of data collection can produce inconsistent behavior including increased outgoing traffic. To encourage further analysis, we release our measurements as an open dataset.
papers.authors: Judit Borcsiczky, Lukas Moog, Boel Nelson

papers.title: RV2GC: Reconstructing the Garbling Boundary in a RISC-V Garbled Processor
papers.abstract: Programmable garbled-circuit execution must balance the benefits of cross-program reuse against the cost of repeated work during secure execution. A complete garbled processor provides a fixed circuit for many programs, but its evaluator repeatedly visits processor-wide structures even when only a small part performs the current protected computation. We present RV2GC, which reconstructs the garbling boundary around a fixed library of RISC-V instruction circuits. Public scheduling and operand routing operate outside the circuit topologies; persistent label-encoded state connects independently invoked garbled instruction circuits and instruction-specific garbling-free paths through a common interface. A Conditional-execution Stack and protected commits support secret-dependent branches, bounded loops, and secret-indexed memory access under public scheduling, keeping instruction and memory-address sequences independent of private inputs. Across nine benchmarks, measured ARM2GC-to-RV2GC runtime ratios range from 12.81 to 4,043. In terms of circuit size, the largest listed instruction circuit has 3,386 gates, corresponding to 2.044% and 0.393% of the 256-byte and 4,096-byte Amber processors, respectively. Additional comparisons quantify schedule storage, communication, and the cost of secret-dependent execution.
papers.authors: Zixiao Feng, Xiaolin Li, Chenglu Jin, Wei Yan, Yong Zhang, Hongwei Liu, Yong Liu, Qinfen Hao

papers.title: When Static Reachability Says No: Checking Joern-Based Negative Verdicts for Python Against Execution
papers.abstract: A negative reachability verdict removes a finding from human review. We check such verdicts against execution. Our pipeline, SourceLens, maps Semgrep findings to a Python program's call graph, whose edges a query takes from the calls that Joern links in its code property graph. We ran two command-line programs from the PyCG macro-benchmark, in which the benchmark's manual call graph and Joern disagree, under coverage and recorded the calls between their functions. On these edges, 123 functions of asciinema are unreachable from the program's entry points. The project's own integration script executes 86 of them, and all our runs 113. In Sublist3r, 19 of 24 are executed. The latest Joern release gives the same verdicts. The missing calls go through values, such as classes and functions passed around, or have no call expression, as in with blocks and property reads. In asciinema, four missing edges make 50 of the 113 executed functions reachable. The manual call graphs also lack observed calls, in asciinema many of them property reads and with blocks, which the benchmark may not count as calls. A rule that turns negative verdicts into unknown recovers 62 of the 113 and 15 of the 19, mostly through dunder and private method names. It recovers 0 of the 5 security findings with a negative verdict, all in executed functions. Its selectivity cannot be measured, as only 10 and 5 negative verdicts were not executed, and under library entry-point models it degrades every negative verdict.
papers.authors: Artur Zięba-Kozarzewski, Bartosz Grzegorzewski

papers.title: ARBITRA: Robust Document-Level ATT&CK Extraction via Multi-Expert Argumentation
papers.abstract: Cyber threat intelligence (CTI) reports describe adversary behavior in natural language, but converting them into structured MITRE ATT&CK mappings remains difficult: existing methods decompose reports to sentence-level granularity for extraction, while modern LLMs can work with full reports in a single pass but with noticeable performance degradation. We present ARBITRA, which orchestrates multiple role-specialized LLM experts that propose candidate ATT&CK entities from the full report, which are then verified through a per-candidate quantitative bipolar argumentation framework (QBAF) grounded in document evidence and rationales. We additionally construct reasoning-specialized corpora for fine-tuning so experts can act as effective participants during this verification process. Across ATT&CK extraction benchmarks, ARBITRA reaches a stronger precision-oriented operating point than sentence-level pipelines, recent LLM-based extraction systems, and frontier models including GPT-5.5. Under adversarial perturbations simulating conflicting TTP statements, cross-report contamination, and semantic poisoning, ARBITRA limits mean precision degradation to roughly half that of frontier-model baselines for a more robust extraction.
papers.authors: Youngjin Jin, Seungwon Shin

papers.title: AgentHeal: Evaluating Goal-Preserving Resource Recovery of Web Agents under Access Barriers
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents have demonstrated strong capabilities in automating complex information-seeking and transactional tasks across the open web. However, their real-world reliability remains limited by access barriers, such as dead links, authentication walls, rate limits, and anti-scraping defenses. These barriers block the primary execution path, causing agents to abort prematurely, loop indefinitely, or quietly compromise the user's original constraints. Existing evaluations either implicitly assume that target resources are freely accessible or focus on transient perturbations that simple retries can resolve, failing to capture scenarios where agents must actively reroute around impassable bottlenecks. To bridge this gap, this paper introduces AgentHeal, a comprehensive benchmark evaluating goal-preserving resource recovery, defined as the ability of web agents to detect non-transient access barriers, pivot to legitimate alternative sources, and fulfill the user's exact original objective. Spanning nine barrier families across a counterfactual sandbox and real-website replay, our experiments on leading LLM backbones show that average task success drops sharply from 89.4% to 43.7% under access barriers. Further analysis reveals that agents frequently fall for deceptive look-alikes, fail to escalate to users when necessary, violate access policies, or waste computation on futile retries, providing actionable diagnostics for developing resilient web agents.
papers.authors: Zhiyi Liu, Haohua Du, Haoqi Sun, Haisheng Tan

papers.title: Unlocking with the Heart: Investigating User Perceptions of ECG-Based Biometric Authentication
papers.abstract: Password-based authentication remains challenging for many users, especially for those who face usability and accessibility issues. The burden of maintaining security can cause user fatigue, frustration and non-engagement. To address these issues, we conducted a pilot study to assess ECG-based biometric authentication as a passwordless alternative and to gather adult participants' perspectives on this approach. The research consisted of a survey study, an authentication prototype and a follow-up usability experience questionnaire. Our approach combined an online survey of 337 adults examining authentication practices and perceptions, with a separate usability evaluation in which 49 participants interacted with a simulated ECG-authentication and password interface in a health-care application prototype, then completed a post-test usability test questionnaire. The survey examined how adults across age groups use and perceive various authentication techniques, their experiences with biometrics, their views on security and convenience, and their willingness to adopt ECG authentication. In parallel, the usability prototype and questionnaire captured participants' responses after hands-on interaction with an ECG authentication prototype.
papers.authors: Farnaz Farid, Linet Momposhi, Tamara Watson, Alana Maurushat, Abubakar Bello, Farhad Ahamed

papers.title: CARI: Cross-Boundary Adversarial Runtime Injection in Coding-Agent Workflows
papers.abstract: Coding agents increasingly develop, test, and integrate software whose components are owned by different developers, teams, or services. This exposes a distinct attack surface: a malicious or compromised peer development role can manipulate a live component of the software under development (e.g., a backend service, test harness, CI job, or deployment service) and influence the runtime feedback that another role's coding agent must process to complete its task. Although such a component has legitimate diagnostic authority to report its own state, it has no action authority over the victim's local files, credentials, shell, or development environment. We introduce Cross-Boundary Adversarial Runtime Injection (CARI), a direct runtime-feedback injection setting that exploits this authority mismatch. Rather than explicitly compromising the victim's prompt, model, tools, or local environment, the attacker covertly embeds malicious instructions in task-relevant runtime feedback produced by a peer-controlled development component. The victim then interprets that feedback as part of normal debugging or recovery, and may translate the diagnostic guidance into unauthorized victim-side actions. We instantiate ten different attacks based on CARI, spanning resource exhaustion, information exposure, and development-state manipulation. Across four programming languages and five code-capable models, CARI succeeds in 2,845/3,000 (94.8%) trials. Furthermore, CARI transfers effectively to product-level coding agents, achieving 61.3% attack success on Codex and 58.7% on Claude Code. By contrast, prompt-level defenses exhibit a security-utility trade-off: generic warnings are ineffective, whereas explicit policies suppress attacks but substantially over-refuse legitimate actions.
papers.authors: Jie Fu, Shuang Wu, Ashish Kundu, Wendy Hui Wang, Yuan Hong

papers.title: Enhanced image forensics through partial C2PA-based provenance information
papers.abstract: Cryptographically verifiable C2PA-based Content Credentials (CCs) can be attached to freshly acquired or generated digital images but also to already existing ones with no previous provenance information, for instance after processing through trusted C2PA-enabled software tools. The latter case leads to images with so-called partial CCs, which capture only the last operations applied, while prior provenance remains unknown and can be investigated through signal forensics. This paper addresses the forensic analysis of such images, highlighting the opportunity to leverage the partial CCs as additional trusted knowledge to adapt forensic detectors towards the statistical characteristics of the image under analysis and mitigate potential distribution shifts. To this end, a two-step strategy is envisioned: (i) reconstructing the operations applied by the last signer through a structural analysis of the partial CCs; (ii) exploiting the obtained reconstruction to enhance the forensic detector of the analyst through an adaptation process. An empirical analysis on partial CCs produced by commercial C2PA-enabled software tools through different editing operations is carried out, providing evidence on the feasibility of the reconstruction in practical cases. An experimental case study on the forensic task of synthetic image detection is then presented, showing that the proposed strategy can significantly enhance the performance of state-of-the-art detectors on test images that are postprocessed via C2PA-enabled software tools after being generated/acquired.
papers.authors: Riccardo Ziglio, Eleonora Marchesini, Andrea Montibeller, Giulia Boato, Silvio Ranise, Cecilia Pasquini

papers.title: STAR: Scalable TEE-based Anonymous Rate-limiter
papers.abstract: Protecting Internet services from attacks such as TLS/HTTP floods requires rate limiting, yet identifying users to enforce these limits can compromise their privacy. Anonymous rate limiting promises to reconcile these goals, but existing schemes either struggle to scale or assume that services and authorities do not collude. We present STAR, which uses server-side trusted execution environments (TEEs) to overcome these limitations. By enabling lightweight cryptographic operations, TEEs make authentication efficient, but introduce a privacy challenge: malicious services can observe memory-access patterns to infer user secrets. We address this threat through countermeasures against secret-dependent memory accesses and assess our implementation using dynamic analysis. To extend these efficiency gains across servers, we also design a secure sharding mechanism that distributes client requests. We demonstrate that strong privacy guarantees can coexist with efficient authentication at scale; STAR processes authentication requests in tens of microseconds and handles approximately 13.9K requests per second per CPU core.
papers.authors: Kosei Akama, Yoshimichi Nakatsuka, Koichi Moriyama, Keisuke Uehara

papers.title: A Minimally Informed Black-Box Fake-Report Attack on DRL Traffic-Signal Control
papers.abstract: Deep reinforcement learning (DRL) traffic-signal controllers may use vehicle-to-infrastructure (V2I) reports, exposing their perception layer to false-data injection. Existing demonstrations typically assume either white-box access to the controller's weights or full observability of the traffic state. We study the impact of a weaker and more realistic adversary who has no access to the RL model and whose traffic observations are limited to her own approach. This black-box, minimally informed attacker trains an imitation surrogate of the controller. She then crafts bounded fake reports, restricted to inflating vehicle counts on her own approach, that transfer to the real controller. We demonstrate that despite the loss of accuracy relative to an attacker who can observe the entire state and action space, this limited attacker can significantly increase the average waiting time for other approaches while barely changing the waiting time on her own approach, i.e. externalizing the added delay onto the other approaches. Because the only realizable move is to inflate one's own reported queue, we find that a zero-knowledge attacker that simply reports the maximum feasible queue is as damaging as the surrogate-based one, while an unstructured random inflation is not: the surrogate is not required to reproduce the degradation, and the exposed vulnerability is the V2I sensing channel itself. The surrogate's role is directional control, selecting a disruptive or a selfish objective at the same budget. The attack persists under +/-20% uniform demand variation. Finally, on a common per-lane budget we place the attacker on a knowledge ladder against white-box adversaries, and find the black-box surrogate matches a realizable white-box attacker that uses the victim's own gradients; only abandoning realizability raises the damage further.
