Despite their growing capabilities, these agents remain vulnerable to real-world attacks such as indirect prompt injections, which manipulate agents through malicious instructions embedded in external environments. While existing risk assessment work has primarily focused on the injection content, the effect of where an injection appears has not been systematically characterized. Studying injection placement requires agents to operate over longer-horizon tasks and interact with diverse environmental surfaces. Thus, we build three agentic testbeds spanning tool use, coding, and daily workflow domains with diverse injection surfaces. Holding the injection content fixed, we find that agent susceptibility varies across injection placements. We refer to this phenomenon as the trust region effect: agents implicitly assign different levels of trust to different regions of their environments. For example, an agent powered by GPT-5.4 follows an unsafe injection instruction placed in a repository documentation file (i.e., a README or TODO file) 2.6 times more often on average than the same instruction placed in a code or data file. Building upon this observation, we develop learning-based attackers that generate injection content and select better injection placements. Our approach demonstrates that both where an injection is placed and what content it contains can affect the strength of indirect prompt injection attacks. To the best of our knowledge, this work provides the first systematic characterization for the effectiveness of different injection placements, spanning both coarse-grained environmental surfaces and fine-grained positions. The uneven trust that agents implicitly place across their environments provides important insights for future attack and defense design.
papers.authors: Chengquan Guo, Xiaodong Liu, Weiwei Yang, Mingqian Feng, Jialin Song, Qiyao Ma, Carolyn Buractaon, Christopher White, Bo Li, Jianfeng Gao

papers.title: Jailbreak Connectivity: Towards Diverse, Transferable, and Universal Multimodal Large Language Model Jailbreak
papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are vulnerable to visual jailbreak attacks that bypass safety safeguards. Existing methods typically optimize isolated adversarial examples, limiting attack diversity, transferability, and generalization. We propose Jailbreak Connectivity (JC), a framework based on the observation that effective adversarial inputs can be connected through low-loss regions in image space. JC optimizes continuous adversarial paths: path sampling yields diverse jailbreak images, lightweight surrogate classifiers guide cross-model transfer, and a distribution-level objective enables universal attacks across harmful queries. On MM-SafetyBench, JC achieves average attack success rates of 84.01%, 85.77%, and 97.95% on Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct, InternVL3.5-8B, and Gemma-3-12B-IT, respectively, exceeding the strongest baselines by up to 68.36 percentage points. In black-box evaluations, JC improves attack success rates over FigStep by 24.69 and 27.34 percentage points on GPT-5.6 and Gemini 3.1 Pro, respectively. These findings reveal structured vulnerabilities in MLLM safety alignment and inform more comprehensive security evaluation.
papers.authors: Xu Zhang, Ziqing Hu, Shuo Han, Ren Wang

papers.title: Poisoned Skills: Propagating Jailbreaks Through Agent Markdown Files
papers.abstract: Modern agent frameworks allow users to provide Markdown files containing system prompts, tool descriptions, and skill definitions (e.g., SKILL.md), which are incorporated into the agent's context during initialization. In this work, we investigate whether this configuration mechanism can also serve as an injection channel: can a jailbreak embedded in a Markdown skill file propagate through an agent and induce prohibited behavior? To answer this question, we construct a LangChain-based question-answering agent whose system prompt is assembled from a user-provided Markdown file. We embed a jailbreak combining persona manipulation with a GPTFUZZER-based attack and evaluate its effectiveness across seven contemporary open-weight models using 270 forbidden questions spanning nine harm categories. Under a benign system prompt, the models exhibit near-complete refusal behavior, with a mean attack success rate (ASR) of just 0.5%. In contrast, the injected skill file raises the mean ASR to 45%, reaching 68.9% for individual models. We further evaluate two payload obfuscation strategies: an invisible zero-width character-based stealth payload and a phonetic payload based on grapheme-to-phoneme transformations. Neither outperforms the plain-text injection; notably, the phonetic variant reduces mean ASR to 30%. These findings identify Markdown skill files as an underexplored attack surface for AI agents and suggest that vulnerability to configuration-based jailbreaks depends more strongly on the underlying model than on the specific payload obfuscation technique.
papers.authors: Kashyap R Manjusha, Murali Emani

papers.title: Efficient SIMD SHAKE through Cost-Aware Permutation Scheduling
papers.abstract: Lattice-based cryptography uses SHAKE to expand seeds into byte strings for matrix generation and sampling. SIMD Keccak implementations process multiple hash streams in parallel. Differences in stream lengths and input dependencies can prevent full SIMD utilization. We present a cost-aware method for scheduling Keccak permutations across hash streams during a single execution of a cryptographic algorithm. The method groups ready streams and divides long streams into segments for regrouping. A model of permutation calls, state movement, initialization, and input preparation guides the selection of stream groups, segment lengths, and state placements. We evaluate ML-KEM and HAETAE on an Apple M5, a Cortex-A72, and an Intel Core i5-11500, using Keccak kernels that process two, four, or eight streams per call. ML-KEM achieves speedups of up to $1.31\times$ for encapsulation and $1.44\times$ for decapsulation, while HAETAE achieves up to $1.28\times$ for signing and $1.26\times$ for verification.
papers.authors: Hang Zhang, Ya Shi, Ying Liu, Xianhui Lu

papers.title: Beyond the Event Horizon of Keccak, Extending the Observation from 2011 and applications
papers.abstract: In 2011 we observed that a single path in the Keccak sponge from a state whose capacity has all zero bits back to such a state yields an explicit, infinite family of second preimages for every message of at least one full rate block. Finding such a path costs about 2^(c/2), which lies "beyond the event horizon" for SHA3-256 (c=512). In this paper we give four novel theorems around that observation. First, the capacity can have any value x: a two-block meet-in-the-middle loop from x back to x, found at heuristic cost about 2*2^(c/2), gives the same unlimited family of second preimages requiring no further search, with connectors to and from x at about the same cost again (Theorem 1). Theorem 2 extends this to k-block loops and to cycles of the capacity map. A single-state bridge, a state S with cap(f(S)) = cap(f^-1(S)), where cap denotes the capacity part of the state, also gives such a family but costs about 2^c. Theorem 3 gives cheap collisions and a bridge-amplified multicollision: one inner collision and one connector yield equal-length Joux-style 2^k-multicollisions for every k, instead of Joux's k collision searches. Building on paths to a given inner state, Theorem 4 uses k bridges on the same capacity value x to give k^L full-state multicollisions of 2L+1 blocks after a prefix to x, for every L, at a fixed heuristic cost of E[T_k] ~ Gamma(k+1/2)/Gamma(k)*sqrt(2*2^c/q) with q=2p(1-p), about sqrt(4k)*2^(c/2) for balanced search (p=1/2), that does not depend on L; a binary Joux construction producing at least as many messages needs about ceil(L*log2(k)) collision searches, each of generic order 2^(c/2). Fixed-cost multicollisions were known for CubeHash, but they use the all-zero fixed state and their messages differ in length; to our knowledge, the k^L count of equal-length messages from k>1 bridges at an arbitrary x is new. It has no impact on SHA3-256. We give verified full-round examples on Keccak-f[200] and on Keccak-f[1600] with c=32, a full-round Keccak-f[1600] bridge with c=80, and a full-round c=80 example from the standard IV: an IV transition and three bridges (2^42.61 calls in total) give 3^3=27 distinct 1710-byte messages with a common digest. The second part of the paper offers novel protocols built on the asymmetry between minting and forging Keccak bridges. They include proof of work with hardness-adaptive capacity, dual-capacity commitments anchored by the real SHA3-256 digest, bridges as zero-knowledge-committed tokens, and a self-enforcing bounty market for reduced-round security. To our knowledge, these are the first unkeyed Keccak-based protocols that deliberately set the capacity so that minting a generic bridge takes a feasible O(2^(c/2)) permutation calls, while the tunable hardness parameter c makes forging a bridge infeasible, since it requires O(2^c) permutation calls. We prove the four theorems, machine-check the stated algebraic results in Lean 4, and provide reproducible experiments and open-source proof-of-concept code. The applications are design proposals whose end-to-end security remains open.
papers.authors: Danilo Gligoroski

papers.title: Barriers to Identity-Based Encryption in Generic Group-Action Models
papers.abstract: Identity-based encryption (IBE) is required to support a superpolynomial-size identity space using only polynomial-size public parameters. This compression requirement underlies known barriers to IBE in the generic (pairing-free) group model. Cryptographic group actions, motivated prominently by isogeny-based cryptography, support many advanced primitives beyond public-key encryption. However, no generic construction of IBE from the basic group-action interface is known. Existing generic-group barriers do not resolve this question as they do not translate to generic group-action models. We establish the first tight barriers to IBE in two variants of the generic group-action model. In the type-safe generic group-action model, we prove that an IBE scheme with negligible correctness error and $n$ non-origin action-set element-handles in its public parameters can support at most $n$ identities, even for a weak notion of fully selective security. We show that this bound holds irrespective of the number of action-set element-handles in identity secret keys. We further establish that this bound is tight by demonstrating a matching construction. We then extend this tight characterization to a natural class of IBE schemes in the random-representation generic group-action model (including against representation-sensitive adversaries) under conditions ensuring that identity keys retain no hidden action-set encodings and discarded private encodings leave no residual information. We give a natural syntactic condition for the latter property. For actions additionally equipped with an inversion-like twist, we obtain a more general upper bound (including the same tight bound for odd-order actions). Our results provide the first formal evidence that IBE is likely to require additional algebraic structure or non-black-box techniques beyond the generic group-action interface. More broadly, we provide a new framework for proving lower bounds in generic group-action models.
papers.authors: Sikhar Patranabis

papers.title: An Algebraic Polynomial Evaluation Datastructure for Fields of Large Characteristic
papers.abstract: In this work, we study (multivariate) polynomial evaluation datastructures, i.e. algorithms that can evaluate a multivariate polynomial at any input point, using random access to some precomputed encoding of the polynomial. Multiple constructions have been proposed in the literature, with the work by Bhargava, Ghosh, Guo, Kumar and Umans (2024) achieving optimal datastructure size and query complexity, up to polynomial factors. For $n \in d^{o(1)}$ this is equivalent to having datastructure size $d^{n + o(n)} (d n \log q)^{O(1)}$ and query complexity $(d n \log q)^{O(1)}$ for an $n$-variate polynomial of total degree $d$ over $\mathbb{F}_q$. However, the algorithm of Bhargava et al. is not algebraic, since it requires lifting prime field elements to $\mathbb{Z}$. An algebraic algorithm would be desirable, as an algebraic model of computation is natural for studying polynomial evaluation and is the standard model in algebraic complexity theory. One approach to finding algebraic polynomial evaluation datastructures is to use univariate polynomial interpolation to reconstruct the polynomial along algebraic curves. This approach was first made explicit by Bhargava, Ghosh, Kumar and Mohapatra (2023), who used it to build an essentially optimal algebraic polynomial evaluation datastructure for fields of small characteristic $p = \mathrm{char}(\mathbb{F}_q) \in d^{o(1)}$. Over these fields, their construction refutes a previous conjecture by Miltersen. For fields of larger characteristic, it remains an open problem to find an algebraic algorithm with optimal datastructure size and query complexity. In this work, we propose a new way to construct algebraic curves over prime fields that allow polynomial interpolation: by deriving curves from the base-$\beta$ representation of (lifts of) prime field elements, we are able to recursively reduce the evaluation problem to points in boxes of decreasing size. This leads to a datastructure whose performance scales much more favourably with $p$. Concretely, we improve the dependency of the query complexity on $p$ from $p^{O(1)}$ to $d^{2\log_2 \ln\ln p} \ln p$, and completely remove the dependency on $p$ from the datastructure size. Its query complexity is still slightly super-polynomial in $d \log p$. Nevertheless, a variant of our results is enough to disprove Miltersen's conjecture for all finite fields, including prime fields. We further show that for a certain class of datastructures, which captures natural generalizations of our approach, the query complexity is lower-bounded by $d^{(1 - o(1))\log_3\ln\ln p}$. Consequently, within this class, our construction is optimal up to a constant in the exponent.
papers.authors: Hiroki Okada, Rachel Player, Simon Pohmann

papers.title: Faster complete formulas and their application to curves with efficient endomorphisms
papers.abstract: We revisit scalar multiplication on prime curves $y^2 = x^3 + b$ with $p \equiv 1 \pmod 3$, the family including secp256k1, BN, and BLS curves. We apply a 15-year-old technique in a novel way to improve the best complete addition from $12$ to $11$ multiplications (or $10$ for mixed coordinates) for the first time in 10 years: its final stage is a 3D cross product, which needs only five multiplications. We implement the new formulas on the \texttt{libsecp256k1} library, with an improvement of $5.2$\% in constant-time fixed-base scalar multiplication. Furthermore, we propose a complete tripling formula with the same cost as incomplete tripling in Jacobian coordinates, and combine both formulas into an exception-free width-3 $\tau$-NAF with $\tau = 1 - \omega$ and a six-point precomputed table. In an operation-count model it is about 14\% faster than exception-free GLV-based scalar multiplication at 256 bits and 3--7\% faster than the fastest incomplete GLV. A constant-time implementation in RELIC confirms the model on the BLS families: in $\mathbb{G}_1$ of BLS12-381, BLS24-509 and BLS48-575 the $\tau$-NAF is 9--13\% faster than GLV with the same complete formulas, and the regular variant is 10--12\% faster than regular GLV with complete formulas and 5--9\% faster than regular GLV with incomplete Jacobian formulas. In $\mathbb{G}_2$ of the same curves, where GLS gives the baseline, the $\tau$-NAF stays 10--11\% faster than GLS with complete formulas and 7--9\% faster with Jacobian formulas, while the regular variant gains at most 6\%. We also develop an `imaginary' version of Toom-Cook that is useful for the $\mathbb{G}_T$ extension field arithmetic, yielding a 4--6\% improvement in $\mathbb{G}_T$ exponentiation for BLS24-509 and BLS48-575. A cyclotomic cube at 0.77 multiplications carries the $\tau$-adic method over to $\mathbb{G}_T$, where it makes exponentiation 3\% faster on BLS24-509 and 11\% faster on BLS48-575.
papers.authors: Diego F. Aranha, Paulo L. Barreto

papers.title: PIR through the Lens of Probabilistic Inference
papers.abstract: Private Information Retrieval (PIR) allows a client to retrieve an entry of a database while revealing no information about the requested index to the servers. Classic information-theoretic PIR protocols of Chor et al. (FOCS '95, JACM '98) and Ambainis (ICALP '97) achieve sublinear client computation and communication complexity with a constant number of servers, but require each server to perform computation linear in the database size. In this work, we ask for which classes of structured databases the server computation can be substantially reduced while preserving the communication complexity and privacy guarantees of these protocols. Our main contribution is a new connection between server computation in information-theoretic PIR and probabilistic inference. We show that the computation performed by every server in both the Chor et al. protocol and the recursive protocol of Ambainis can be viewed as computing a marginal probability of a product distribution. Consequently, efficient exact probabilistic inference algorithm immediately yields a faster server algorithm for PIR. We formalize this connection through the notion of inference complexity, which captures the complexity of evaluating these marginals. Using this framework, we obtain improved server computation for several broad classes of functions, including read-once arithmetic formulas, graphical models of bounded treewidth (and consequently arithmetic circuits of bounded treewidth), functions with low communication complexity, and functions with sparse Fourier representations. The resulting protocols preserve the communication complexity, client computation, and number of servers of the underlying PIR constructions while substantially reducing server computation for these structured function classes. Finally, we complement our algorithms with conditional lower bounds. Assuming the randomized Circuit Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis (rCSETH), we show that, for every constant \(\varepsilon>0\), there exists a constant \(c\) such that no uniform algorithm can compute the first (virtual) server's response in the Chor et al. or Ambainis protocol on all \(n\)-input Boolean circuits of size at most \(n^c\) in time \(O(N^{1-\varepsilon})\), where \(N=2^n\). Thus, under rCSETH, substantially sublinear server computation cannot be achieved uniformly for all polynomial-size Boolean circuits.
papers.authors: Dana Dachman-Soled

papers.title: Shor's algorithm compiled on cat qubits: 22 593 qubits for RSA-2048 in 3.14 days
papers.abstract: We present an end-to-end resource estimation of Shor's algorithm on superconducting cat qubits, from its mathematical description to the allocation and scheduling of physical qubits on a chip layout. After proposing a comprehensive view of the modern versions of Shor's algorithm for RSA, ECDLP and FFDLP, we make explicit their logical circuits and the trade-offs they enable. We compile the dominant subroutines down to physical-qubit operations on two architectures: one based on repetition cat codes and one based on LDPC cat codes. We design a parity-Cnot gate for cat qubits, extend a multi-target Cnot gate to the LDPC-cat architecture, and adapt an active injection procedure to cat-qubit architectures. Building on these primitives, we adapt to cat-qubit architectures the adder from Gidney’s 2025 resource estimate for factoring RSA-2048. We combine our adder compilation and a coarser resource estimate for the phaseup with the factory designs and lookup compilation from the FeMoco resource estimation of Kroell et al. Together, these compilations lead to chip layouts and schedules for factoring RSA-2048. Assuming a 1$\mu$s error-correction cycle time, a 10$\mu$s reaction time, circuit-level phase-flip noise with probability $p_Z = 5 \times 10^{-4}$ and no bit-flips, factoring RSA-2048, the configuration we compile in full, requires about 23 000 cat qubits and 3.14 days. Reusing the operations compiled for RSA-2048, solving ECDLP on secp256k1 requires at most 30 000 cat qubits and 1 hour, and FFDLP-512, which we propose as an intermediate benchmark, about 6\,700 cat qubits and 21~minutes. Trading space for time, RSA-2048 runs in 1.25 hours on about 611 000 cat qubits. The requirement on no bit-flips (which corresponds to a bit-flip time of about 100 years) can be relaxed to a bit-flip time of about one hour by using an additional concatenation layer into a distance-3 bit-flip error-correcting code. In that case, we estimate that the cost of RSA-2048 increases to about 45 000 cat qubits.
papers.authors: Axel Pappalardo, Dahmun Goudarzi, Victor Hertz, Hugo Jacinto, Larissa Kroell, André Schrottenloher, Peter Shanahan, Élie Gouzien, Rémi de La Vieuville, Vivien Londe

papers.title: Rerandomizable Garbling Beyond BHHO-KMHE and a Construction from LWE
papers.abstract: Rerandomizable garbling schemes (RGS) are a fundamental primitive enabling advanced cryptographic constructions such as multi-hop homomorphic encryption (Gentry, Halevi, Vaikuntanathan, CRYPTO 2010), iO-combiners (Ananth, Jain, Naor, Sahai, Yogev, CRYPTO 2016), and YOSO-style MPC (Acharya, Hazay, Kolesnikov, Prabhakaran, TCC 2022 and CRYPTO 2024). All known RGS instantiations rely on discrete-logarithm-type assumptions, concretely via the BHHO scheme (Boneh, Halevi, Hamburg, Ostrovsky, CRYPTO 2008) and its recent pairing-based variant (Heitjohann, von der Heyden, Jager, CRYPTO 2025). This reliance stems from the use of key-and-message homomorphic encryption (KMHE) that supports rerandomization and strong "key-privacy under leakage", which hides the applied homomorphic transformations and is currently only achievable using BHHO-style bitwise encryption in combination with permutation-based homomorphisms. Our first main contribution is a new garbling technique that shifts the burden of hiding homomorphic transformations from the encryption scheme to the garbling itself. This allows us to construct RGS from KMHE schemes with substantially weaker properties, avoiding the need for bitwise encryption and permutation-based homomorphisms, and enabling the construction of RGS from KMHE with other homomorphisms, such as additively-homomorphic ones. As a second contribution, we give a concrete lattice-based instantiation of the required KMHE primitive, based on LWE. This construction is a variant of the GSW FHE scheme (Gentry, Sahai, Waters, CRYPTO 2013), which uses new techniques for rerandomization and is tailored to the requirements of our new garbling scheme by supporting a "homomorphic"/"lossy" mode. This yields the first RGS construction that does not rely on discrete-logarithm assumptions and may provide post-quantum security.
papers.authors: Raphael Heitjohann, Jonas von der Heyden, Tibor Jager

papers.title: Beyond LWE: Post-Quantum Assumptions under a Counterfactual Break of the Dihedral Coset Problem
papers.abstract: A refuted 2026 claim of an efficient quantum algorithm for the Dihedral Coset Problem (DCP) motivates this survey of the consequences of a genuine breakthrough. We distinguish a noiseless cyclic coset-state solver, a solver with a prescribed failure exponent, and an extrapolated-state solver. Regev's rare-corruption observation already makes the first hypothesis sufficient for lattice algorithms at some polynomial approximation factors; the witnessing algorithm determines the quantitative bounds. We compose unstructured reductions with explicit sample, state-preparation and success conditions, and compare their sufficient guarantees with more than thirty lattice and non-lattice assumptions. We restate the structured state conversion of Wen and Zheng and audit its forward parameter certificate; the printed bound supplies no certificate at the ML-KEM ring and modulus. We use an explicit affine embedding for heuristic gap estimates, explain the lossiness connection from decision NTRU to search Ring-LWE, and distinguish ordinary from module uniqueness. Chen's withdrawn 2024 quantum algorithm for LWE and a proposed repair of its post-processing would, if correct, reach only a many-sample, small-noise LWE regime that the failure-exponent hypothesis already covers for exponents below $1/2$, and no deployed parameter set. Tables separate rigorous consequences, heuristic comparisons and unverified applications, and distinguish solving a proof assumption from attacking a scheme. Classical structural attacks on Classic McEliece, which do not involve DCP but put the concrete security of the scheme under revision, are summarised here and analysed in detail in a companion paper. The survey closes with open questions and a scenario-planning checklist that requires a complete efficient reduction.
papers.authors: Ramses Fernandez

papers.title: HqcLethe: Streaming HQC Encapsulation for Tiny Stateless Servers
papers.abstract: Stateless post-quantum authenticated key exchanges such as post-quantum WireGuard hedge against unexpected cryptanalytic advances by combining a lattice KEM with code-based Classic McEliece. However, recent attacks have led Germany's BSI to advise against McEliece, which leaves these protocols with lattices alone. HQC, the code-based KEM that NIST selected, could restore diversity, but its keys do not fit in a single packet, so a server would have to buffer multi-packet handshakes. This would leave an attack surface for memory exhaustion, which is what WireGuard's stateless handshake was designed to avoid in the first place. McTiny demonstrated that stateless key encapsulation for Classic McEliece is possible by streaming key blocks one-at-a-time. However, HQC's encapsulation does not split as easily into individual packets, as cyclic polynomial multiplication, unlike matrix-vector multiplication, is inherently non-local. We present HqcLethe, a stateless key exchange that streams an HQC encapsulation in packet-sized pieces. It uses the Chinese remainder theorem to split the polynomial multiplication into independent remainders, one per packet, and masks them so that they reveal no more than an ordinary HQC ciphertext, which we prove in Rocq with SSProve; we also verify session secrecy, server authentication and forward secrecy in ProVerif. Client puzzles bound CPU exhaustion, and HqcLethe removes memory exhaustion: on a Raspberry Pi 3B+, each worker runs in a fixed 1.2-1.6 MiB. At category 5 it sends 27x fewer bytes and uses 9.0x less server CPU than McTiny, the earlier stateless code-based design.
papers.authors: Wind Wong, Klaus v. Gleissenthall

papers.title: Unshuffling Fisher-Yates: Practical Recovery of Length-128 Permutations and Application to ML-DSA
papers.abstract: Shuffling is a standard hiding countermeasure against (single-trace) side-channel attacks on the number-theoretic transform (NTT) of lattice-based post-quantum schemes, such as ML-DSA. The Fisher-Yates algorithm can be used to generate the underlying random permutation. Recovering this permutation itself from a single trace has so far only been studied for short sequences. We present a practical attack on a software implementation of Fisher-Yates for sequences of length 128, the number of butterfly operations in one layer of ML-DSA’s NTT. We identify the exploitable leakage of the algorithm, detect and remove the timing variations caused by rejection sampling and extract Hamming weight and identity leakage from a single trace per shuffle. We encode these hints as a constraint-programming problem with a soft objective function and enumerate the most likely permutations in order of descending likelihood. Applied to a shuffled ML-DSA-44 NTT, the recovered permutations are used to re-order the butterfly leakage, and recover the secret polynomial s1 either directly or up to a few coefficients that are enumerated directly. Protecting ML-DSA’s NTT with Fisher-Yates-based shuffling does, therefore, not, by itself, prevent side-channel-assisted key recovery.
papers.authors: Jonas Schupp, Anna Baumeister, Antonia Wachter-Zeh, Georg Sigl

papers.title: When Algebraic Structure Meets Too Many Hints
papers.abstract: The hint framework of Dachman-Soled, Ducas, Gong, and Rossi (CRYPTO 2020), together with the later too-many-hints analyses from May and Nowakowski (ASIACRYPT 2023) and Cao, Jiang, and Cheng (CRYPTO 2025), gives a classification of secret-dependent hints and LLL-breaking hint thresholds for LWE schemes. These values are now frequently adopted as the default benchmark for side-channel security evaluation. We show that applying them as a security metric is problematic. DDGR categorizes hints based only on their local algebraic form, while the threshold analyses assume uniformly sampled hint vectors. Neither captures how the specific algebraic form of a hint governs the geometry of the resulting sparsified lattice. A hint’s class label and the corresponding uniform threshold therefore cannot, on their own, capture its real cryptanalytic power. We illustrate this mismatch with two forms of structured leakage that naturally appear in ring and module lattice implementations, validated via synthetic experiments on Kyber-512. NTT-domain residues qualify formally as mod-$q$ hints, yet they recover the full Kyber-512 secret with roughly half as many hints as the uniform mod-$q$ bound predicts. Finite-precision FFT samples fall into the weaker approximate-hint class, and still only need $25\%$--$55\%$ of the hint budget required for uniform perfect hints. The gap stems from algebraic structure: these hint families carry additional ring structure that enables tailored lattice recovery strategies, a distinction invisible under the uniform-sampling model. We do not propose new attack optimizations. Our findings indicate that DDGR hint classes and too-many-hints thresholds are syntactic descriptions, not standalone security metrics for real leakage traces. Evaluating a side-channel leak requires considering the algebraic structure of the hint vectors, not just their category and quantity.
papers.authors: Dongshu Cai, Yijian Liu, Xianhui Lu

papers.title: Towards Quantum Sensing for Side-Channel Analysis
papers.abstract: Side-Channel Analysis is an established field of research to assess implementation vulnerabilities of cryptographic algorithms. One typically exploited side-channel is the electromagnetic (EM) near-field, which is proportional to the data-dependent currents flowing through an Integrated Circuit (IC). The field of Quantum Sensing (QS) based on Nitrogen-Vacancy (NV) centers has shown promising approaches for different measurement configurations like scanning or spatially resolved wide-field imaging. Already today, QS has been used in the analysis of (quasi-)static magnetic fields on ICs in spatially-resolved wide-field magnetometers. In this work, we study the applicability of QS for the analysis of dynamic EM fields of ICs. For the first time, we demonstrate spectral-temporal analysis of the EM-side-channel using an NV-center-based Radio-Frequency spectrometer. Our sensor has a real-time bandwidth of 1.1 GHz with adjustable center frequency and directly probes the frequency spectrum via NV center interactions in the time domain. The approach circumvents any computations like Fourier transforms or performing frequency sweeps, enabling GHz-realtime bandwidths. We use this spectrometer to analyze the EM emanations of an RSA decryption and perform leakage detection of a software implementation of the Number Theoretic Transform - a building block of all current lattice based post-quantum algorithms - running on a Cortex M4 commercial off-the-shelf microcontroller.
papers.authors: Oliver Butowski, Paul Haas, Jonas Hasenkrug, Niklas Mathes, Emanuele Strieder, Michael Kunzer, Jan Jeske, Nisha Jacob Kabakci, Marc Stöttinger

papers.title: Peak-DNA: Recurrent Morphology in Global Narrative Propagation
papers.abstract: Global narrative streams exhibit noisy, fragmented, and asynchronous amplification bursts, making direct waveform comparison unreliable for recurrence analysis. This paper introduces Peak-DNA, a framework for identifying recurrent propagation morphology in global narrative streams. The proposed framework transforms hourly GDELT activity into normalized macro-peak episodes through denoising, macro-peak consolidation, and temporal alignment, and compares propagation morphology using DTW-based similarity analysis. Using GDELT narrative streams, we analyze five high-amplification narrative domains: Iran, Defense, AI, Space/Elon, and Quantum/PQC. The results show that amplification events repeatedly converge toward morphology-level propagation patterns within each narrative domain. DTW-based similarity analysis further demonstrates strong intra-domain structural compactness despite heterogeneous publication dynamics and severe observational noise. These findings suggest a measurable morphology layer beyond semantic content or anomaly intensity, providing an initial structural foundation for recurrence-aware narrative monitoring, propagation family discovery, and longitudinal Narrative Genome analysis.
papers.authors: Joosung Kim, Luyonghe Li, Shanwen Wu

papers.title: They Will See Johnny's Message: A Measurement Study of Post-Quantum Cryptography Across Email Delivery Paths
papers.abstract: Harvest-now, decrypt-later (HNDL) attacks make the transition to post-quantum cryptography (PQC) urgent for email. This paper presents a systematic measurement that jointly examines PQC deployment across email service stages, negotiation by communicating peers, and usable message encryption. Endpoint-level support alone does not establish PQC readiness across email workflows because submission, relay, and access use independently negotiated Transport Layer Security (TLS) connections. We therefore combine three snapshots of relay, submission, access, and webmail services associated with the Tranco Top~1M domains with controlled tests of mail clients, sending servers, and OpenPGP and S/MIME implementations. Our measurements reveal a transition concentrated among a few providers, with available capability not consistently translating into actual use. Fewer than half of the domains in each service panel support PQC, and Google alone accounts for approximately 87\% of hybrid-capable relay domains. Only two of eight tested sending providers negotiate PQC with our receiver, although five accept it inbound. When TLS groups are restricted to PQC, four of the six incompatible senders fall back to plaintext where unencrypted SMTP remains permitted. At the message layer, limited native key generation, key-format incompatibilities, and backend integration failures further constrain usable PQC encryption.
papers.authors: Jaehwan Park, Sunghyun Park, Kevin Nam, Doowon Kim

papers.title: Falcon Key Recovery from Joint Sampler Leakages
papers.abstract: Falcon and the forthcoming FN-DSA standard based on it generate signatures via discrete Gaussian sampling, during which power consumption leaks information about secret-dependent intermediate values. While prior attacks exploit sampler leakages individually or in pairs, we present a unified key-recovery framework that fuses three observations from each SamplerZ call: the signed-exponent class e(k) of the integer center, the random-sign bit b, and a multi-class proposal magnitude z0. These fused observations define magnitude-preserving intervals or rays for accepted sampler outputs. Leveraging an exact public linear relation that holds in the absence of modular wraparound, we map these candidate sets directly into slab and halfspace constraints on the secret key. The resulting system is solved via smooth softplus interval regression and bounded integer reconstruction with public-key validation, entirely bypassing computationally intensive lattice reductions such as LLL or BKZ. For PQClean Falcon-512 running at-O3 on an ARM Cortex-M4, our 17-class center classifier achieves 99.34% call-level accuracy on held-out test signatures from the profiling keys. The resulting attack recovers all 50 disjoint evaluation keys using at most 34 signatures (median 11), with a median post-classification key-recovery runtime of 17.54s per key. Furthermore, on c-fn-dsa, where center conversion relies on a single constant-time CLZ instruction, a reduced-resolution 7-class classifier combined with proposal leakage still recovers 38 of 50 keys within 200 signatures. These findings demonstrate that instruction-level normalization alone cannot prevent key recovery, underscoring that side-channel countermeasures for FN-DSA must protect all sampler leakage channels jointly.
papers.authors: Youngchang Kim, Yongseong Park, Jaeho Jeon, Young-Sik Kim

papers.title: Quantum Multi-Collision Lower Bounds for Arbitrary Bounded Types
papers.abstract: We study quantum collision finding for functions of prescribed exact type. For fixed constants $k\ge r\ge2$ and $N=kn$, consider functions $f:[N]\to\mathbb Z_q$ of type $(k^n)$, with exactly $n$ distinct output values and $k$ preimages for each value. We prove that the worst-case bounded-error quantum query complexity of finding $r$-collisions in $\ell$ distinct equality classes is \[ \Theta_{k,r}\!\left( \ell^{\,2^{r-1}/(2^r-1)} N^{(2^{r-1}-1)/(2^r-1)} \right) \] for $1\le\ell\le N^{2^{-r}}$. The result is uniform over all feasible alphabet sizes $q\ge n$. Our proof uses the compressed permutation oracle (CPO). We establish a recurrence for intermediate collision counts and control its accumulated error to obtain database tails exponentially small in $\ell$. The improved CPO soundness estimate then converts these database bounds into function-query lower bounds. Moreover, we extend the analysis to arbitrary exact types with bounded class sizes, without requiring any particular class size to occur linearly often. The resulting lower bounds are tight when forward permutation access is additionally available, although they need not be tight for the original function-query problem. Finally, a sampling reduction relates our collision bounds to sparse $k$-distinctness instances. A separate analysis using Belovs's transfer framework recovers the same lower-bound exponent, establishing a concrete connection between the two approaches.
papers.authors: Tianci Peng, Shiqi Hou, Xiaoyang Dong

papers.title: Classical Verification of Quantum Computation Beyond the Polynomial Hierarchy
papers.abstract: It is not known whether a classical polynomial-time verifier can verify arbitrary polynomial-time quantum computations with an efficient quantum honest prover without computational assumptions. We show that, relative to a classical oracle, such verification is possible for a language beyond the polynomial hierarchy that is decided exactly in quantum polynomial time. The protocol is public-coin, with perfect completeness and soundness error at most 1/4. To our knowledge, no language with such a proof system was previously proved to lie outside AM relative to an oracle. For every unbounded polynomial-time computable function, the oracle can be chosen so that the message count and the oracle query counts of the quantum algorithm, verifier, and honest prover are bounded by this function of the input length. The message count is optimal up to a constant factor, since for a suitable oracle every interactive proof system for the language uses at least a constant fraction of the messages of our protocol on infinitely many lengths, with a constant depending on its verifier. The language is a variant of recursive Fourier sampling in which code tables encode secrets that address data tables. The tables are evaluated recursively, and the oracle stores only the leaves. The quantum algorithm recovers every secret exactly, and the verifier checks the prover's secrets recursively against random code entries. The recursion restricts the input in a correlated way, as the same secret fixes the code bits and chooses the free coordinate, so Håstad's switching lemma does not apply. We prove a switching theorem for these restrictions, which may be of independent interest. For instances of sufficient height, no constant-depth circuit of size $2^{\mathrm{poly}(n)}$ changes its output with probability above $2^{-Ω(n)}$ when the answer of a random instance is flipped by changing a single leaf.
papers.authors: Atul Mantri

papers.title: Watermark Basins: Black-Box Detection of Distilled LLMs
papers.abstract: Proprietary language models and their reasoning traces are vulnerable to API-based distillation, where an adversary trains a student model on the teacher model's outputs. To obtain evidence of distillation, model providers can watermark the teacher's outputs, aiming to leave a radioactive signal in the student's outputs. Existing black-box detectors search for such radioactivity using token-level statistics of the suspect model's outputs. However, token-level signals are not always detectable, for instance when the distillation traces are sampled at a low temperature. In this work, we discover the watermark basin, a persistent signal that enables more reliable watermark detection: during fine-tuning, watermarked teacher traces embed a distinct, key-specific geometric signal in parameter space that lies orthogonal to the ordinary task-specific fine-tuning subspace. Building on this, we introduce Watermark Basin Alignment (WM-Basin), a black-box watermark detector that queries the suspect model through its API, without access to its weights or logits. WM-Basin maps generated text to gradient representations using a fixed clean probe model, projects out the ordinary fine-tuning task directions, and tests whether the residual gradient aligns with the watermark basin induced by the watermark key. We evaluate WM-Basin extensively across diverse teacher models and student architectures (from 135M to 8.2B parameters) distilled on mathematical reasoning. At a strict 0.1% false-positive rate, WM-Basin detects 79% of distilled models at n-gram=1 and 45% at n-gram=3, substantially improving over the state-of-the-art token-level baseline (29% and 1.3%, respectively). Because the watermark signal resides in a persistent basin, it survives post-distillation modifications including quantization, pruning, and reinforcement-learning post-training.
papers.authors: Hongyan Chang, Hady Elsahar, Tom Sander, Pierre Fernandez, Saeed Mahloujifar, Sylvestre-Alvise Rebuffi, Tomáš Souček, Tuan Tran, Valeriu Lacatusu, Surya Parimi, Rashel Moritz, Vanessa Stark, Alexandre Mourachko

papers.title: OblivDGL: Oblivious Deep Graph Learning Made Practical
papers.abstract: The rapid deployment of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) within Machine Learning as a Service (MLaaS) has opened up new privacy concerns. Both sensitive graph data and proprietary GNN models are submitted to and processed in third-party MLaaS platform for training and inference. To alleviate those concerns, recent efforts have been made to design tailored secure computation protocols for GNNs. Unfortunately, existing designs cannot accomplish security, functionality, and scalability simultaneously. They leak a certain degree of graph information, offer limited support on secure training of GNNs, and can hardly scale to large graphs. In this paper, we design and implement OblivDGL, an oblivious deep graph learning framework for secure GNN inference and training. Our design is inspired by Deep Graph Library (DGL), an industrial practice for graph learning. At its core, we distill the secure computational patterns of GNNs into a generalized form, and empower both secure GNN training and inference through a novel oblivious message passing paradigm. To realize such a paradigm, we design a new oblivious graph representation, and realize it by function secret sharing (FSS), a lightweight secure computation technique with low latency. Compared to prior secure GNN systems, OblivDGL achieves the most stringent privacy guarantees, i.e., revealing no private information except for the total number of edges and nodes. One standout feature of OblivDGL is the scalability of processing encrypted graphs by carefully tailored parallelization designs. Extensive evaluations on four benchmark graph datasets demonstrate that, compared to state-of-the-art secure GNN frameworks, OblivDGL reduces communication cost by up to 1024x and achieves up to 14.3x speedup in runtime during secure training. For secure inference, OblivDGL achieves up to 754x lower communication and a 4.19x speedup.
papers.authors: Yiming Qin, Xiaoning Liu, Shangqi Lai, Joseph K. Liu, Xingliang Yuan

papers.title: No Tokenizer, Still a Gap: Cross-Lingual Fairness of Homoglyph and Invisible-Character Watermarking
papers.abstract: Homoglyph and invisible-character watermarks are edit-based watermarks. Instead of changing how a model generates text, they hide a signal in the text after it is written. They swap some characters for homoglyphs, which look the same, or very similar, but have different Unicode code points, or they insert characters that do not display, all without access to the model that wrote the text. Generation-time watermarks work less well for lower-resourced languages due to how tokenizers split their text. Because they work on individual characters, these watermarks never touch a tokenizer, so we ask whether they escape this gap. Across 40 language varieties in 24 scripts, we measure capacity (the hidden bits each character can carry), how much of it survives routine handling and targeted removal, and how much text a keyed detector needs. Capacity varies 3.3-fold and script accounts for 96\% of that variation. Within Latin script, resource level makes no detectable difference ($ρ=+0.095$, $p=0.78$), but across scripts capacity rises with it ($ρ=+0.54$, 95\% CI $[+0.14,+0.83]$), because lower-resourced languages tend to use scripts with few homoglyphs. Ordinary copy-paste, which strips invisible characters, widens the gap: a detector then needs about 2 code points of English or Persian but 93 of Lao. Removing the tokenizer does not remove the inequity, but instead only changes its source.
papers.authors: Alexander Nemecek, Yuqiao Xu, Joseph Falkenburg, Erman Ayday

papers.title: Analyzing Compiler-induced Constant-time Violations with Compiler at Scale
papers.abstract: The constant-time programming policy is a de facto standard for cryptographic libraries to prevent timing side-channel attacks. However, compiler optimizations may break constant-time source code during compilation. Systematically preventing this requires understanding where a violation arises, how it is introduced, and which compiler configurations are problematic. Existing approaches analyze a single compilation point, either the final binary or one intermediate representation, and thus only partially answer the three questions. We propose CTGREP, a compiler-based framework that answers all three questions by applying differential analysis across the entire compilation chain. We use CTGREP to analyze seven complete cryptographic libraries across three Clang versions, six target platforms, and thousands of compiler configurations. We systematically detect compiler-induced constant-time violations in the wild and collaborate with library developers to address 48 cases. We further identify seven new problematic LLVM passes, bypass and improve the state-of-the-art compiler-flag-based mitigation. Finally, we quantify how the compiler version, target platform, and optimization configuration affect the violations. By covering entire libraries across the full compilation chain, CTGREP effectively detects remaining compiler-induced constant-time violations and complements the community's ongoing hardening efforts.
papers.authors: Jing Liu, Lucía Martínez Gavier, Zhiyuan Zhang, Marcel Böhme, Gilles Barthe

papers.title: GKS Fully Homomorphic Encryption: Security Analysis
papers.abstract: All traditional encryption schemes share a fundamental operational vulnerability: encrypted data must be decrypted before it can be used. Fully homomorphic encryption eliminates this vulnerability by enabling computation directly on encrypted data, but existing FHE schemes impose substantial practical constraints that limit deployment. This paper presents a formal security analysis of the Gribov-Kahrobaei-Shpilrain (GKS) private-key FHE scheme. GKS requires no bootstrapping or de-linearization, produces bit-exact decryption, supports native encrypted search, and scales to unbounded depth.
papers.authors: John Graham, Soundes Marzougui, Miloš Pavlović, Vladimir Shpilrain

papers.title: Alg\{Ossa\}: Decentralized Secure Aggregation with Rotating Committees and Eventual Delivery
papers.abstract: Secure aggregation lets clients reveal only an aggregate of their private contributions, supporting a variety of applications, including privacy-preserving sensing, collaborative analytics, and federated learning. Building on the single-server, committee-aided model for one-shot clients used by OPA and Willow~(CRYPTO~'25), we present Ossa, a generic construction with a modular security analysis. Ossa realizes the standard secure aggregation functionality with non-selective abort against a malicious server, but leaves role selection unspecified and provides no delivery guarantee. We therefore present AlgOssa, which integrates Ossa into an Algorand-style consensus backbone in which cryptographic sortition selects fresh potential leaders and verifier committees in each round and refreshes the decryptor committee from finalized chain state at key epochs. AlgOssa further selects the server from among the potential leaders, and we establish an explicit lower bound on the probability that the selected server is honest. Consequently, the probability that a round delivers a non-empty aggregate is bounded below by a positive constant, yielding an eventual delivery guarantee across repeated rounds. This variable delivery cadence fits delay-tolerant statistical sensing and, with persistent buffering and staleness control, buffered asynchronous federated learning. Our generic core supports classical and post-quantum instantiation routes; we evaluate complete local classical rounds and demonstrate the feasibility of the post-quantum route.
papers.authors: Xiangyu Su, Yuma Tamagawa, Mario Larangeira, Zengpeng Li, Keisuke Tanaka

papers.title: CASEL: Consequence-Aware Selective Execution for Reliable Long-Horizon Tool-Using Agents
papers.abstract: Tool-using language agents increasingly modify external systems, yet most runtime safeguards allocate scrutiny by generic uncertainty scores or coarse mutation heuristics. We introduce CASEL (Consequence-Aware Selective Execution Layer), a model-agnostic runtime allocation policy that combines calibrated failure probability, state-dependent consequence, reversibility, ambiguity, and evidence freshness to choose, for each proposed tool call, among direct execution, verification, sandboxing, clarification, approval, and abstention by minimizing a per-mode cost. We formalize direct execution as selective prediction and state and test the validity conditions of a finite-sample threshold and a trajectory risk ledger. In a controlled simulation over 20 seeds with 120,000 test actions each, in which every method has the same intervention menu and the same compute cost, CASEL reduces harmful-side-effect trajectories from 14.75 percent for an uncertainty-ranked gate to 7.02 percent and mean normalized harm from 0.184 to 0.123. A gate ranked by the product of failure probability and consequence reaches similar harm (5.82 percent, 0.120) but sends 45 percent more actions to human approval, and removing reversibility-aware routing raises the rate to 15.53 percent. A trajectory-level risk budget, in contrast, increases harm at equal cost (11.82 percent). Intervention effectiveness is assumed, not measured: the results rank allocation rules under the simulator's assumptions and do not establish deployment effectiveness.
papers.authors: Yanyan Zhang, Fei Shen, Ting Yan, Hao Zhang

papers.title: BUSTA: Teaching Small Language Models to Reason About Binary Execution
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLM) are increasingly applied to Reverse Engineering (RE) workflows. RE, however, differs from common LLM coding tasks as it requires models to reason about low-level program behavior. Furthermore, the deployment of tooling in resource-constrained sandboxed RE environments limits the ability to use frontier-scale solutions. We examine whether a targeted LLM training approach can transfer distinct RE skills to open models via inverse basic-block execution: given an x86-64 basic block and a desired output register state, the model predicts the input register values that produce it. Fine-tuning \texttt{Qwen3-1.7B} and \texttt{Nemotron-3-Nano} with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) raises knowable-register prediction accuracy from 73.2\% to 85.3\% and from 63.3\% to 95.2\%, respectively. Frontier models still score highest (up to 99.2\%), but our fine-tuned \texttt{Nemotron-3-Nano} comes within four points at a fraction of the parameter count. We release both fine-tuned models and the training dataset.
papers.authors: Ritika Poddar, Aidan Fennelly, Deirdre Murphy, Eric Wolos, Corre L. Steele, Michael Doyle

papers.title: Reverse Substitution in Secret Sharing: The Critical One-Half Threshold and a Route to Superpolynomial Lower Bounds
papers.abstract: The contribution vector (convec) of a secret-sharing scheme is the vector of its normalized share sizes. The average and maximum coordinates of a convec give, respectively, the average and maximum information ratios of the scheme. Obtaining superlinear lower bounds on these quantities for unrestricted perfect secret sharing has remained a challenging open problem for about four decades. In this paper, we study substitution, a natural way to build complicated access structures from simpler ones: one participant of an outer access structure is replaced by an inner access structure. Given secret-sharing schemes for the two factors, the standard forward construction composes them into a scheme for the composite access structure. We study the converse question. Given an arbitrary scheme for the composite access structure, we ask to what extent its convec admits a reverse factorization into convecs for the outer and inner factors, up to a common multiplicative loss. Exact reversal is false: we give a counterexample whose optimal reverse factor is \(8/9\), with a composite scheme that is scalar-linear over every finite field. On the positive side, we prove that a factor \(1/2\) is always attainable, and that every fixed instance admits a strictly larger factor. For a recursive family built from Csirmaz’s classical access structure \(\mathcal C_k\), whose distinguished set has size \(k\), we identify a critical reverse factor that determines when the resulting lower bound becomes superlinear. This critical factor exceeds one half by only an amount of order \((\log k)/k\). Crossing it yields superlinear lower bounds, while any fixed positive excess above one half gives a route to superpolynomial lower bounds. Using only Shannon inequalities, the corresponding recursive factor cannot cross the critical value. Thus any improvement sufficient to pass this threshold must exploit constraints beyond the Shannon inequalities.
papers.authors: Shahram Khazaei

papers.title: Tractable, Not Truncated: Colored-Noise TRNG Security via Fractional Brownian Motion
papers.abstract: Oscillator-based true random number generators derive randomness from timing fluctuations driven by thermal and flicker noise, and flicker gains weight as technology advances and transistors shrink. Its long memory leaks information about past, which existing models either discard or truncate, overstating security. We introduce a rigorous and tractable framework for colored noise, including the white and flicker noise of oscillators. We model the oscillator phase by fractional Brownian motion and prove a quasi-renewal property: the phase uncertainty left after conditioning on the entire past depends only on the elapsed time. This yields closed-form worst-case min-entropy and sampling requirements. We also extend spectral and Allan-variance analysis to finite samples, so the noise parameters are estimated consistently from a single timing trace. The pipeline from measurement to sampling requirement is closed-form and needs no simulation. Experiments across FPGA and ASIC platforms show that flicker dominates: its variance meets white noise within about 100 cycles and accounts for more than 99% of uncertainty behind the targeted 0.99 min-entropy rate. Methods relying exclusively on thermal noise require adjustment or redesign: incorporating flicker noise enables a two-to-three orders of magnitude increase in bitrate.
papers.authors: Maciej Skórski, Nathalie Bochard, Licinius Benea

papers.title: SecDMP: Provably Secure Data Memory-Dependent Prefetching (Extended Version)
papers.abstract: Data memory-dependent prefetchers (DMPs) are a microarchitectural optimization recently introduced in mainstream desktop and server CPUs. Although DMPs offer performance improvements, they have been shown to enable side-channel leakage of secrets, even from constant-time code that has been hardened against Spectre attacks. Unfortunately, existing defenses either incur significant performance overhead or, as we show, fail to prevent all DMP leakage. In this work, we address this gap by designing a defense that is both secure and efficient. First, we propose a classification of DMP leakage, categorize existing and novel attacks, and analyze which leakage classes are mitigated by existing defenses. We validate this analysis empirically by implementing the first open-source DMPs on a RISC-V processor, showing that the only existing defense that aims to preserve DMP performance fails to protect against entire leakage classes. Next, we propose SecDMP, a provably secure and efficient hardware-based defense. SecDMP requires secrets to be marked in memory and ensures that DMPs never encode these secrets in the microarchitecture---without compromising performance for public data. We formally prove that SecDMP introduces no leakage beyond a baseline semantics without DMPs. Notably, when combined with speculative-execution defenses, SecDMP restores complete microarchitectural security for constant-time code. Finally, our empirical evaluation shows that SecDMP prevents all DMP leakage while incurring minimal performance overhead and hardware cost.
papers.authors: Jens Sprengers, Marton Bognar, Lesly-Ann Daniel, Frank Piessens

papers.title: Radical isogenies on every model
papers.abstract: Radical isogeny formulae compute a cyclic chain of $N$-isogenies with one $N$th root per step and without sampling torsion points, but for general $N$ they were only known in Tate normal form. We give radical steps of every odd degree $N$ directly on short Weierstrass, Montgomery, twisted Edwards, Huff, extended Jacobi quartic, twisted Hessian, Legendre and Jacobi intersection curves, on Kummer lines, and on all curves with a rational point of order~$2$. Our approach is model-independent. The Tate normal form data is obtained from the $x$-coordinate of the kernel generator by a shifted recursion, and the codomain is recovered in the original model by locating the image of a distinguished torsion point, without square roots. In Tate normal form we lower the cost of a step from $12.5N$ to $10N$ multiplications plus one exponentiation, and short Weierstrass curves come close at $10N+35$. Montgomery and twisted Edwards curves cost $10.5N+O(1)$. However, pushing a point through their steps costs only $2N$ multiplications without precomputation, against $2N+16$ plus a shared $2N-7$ in Tate normal form, which makes them the cheapest models for chains that transport torsion points, e.g.\ for all $N\ge19$ when two points are pushed. The other models cost between $11.5N+O(\log N)$ and $15.5N+O(\log N)$ per step. All algorithms are inversion-free, with exact operation counts.
papers.authors: Thomas Decru

papers.title: Constraining the Commit Boundary: A DIO/ODI-Informed Authorization Guardrail for Agentic Entity Resolution
papers.abstract: Agentic Entity Resolution (ER) systems iteratively plan actions, retrieve evidence, revise hypotheses, and propose graph mutations. An erroneous identity hypothesis may condition later retrieval and produce apparent confirmation. This paper proposes a Digital Identity Optimization (DIO) and Ontology of Digital Identity (ODI)-informed authorization boundary between evidence available for agent reasoning and evidence eligible to authorize persistent identity-changing mutations. A domain-governed constraint-binding function maps selected reconstruction-failure distinctions to explicit identity-preserving constraints. An abstract two-phase supervisor permits a commit only when claim-specific authorization-eligible evidence supports every required proposition, relevant conflicts are resolved, the operation remains within its authorized scope, and relevant state and policy versions remain valid. Admission as UNVERIFIED does not confer authorization eligibility. Separate claim-specific promotion governs evidentiary use; insufficient support or unresolved material conflict leads to deferral. The contribution is a specification connecting diagnostic-to-constraint mapping, evidence promotion, proposition coverage, conflict handling, scope binding, and commit-time version integrity. A proposed evaluation protocol is designed to assess the mapping's incremental value beyond generic authorization and conventional identifier rules. This is a conceptual architecture without implementation or empirical validation, not a theorem of semantic correctness. Its property depends on domain-policy adequacy, evidence promotion, and enforcement. It does not prevent erroneous hypotheses or hypothesis-conditioned retrieval; dependency-aware evidence flow remains future research.
papers.authors: Daniel Beránek

papers.title: When Is a Relation Worth Trusting? Manipulation Costs, Exposure, and the Trust Trap in Multi-Relational Graph Learning
papers.abstract: Multi-relational graph detectors learn from clean data how much to trust each relation, but an adversary pays a different price to manipulate each relation and each action; taking such costs as given, we ask when using a relation is worse than ignoring it. Our first main result proves that degree gating strictly beats every selection or reweighting of a relation when part of the population is isolated on it and the attacker cannot afford to open the gate, and that this window is sharp; on real graphs, validated gating gains exactly on the relations that meet these conditions and nowhere else. Our second shows that a per-node exposure bound, which extends to message passing, tells a platform which relation to harden: exposure per unit cost, computed without any attack, picks the relation whose hardening raises the exact trap threshold most in 15 of 16 cases, against at most 7 for informativeness, cheapness, or an analysis with equal edit costs. Supporting tools give exact worst cases for linear relational models, certified brackets for R-GCN and tree ensembles, and a finite-sample guarantee for adversarial validation, under which clean-trained graph detectors fall below their graph-free counterparts in 58 of 90 settings on six graphs. A selection protocol built on these results is never significantly worse than ignoring the graph; with at most four relations it mostly abstains, as validation alone would, and its cost-aware proposals help when relations are many, so far shown on synthetic graphs. Without cost information, the safe choice is to abstain.
papers.authors: Vincess Dongmo, Astride Melvin Fokam Ninyim

papers.title: Blindfold: Keeping the Audit Coin Secret from LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Audit-based certification bounds the violation rate of an LLM agent by auditing a random fraction $\varepsilon$ of actions and reweighting the audited labels; its validity is meant to rest only on the defender's audit coin. We show that it also rests on a confidentiality property: the coin must not interfere with the agent's view before the action commits, at a time the agent chooses. We call this pre-commit noninterference (PNI) and measure its violation by $D_{\mathrm{A}}$, the total-variation distance between the agent's views under the two coin values. PNI is necessary and sufficient for an unbiased certificate against adaptive agents, the worst-case bias is $(1-\varepsilon)D_{\mathrm{A}}$, and no procedure that sees only audited labels can pay less. Leakage composes across steps, a resource shared across episodes opens a channel of computable size, and raising the audit rate cannot restore validity. On a monitor we built, a silent audit changes no output but adds latency that tool timestamps expose, and the agent can enlarge it. A real LLM agent follows an injection that names a visible audit notice (generic, tool, and timing clauses have no effect); over that channel the plain certificate fails on measured labels and, by a post-hoc analysis, in a live run on a pre-registered schedule, while a silent audit restores it. A fresh coin per audited call closes the timing channel; padding only narrows it.
papers.authors: Wei Zhu, Meiyun Zuo, Huiping Sun

papers.title: RePAIR: Inverting Backdoor Attacks in Semantic Segmentation
papers.abstract: Despite significant advances in computer vision, semantic segmentation models remain vulnerable to backdoor attacks, posing a security risk. These attacks redirect pixels of a chosen victim class to an attacker-specified target class when a trigger is present, while preserving clean predictions. Existing defenses are largely derived from image classification, while dedicated segmentation defenses remain scarce and typically require retraining or model modification. We introduce RePAIR, a post-hoc, label-free, attack-unaware defense based on the observation that backdoor-induced shifts can be stronger in the classifier head than in internal representations, leaving recoverable victim-class semantics. RePAIR infers the victim-target relation from an unlabeled, potentially contaminated image pool, constructs a safety-approved semantic reference, and localizes suspicious pixels by comparing head predictions with internal semantic evidence. It then applies feature-space and output corrections toward the inferred victim semantics, while conservative localization and output constraints limit changes to benign predictions. We model the attack as adversarial probability transport and repair as its approximate reversal, deriving bounds and sufficient conditions for localization, residual attack success, clean-side changes, defense-induced target predictions, and attack-unaware pair identification. Experiments across segmentation architectures and attack settings show that RePAIR substantially reduces attack success while largely preserving clean performance.
papers.authors: Arnold Brosch, Kira Maag

papers.title: The Content Leash: Mitigating Degenerate Solutions in Invertible Speaker Anonymization
papers.abstract: Voice anonymization aims to protect a speaker's identity while preserving the linguistic content of speech, enabling voice data to be shared and processed with reduced privacy risk. This work focuses on reversible voice anonymization, where the original voice can be recovered by an authorized user rather than being permanently discarded. However, existing approaches can achieve apparent speaker anonymization by degrading the speech itself, while their effectiveness may also depend on the speaker-verification representation used during training. This creates a need for methods that protect speaker identity without sacrificing speech intelligibility and that remain effective against unseen speaker verifiers. We introduce content preserving training constraints to improve the privacy-utility trade-off by preventing anonymization from being achieved primarily through speech degradation. We further introduce a verifier-generalization strategy that incorporates a stronger speaker-verification representation during training, improving anonymization robustness beyond the verifier used in the original training setup. The resulting approach maintains intelligible speech, strengthens anonymization, and preserves reliable voice restoration, with evaluation on unseen speakers and held-out speaker verification models. On 38 unseen speakers, the approach raises the attacker's equal error rate from a measured floor of 2.8% to 26.3%, and to 27.9% against a held-out verifier, with 11.8% word error rate and 94.9% speaker similarity on key-based restoration. These improvements advance reversible voice anonymization toward practical privacy-preserving speech applications, where anonymized speech can be safely processed or shared while the original voice remains recoverable under authorized conditions.
papers.authors: Nirjon Mobarak Talukder, Rafid Ahmed, Mohammad Ishrak Abedin, Abu Raihan Mostofa Kamal

papers.title: Quantifying and Prioritizing Stealthy Source-Manipulation Threats Against Multi-Source Anomaly Detectors
papers.abstract: Security pipelines often fuse several data sources and protect a downstream model with a cross-source anomaly detector. Such detectors are usually judged by their clean false-positive rate and by how well they catch random corruption. Neither metric captures an adversary who controls some sources and targets a specific downstream decision. We propose a threat-quantification score, the \emph{task-conditioned visibility margin}, defined as the least detector evidence a manipulation must reveal per unit of harm to the downstream task. The margin has a closed form, takes about $85\,μ$s per certificate, yields a minimum-evidence attack, and identifies task-relevant directions the detector cannot see. On a 17-channel industrial telemetry benchmark, a detector that flags 82.8\% of random single-channel corruptions is first-order blind on 64.7\% of task/subset pairs in an audit of one- to four-channel subsets. Task-conditioned manipulations cause more than twice as many falsely reassuring errors as generic stealthy ones, and more of them evade the alarm on four of five splits, mainly at small budgets. Used to prioritize audits on held-out subsets, the margin finds a median of four verified failures in ten checks, compared with none for random order and two for alarm-based ranking, and performs comparably to the task-gradient baseline. It also ranks vulnerable configurations of the learned GDN and TranAD detectors and of a five-source crop-yield panel.
papers.authors: Indraveni Chebolu, Seema Panghal, Arnab Mallick, Ch A S Murty

papers.title: FIDES-Live: Evaluating Behavioral Concordance in Sequential Trading Agents
papers.abstract: Sequential trading agents produce decisions, orders, execution receipts, account states, and reports that need not agree, even when the final portfolio value is correctly computed. We present FIDES-Live, an operational extension of FIDES from generated strategy concordance to the audit of sequential agent traces. The protocol separates structured decision validity, optional numerical commitment adherence, execution and ledger reconciliation, and receipt- grounded reporting, with explicit coverage and unscorable outcomes. We retrospectively audit ten requested inference routes over 7,299 cryptocurrency account-rounds and a 310-round equity pilot, using real market observations and local paper execution. Cryptocurrency decision validity is 97.35% and structured reporting accuracy is 90.81% among scorable responses, but route-level decision and reporting performance can diverge sharply. Commitment adherence is 94.36% overall; it falls to 62.63% on constraints emitted with nonempty order proposals, compared with 97.56% for valid empty proposals. All retained cash and position transitions reconcile with recorded fills, while execution controls and unavailable quotes explain separate rejection populations. Short-window marked returns provide descriptive context rather than a new test of whether concordance predicts alpha. These observations motivate reporting concordance, evidence coverage, activity, and financial outcomes separately. They do not establish long-run trading skill, semantic faithfulness of explanations, or causal benefits from audit feedback.
papers.authors: Arther Tian, Alex Ding, Simon Wu, Aaron Chan

papers.title: ORBITAL: Optimization of Robust Brain--Computer Inference Through Architecture-Aware Low-Precision Compression
papers.abstract: Compact electroencephalography (EEG) decoders enable embedded brain--computer interfaces (BCIs), but compression can alter adversarial robustness without proportional hardware savings. We present ORBITAL, a robustness-constrained framework combining hardware-realizable structured compression, recovery-aware operating-point selection, multi-attack evaluation, and native edge validation. Across nine subjects and three seeds on BCI Competition IV-2a, S25-TRADES achieves the highest observed mean true-union robustness among compressed EEGNet models (23.06% vs 21.27% for standard Full), with 26.27% fewer parameters and 25.10% fewer MACs. Matched controls identify TRADES as the main source of robustness recovery, improving S25 union accuracy by 6.74 percentage points over clean recovery (p=0.0039), while per-example analysis reveals boundary redistribution rather than uniform margin expansion. On Jetson Orin Nano, FP16 compression reduces board energy by up to 16.20% and latency by 8.00%. Despite 99.3% prediction agreement, native INT8 Q/DQ incurs about twice the FP16 latency and energy, demonstrating the need for joint robustness and hardware-aware optimization.
papers.authors: Saim Rehman, Muhammad Shafique

papers.title: Detecting and Mitigating Query-Based System Prompt Leakage Attacks
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) rely on proprietary system prompts to enforce task directives, safety policies, and access controls. These prompts are vulnerable to query-based leakage attacks, where black-box adversaries extract confidential instructions through adaptive, multi-turn interactions. Existing defenses often assess queries independently, missing malicious behavior that emerges across interactions. We present AdvGuard, a model-agnostic framework for detecting and mitigating system prompt leakage. AdvGuard models cross-query relationships using a bounded semantic interaction graph, statistically filters candidate components, and converts them into line graphs for graph convolutional network (GCN) classification. This approach captures multi-hop patterns in query similarity that distinguish coordinated extraction from benign workflows. A lightweight prompt-level detector provides protection before sufficient interaction history accumulates, and the framework supports black-box LLM deployments. In mixed-query evaluations, AdvGuard improves recall by up to 36% over the strongest baseline while maintaining a false positive rate of at most 3.4%. In multi-turn workloads, it achieves 97.23%-99.1% F1 with 100% recall. Leave-one-attack-family-out tests yield 99.98% mean recall and 99.99% mean F1, with no observed false positives. Integrated into the adaptive PLeak and LeakAgent attack loops, AdvGuard limits exact-match leakage to 0.00-0.01 and substring-match leakage to 0.01-0.09 across evaluated victim models. These results demonstrate robust detection of unseen attack families and substantially reduced prompt reconstruction.
papers.authors: Tushar Nayan, Pratik Poudel, Qian Lou, Yuede Ji, Jason Liu, Ruimin Sun

papers.title: When POST Becomes GET: Investigating HTTP Method Interchangeability and Its Security Implications
papers.abstract: HTTP method semantics are a common boundary between safe retrieval and state-changing operations; however, deployed web applications do not always enforce this boundary consistently. In this paper, we study HTTP method interchangeability, a behavior where a POST request can be rewritten as a GET request to the same endpoint, with POST body parameters moved into the query string, while preserving an equivalent observed response. We present Method Interchange Detection Engine (MIDE), an automated pipeline that crawls web applications in a browser, records POST requests generated by page loads and user-interface interactions, converts supported POST bodies into GET candidates, and compares replayed responses with the original POST response. To avoid counting generic or parameter-independent responses as interchangeable, MIDE also sends a no-query GET baseline. We treat as high-confidence evidence of interchangeability only the cases where the converted GET matches the POST, while the baseline does not. We perform a large-scale unauthenticated experiment on the Tranco top 10k. We find high-confidence interchangeable requests on 407 of 10,000 tested sites (4.1%), 407 of 3,200 sites with captured POSTs (12.7%), and 407 of 2,734 sites with replayed POSTs (14.9%). A targeted Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) token-replay check finds cases where invalid tokens are rejected for POST but accepted for the equivalent GET. We also observe Web Cache Deception (WCD) conditions and cacheable GET responses for interchangeable request instances. These results demonstrate that method interchangeability is observable in real web applications and can expose method-scoped defense gaps.
papers.authors: Matteo Golinelli, Seif Errahmane Hannachi, Bruno Crispo

papers.title: Penny for Your Prompts: A Measurement Study of Contextual Leakage in AI Chat Platforms
papers.abstract: AI chatbot platforms have become one of the most popular web interfaces users interact with online, routinely receiving personal and intimate information shared under an expectation of privacy. Yet, on the web application side, these platforms have the ability to embed third-party analytics, advertising, and session replay scripts that operate silently alongside the chatbot, creating an underexamined channel for conversational data leakage towards third parties. We conduct the first systematic large-scale measurement study of contextual leakage in AI chatbots, auditing the web interfaces of 42 general-purpose and domain-specific (health, legal, and education) platforms. Beyond standard network interception, we instrument the browser at the JavaScript engine level to attribute each data flow to the exact user action that triggered it, and the DOM capture mechanism used to retrieve its content, a granularity invisible to network-layer analysis alone. We find that 21 of these platforms leak conversation titles to third-party trackers, while nine leak verbatim user prompts. Beyond content, we observe a substantial amount of chatbot platforms sending user emails to third-party trackers, enabling the association of conversational context with a user's identity. Our findings cast traditional web privacy issues under a new light, highlighting the privacy issues that are inherent in how users interact with modern AI chatbots.
