The modification retains the original matrix-width and row-labeling restrictions, keys, decryption, and ciphertext size, requiring only additional encryption randomness and finite-field arithmetic. We also attack both multi-authority attribute-based inner-product functional encryption constructions of Datta and Pal (PKC, 2023) and establish correctness and matrix-substitution invariance of the same repair. We prove static security of the repaired small-universe construction under asymmetric DBDH. For the large-universe construction, we identify a missing source-group encoding in the original reduction and give a complete static security proof under an augmented $L$-DBDH assumption, whose generic bilinear group hardness we establish.
papers.authors: Xingwang Wang

papers.title: On the Subtleties of Non-Malleability in IVC: Notions, Attacks and Constructions from Falsifiable Assumptions
papers.abstract: We investigate non-malleable Incrementally Verifiable Computation (IVC), a subject that has received limited attention. We focus on whether and how simulation-sound IVC can be obtained from falsifiable assumptions. We provide additional evidence of the unique aspects of non-malleable incremental proofs, identifying definitional challenges in formalizing simulation-sound IVC, and showing how existing IVC designs from falsifiable assumptions cannot exhibit simulation-soundness "for free" (without modifications). In addition to a new family of definitions of simulation-sound IVC, our main results are the following. - A general negative result: common Valiant-style proofs are malleable. We isolate and formalize a feature shared by the dominant Valiant-style IVC designs (Valiant, TCC 2008) related to the ability to merge proofs together. We show that, assuming one-way functions, natural zero-knowledge versions of Valiant's design are malleable. As an implication of our framework of attacks, we show that the only IVC for NP from falsifiable assumptions (Datta et al., CRYPTO 2025) cannot satisfy any form of simulation-soundness; this is the case even when instantiating this scheme from non-malleable building blocks. - A positive result: first IVC from falsifiable assumptions with non-malleability features. We construct an IVC satisfying a non-trivial form of simulation-soundness under subexponential iO and either subexponential LWE or subexponential bilinear-map assumptions.
papers.authors: Matteo Campanelli, Suvradip Chakraborty, Chaya Ganesh

papers.title: Chosen Commitments and Certified Decoding Regions in the Adaptive Threshold Schnorr Attack
papers.abstract: Crites and Stewart reduce an adaptive forgery attack on threshold Schnorr signatures with $N$ parties and threshold $\tau$ to one call to a sparse linear search oracle, which they show to be bounded distance decoding of a diagonally scaled Reed–Solomon code and whose sparse answer, a witness, names the parties to corrupt. Their analysis samples the coefficient vector behind the adversary's commitment uniformly at random and leaves open whether a chosen vector does better. We bound the success of an adversary that follows their template with a chosen vector and recovers witnesses only inside regions built from the radii that seven decoding theorems, three for Reed–Solomon and four for folded Reed–Solomon codes, certify under their own setup hypotheses. When the commitment is fixed through a known coefficient vector before a fresh hash challenge, the attack target is, conditional on the history that fixed the vector, a uniform point of a line. For distinct nonzero Shamir points, our main theorem shows that every such line contains at most $M$ targets with a witness in a finite collection of coordinate and block weight regions fixed before the targets, each permitting fewer than $\tau$ nonzero coordinates, for an explicit integer $M$ depending only on $N$, $\tau$ and the collection. We call the adversary the wrapper when it makes at most $Q$ fresh challenges and no signing query, chooses each coefficient vector from its history before the challenge and keeps it afterwards, and lets its solvers make no further signature hash queries. It accepts only a witness of the same target and representation that lies in the regions of the collection within its corruption cap, corrupts parties only once it holds such a witness, and then forges from that witness and stops. Hence the wrapper succeeds with probability at most $QM/p$, with $p$ the group order, even if its solvers recover every witness in the regions at no cost. On the six pairs $(N,\tau)$ of the original attack, fixed collections built from partitions into consecutive blocks contain all seven certified regions and have $M$ below $2^{24}$, so at the field size proxy $p = 2^{252}$ the bound stays below $2^{-100}$ after $2^{128}$ challenges. For uniform targets we prove much smaller bounds on the witness probability in these regions. For the folded Guruswami–Wang and Ashvinkumar–Habib–Srivastava block regions on partitions into consecutive blocks fixed before the target, this probability is negligible for polynomially many parties, exponentially large fields and $\tau/N$ bounded away from zero. These results also classify the studied decoder theorems. The hardness of the oracle, the success of other strategies and the adaptive security of threshold Schnorr schemes are open.
papers.authors: Hüseyin Eren Demirtaş, Oğuz Yayla

papers.title: Private Information Retrieval with Accountability at Erasure-Optimal Server Redundancy
papers.abstract: Private information retrieval (PIR) hides which database item a client requests. We study PIR that also identifies servers that respond incorrectly. Against a coalition of at most $t$ corrupted servers, the client must retrieve the item and identify every deviating server when at most $d$ deviate. Above that threshold, it must abort and return an empty identification set, with a specified statistical error. We present SynTrace, a single-round compiler for linear PIR supporting audit queries whose honest answers belong to a public code. The client combines the retrieval query with $m$ audit queries using secret linear mixing and independent blinding. Audit syndromes identify deviations before reconstruction. We prove perfect query privacy, zero false-identification probability within the deviation threshold, and statistical realization of an accountable PIR functionality. For Shamir-based PIR, SynTrace uses $k=t+d+1$ servers. Under the stated privacy and download assumptions, tolerating $d$ missing responses already requires this many servers, so identification adds no server overhead. With this number of servers, $m=d$ audit queries suffice with a suitable field, and are necessary within the specified syndrome-span decoder class. Additional audit queries can reduce communication by allowing a smaller field. For one 32 KiB record from a 1 GiB database, with five servers, privacy and robustness against two corrupted servers, and error at most $2^{-40}$, SynTrace uses 2.25 MiB of communication, compared with 8.96 MiB for the homomorphic-MAC construction of Eriguchi, Kurosawa and Nuida (TCC 2022) under the same workload and thresholds. Batched retrievals can share the audit queries.
papers.authors: Myeongjun Kim, Hyunseok Jeong, Mincheol Son, Young-Sik Kim

papers.title: VeilDNS: Post-Quantum DNS Privacy from the First UDP Packet
papers.abstract: DNS was designed around UDP, and most DNS traffic today still follows that design: one query, one response, and no handshake. This makes DNS fast and scalable, but exposes client queries in cleartext. DoT, DoH, and DoQ provide privacy by encrypting DNS messages with TLS. This works once TLS/TCP or QUIC handshakes complete, but cold sessions spend extra round trips and CPU before the first private query can be sent—a cost that grows with post-quantum cryptography. We present VeilDNS, a DNS-native protocol that uses a post-quantum KEM and AEAD to encrypt DNS questions and answers and authenticate the resolver in a single UDP exchange. Given an authenticated resolver KEM key, clients have query privacy from their first UDP packet. VeilDNS supports stateless and stateful modes—the latter reducing recurring computation and bandwidth. An optional mode provides forward secrecy from the second query onward. By preserving the DNS wire format, VeilDNS runs on the standard UDP port 53. Compared with ML-DSA-authenticated Do(T/H/Q) on the well-provisioned network profile, VeilDNS's stateless and stateful modes achieve up to $3.5\times$ higher cold-session throughput, $4.8\times$ lower average latency, $4.7\times$ lower CPU time, $13.7\times$ fewer bytes, and $15.8\times$ fewer packets. On the constrained profile, the throughput gain reaches $12.4\times$. Tamarin establishes query confidentiality, response authentication, and forward secrecy.
papers.authors: Aditya Singh Rawat, Mahabir Prasad Jhanwar, Rei Safavi-Naini

papers.title: A Memory-efficient Implementation of Wiedemann XL
papers.abstract: The signature schemes MQOM, SNOVA, MAYO, and UOV are third-round candidates in the NIST standardization process for additional post-quantum signatures, and their security relies on the hardness of the multivariate quadratic (MQ) problem. XL with block Wiedemann (BW) is one of the most efficient MQ solvers in practice, but its memory demand has led to a debate about its memory access cost: generating the rows of the Macaulay matrix on the fly is widely believed to save memory at a non-negligible computational cost. In this work, we evaluate the memory--time trade-off in practice. We provide the first efficient on-the-fly implementation of XL with BW. We build on the state-of-the-art implementation by Cheng, Chou, Niederhagen, and Yang (CCNY), which uses SSE instructions and supports the fields $\mathbb{F}_2$, $\mathbb{F}_{16}$ and $\mathbb{F}_{31}$; we remove its column-index tables and generate the rows on the fly in the first phase of BW (BW1). We amortize the cost of on-the-fly generation with a new algorithm that computes column indices with $O(n^2)$ instead of $O(n^3)$ table look-ups, where $n$ is the number of variables. In our experiments we observe that our on-the-fly implementation achieves running times comparable to CCNY's with up to five times less memory. We also port both implementations to AVX2 over $\mathbb{F}_{256}$, the main field of UOV, and observe a similar behavior: comparable BW1 running times with less memory for the on-the-fly variant.
papers.authors: Daniel Cabarcas, Tung Chou, Felipe Merino, Javier Verbel

papers.title: Nearly Optimal Hardness for CVP and NCP with Preprocessing
papers.abstract: The closest vector problem(CVP)and the nearest codeword problem (NCP) are fundamental computational problems with connections to learning, coding theory, and cryptography. We study hardness of approximation in the preprocessing model: an algorithm receives the lattice or code in advance, may perform unrestricted computation to produce polynomial-size advice, and must then solve the problem on any target in polynomial time. Unless $\mathsf{NP} \subseteq \mathsf{P/poly}$, no such algorithm achieves an approximation factor of $\bullet$ $M^{1−\varepsilon}$ for NCP over any fixed finite field, or $\bullet$ $M^{1/\min\{p,2\}−\varepsilon}$ for CVP in any $\ell_p$ norm, for every fixed $\varepsilon > 0$, where $M$ denotes the code block length or lattice dimension, respectively. We improve the subpolynomial factors of Khot, Popat, and Vishnoi [KPV14]to polynomial ones, matching the exponents that Song [Son26] proved without preprocessing for binary codes and the $\ell_2$ norm. We further extend Song’s evaluation tables to every fixed prime characteristic and the lattice reduction to $\ell_p$ with $p > 2$. Our main technical contribution is an extension of the moment method, introduced in an OpenAI report [Ope26] and improved by Song [Son26], to the preprocessing setting. In addition, we give a direct reduction from probabilistically checkable proofs (PCPs) whose query locations and families of possible predicates do not depend on the formula. The resulting factor of $M^{\Omega(1/(\log \log M)^2)}$ is already larger than that of [KPV14], and the reduction may be of independent interest.
papers.authors: Giacomo Fenzi, Guy Weissenberg

papers.title: On the Inapplicability of Residue-Confined Error Attacks to CRT-FHE with Non-Degenerate Error Distributions
papers.abstract: This paper responds to the cryptanalysis presented in “Key Recovery from Residue- Confined Errors in the Pradhan CRT-RLWE Construction” (Olejnik and Naskrecki, 2026), which claims key recovery and plaintext recovery against the CRT-FHE scheme introduced in “A New CRT-based Fully Homomorphic Encryption” (Pradhan et al., 2026). We demonstrate that the reported recovery attacks rely entirely on a deliberately con- structed error distribution whose support lies in the kernel of the CRT encoding function. Consequently, the effective encryption error is identically zero, reducing the attacked con- struction to a noiseless RLWE instance. The subsequent key-recovery and plaintext-recovery results therefore follow from the deliberate elimination of the encryption noise, rather than from any cryptanalytic method capable of recovering secrets from properly noise-bearing CRT-FHE ciphertexts. Crucially, the proposed attack neither removes nor estimates errors from normally generated CRT-FHE ciphertexts. Instead, it assumes an artificial error distribution specifically chosen to guarantee their annihilation during encoding. This condition does not hold for the intended centered-binomial error distribution, under which the probability that an entire error polynomial belongs to the encoder’s kernel is negligible at the reported parameters. Thus, the presented recovery procedures do not constitute attacks against the concrete CRT-FHE instantiation with its intended non-degenerate error distribution. We conclude that the reported key-recovery and plaintext-recovery results concern a deliberately degenerate, effectively zero-error instantiation and do not demonstrate a practical security compromise of CRT-FHE under its intended error sampling. We further show that the distributional mismatch identified in the claimed RLWE hardness reduction does not constitute a cryptanalytic attack. In fact, the CRT-encoded error distribution under the intended parameters admits an exact, invertible transformation to ordinary RLWE with an explicitly characterized non-degenerate ternary error law.
papers.authors: Anil Kumar Pradhan, Abhraneel Dutta

papers.title: Notes on BulletProofs++ Range Proofs
papers.abstract: We review the Bulletproofs++ construction which replaces the bit-decomposition inner-product argument of Bulletproofs with a reciprocal set-membership argument over base-$16$ digits. We present a self-contained specification of the $64$-bit range proof as well as a general batched variant parametric in the batch size $M$ and bit width $b$ and prove honest-verifier zero-knowledge and exact-form knowledge soundness. We describe the evaluation and optimizations of our Rust implementation over Ristretto255, which proves up to $7.8\times$ and verifies up to $4.5\times$ faster than regular Bulletproofs. Finally, we correct two formulas of the original paper: the affine $T^3$ term of the scalar polynomial $p_s(T)$ carries a factor of $2$, and the slot-$0$ component of the blinding vector $r_S$ carries the opposite sign.
papers.authors: Philipp Jovanovic, Arnab Roy

papers.title: Revisiting ZMAC+: Birthday-Bound Attacks and a Beyond-Birthday-Bound Repair
papers.abstract: ZMAC+ is a tweakable-block-cipher-based MAC proposed by List and Nandi in ToSC 2017 with claimed beyond-birthday-bound security. We show that a tag-swap mechanism previously observed for a hypothetical two-output extension of DoveMAC also applies to the published ZMAC+ construction. For two-block tags, we give a distinguisher with constant advantage and a fresh-message forgery with constant success probability using $O(2^{n/2})$ queries in the ideal-TBC model, where $n$ is the block length. An internal collision between two message families exchanges their tag blocks; a common extension preserves this relation and leads to a forgery with one additional authentication query. We identify a counting error in the published Lemma~4 and prove a corrected aggregate differential bound. The resulting PRF and MAC upper bounds match the birthday query threshold for bounded message lengths and two-block tags, under explicit field-order conditions. The distinguisher extends to every legal fixed output length $d\ge2$, and the forgery to every legal even $d$. We also retain ZHash and separate the output domains. Under stated field-order, length, and domain-capacity conditions, this modification admits an adaptive PRF bound of order $q^2/2^{n+\min(n,t)}$ for bounded lengths. Finally, a one-query counterexample shows that the ZAE security theorem must retain the per-message length restriction required by its counter-in-tweak encryption component.
papers.authors: Yan Jia, Peng Wang, Lei Hu, Shuping Mao, Tingting Guo, Jiadong Han

papers.title: Mikros: Bitwidth-Aware SNARKs over Extensions of Small Fields
papers.abstract: Provers for succinct non-interactive arguments of knowledge (SNARKs) perform arithmetic over a large field for soundness, even when the witness entries are a few bits wide, which inflates both prover time and memory usage. Recent work makes individual SNARK components bitwidth-aware, so that a lower witness bitwidth means faster proving and lower memory usage, but these techniques cover only part of the prover and exploit the structure of specific fields, typically binary ones. We introduce Mikros, a framework for end-to-end bitwidth-aware SNARK construction based on algebraic vector packing. We pack vectors of length \(N=m\kappa\) over a base field \(\mathbb{F}\) into length-\(m\) vectors over a degree-\(\kappa\) extension field \(\mathbb{E}\), which turns length-\(N\) relations over \(\mathbb{F}\) into length-\(m\) relations over \(\mathbb{E}\) and makes existing linear-time extension-field protocols bitwidth-aware. This technique thus unifies bitwidth-aware inner-product proofs, Hadamard-product proofs, and polynomial commitment schemes, previously obtained by separate constructions, and yields the first bitwidth-aware grand-product proof, hence the first bitwidth-aware permutation argument. Composing them gives bitwidth-aware SNARKs for circuit satisfiability over extensions of arbitrary small fields. For a single instance of circuit satisfiability, the prover cost is proportional to the effective bitwidth, the combined bitwidth of the witness entries and the wiring-position encodings; across instances of the same circuit, the position encoding is amortized and the per-instance cost is proportional to the witness bitwidth. Although Mikros does not rely on binary-field structure, its prover is \(2.19\times\), \(2.55\times\), and \(1.85\times\) faster on batches of \(256\) SHA-256 compressions, Keccak permutations, and BLAKE3 compressions than Flock (B\"unz \etal, IACR ePrint 2026), the state-of-the-art bitwidth-aware SNARK over binary-extension fields.
papers.authors: Mingshu CONG

papers.title: Maximum-Likelihood Decoding of Gabidulin Codes Is NP-Hard Even in Dimension One
papers.abstract: Fix a prime power q . We prove that deciding whether a received word y ∈ F^n_qm lies at rank distance at most n − 2 from the one-dimensional Gabidulin code {λg : λ in Fqm } is NP-complete. Thus maximum-likelihood decoding of Gabidulin codes is NP-hard even for k = 1, an analogue of the Guruswami-Vardy theorem for Reed-Solomon codes. In the Hamming metric, by contrast, hardness at this radius requires the dimension to grow with the length, as in the Guruswami Vardy theorem. The reduction is deterministic; consequently Rank Syndrome Decoding (RSD) and Rank Minimum Distance (RMD) for Fqm -linear codes are NP-complete under deterministic polynomial reductions, whereas the previously known reduction was randomized. The proof goes through a pivot problem that we introduce, Twisted Square Membership (TSM): given Fq -subspaces U, W in FqN , decide whether some non-zero a ∈ U satisfies a^(q+1) in W . Quadratic systems in d unknowns are encoded into TSM, then TSM into Gabidulin decoding. The last step views the received word as an Fq -linear map and decoding at radius n − 2 as the search for an Fq -plane on which it acts as a scalar. With support U + τ W in a cubic extension and map a + τ b → a^(q^2) + τ b^q , two Frobenius twists force solution planes to encode the relation a^(q+1) ∈ W . All constructions are explicit and polynomial, with N = O(qd^2 ), n ≤ N + d, and m = 3N .
papers.authors: Philippe Gaborit

papers.title: The Exact Bit Security of Hash-Based Signatures
papers.abstract: In this work, we analyze the security of hash-based signatures in Lean4. We examine how different ways of accounting for an adversary’s work yield different notions of bit security. As our working example, we study two instances of XMSS with $128$ bit digests. Under most of the accounting modes we consider, we get $127$ bit security for strong unforgeability. However, under the most conservative convention that counts only the adversary’s direct random oracle queries, we only get $122$ bits of security. We prove these bounds in the random oracle model without computational hardness assumptions and give matching attacks. We also prove a tight bound of $127$ bits of strong unforgeability for SLH-DSA-128s. Our work is primarily motivated by recent autoresearch competitions, and it demonstrates the concrete impact of resource accounting. We hope that it helps designers of future challenges make an informed decision when choosing a notion of bit security that reflects their needs.
papers.authors: Mikhail Kudinov, Benedikt Wagner, Emile Wambsgans

papers.title: Exact Error Bootstrapping and Comb Bootstrapping in FHEW/TFHE
papers.abstract: In FHEW and TFHE, bootstrapping evaluates the decryption function via a blind rotation, whose resolution limits the message space. We propose instead to bootstrap the \emph{error}. By rounding the ciphertext at a resolution that is a multiple of the message modulus, we preserve the message exactly. Reduction modulo a small integer then yields a noise-free encryption of the error, which a single blind rotation lifts exactly before it is subtracted. The message modulus is thus constrained solely by the noise and can be much larger than in standard TFHE. Since the error takes far fewer distinct values than the ring degree, a single blind rotation can also refresh several ciphertexts simultaneously. We call this procedure the comb bootstrap. Between refreshes, an integer remains encrypted in a single ciphertext, allowing additions modulo the message modulus and multiplications without programmable bootstrapping. Built on TFHE-rs, for $8$-bit integers on a single thread, our refresh is $3.5$ times faster than that of TFHE-rs, and $9.1$ times faster with the comb bootstrap; multiplication is $6.5$ times faster. In a residue number system, multiplication of integers modulo $\widehat P\ge 2^{32}$ is $19$ times faster than in TFHE-rs. The error bootstrap serves exclusively to refresh ciphertexts; evaluating any other function still requires programmable bootstrapping.
papers.authors: Philippe Chartier, Mohammed Lemou

papers.title: Non-profiled Single-Trace ML-DSA Secret Key Recovery by Horizontal Distribution Analysis
papers.abstract: During the last decade, single-trace side-channel attacks on cryptographic implementations have largely focused on profiled methods, which typically assume that the attacker has a clone device and implementation knowledge to build a leakage model for the target before launching the attack. In this paper, we demonstrate that a much weaker adversary, without the ability to profile, can also mount powerful single-trace attacks. The presented method compares the observed sample distribution with the expected Hamming weight leakage distribution using a Gaussian mixture model as a distinguisher. The horizontal nature of the attack allows us to obtain multiple observations per execution by partitioning and stacking the trace. We show how to select optimal parameters for trace preprocessing and configure the measurement setup so that the noise floor is lowered, enabling the exploitation of weak leakage. We also prove that imperfect classifications can be efficiently corrected using information-set decoding algorithms. The new method is evaluated on an optimized implementation of ML-DSA-65 on ARM Cortex-M4 using the secret key unpacking procedure as an attack point. With an enumeration budget of $2^{70}$ operations in $\mathbb Z_q$, the full secret key is recovered from a single trace in 99% of attacks.
papers.authors: Linus Backlund, Elena Dubrova

papers.title: Revisiting AES Key Wrap: Forgery Bounds, Structural Observations, and Recommendations for the Revision of NIST SP 800-38F
papers.abstract: NIST is revising SP~800-38F, which specifies the AES Key Wrap modes KW and KWP. This paper is an updated and expanded version of our technical comments to NIST. We show that the forgery probabilities stated in SP~800-38F do not account for adaptive attacks, give the resulting forgery probabilities for KW, KWP, and TKW, and show that checking the expected plaintext length can raise the security level of KWP considerably. Revisiting Kelsey's long-message observation, we correct the collision conditions, show that a successful forgery leaks a plaintext prefix, derive an encryption-only distinguisher, and conclude that KW does not have beyond-birthday-bound security. We explain the role of the step counter, analyse the single-semiblock path of KWP and the trade-off between the number of passes and the length limit, and give recommendations for the revision, for implementations, and for future key-wrap designs.
papers.authors: John Preuß Mattsson

papers.title: A Kelsey–Kohno Attack Variant against SHA-2 Message Digests in HSS/LMS and XMSS
papers.abstract: We present a multi-target second-preimage attack on the message hashing of the stateful hash-based signature schemes HSS/LMS and XMSS with SHA-256 and with the truncated SHA-256/192. The attack builds on the herding technique of Kelsey and Kohno: the attacker takes the chaining states that follow the per-signature prefixes of many collected signatures and merges them, level by level through state collisions, into a single chaining state. From that state one search serves all collected signatures at once, which defeats the commitment to the key and to the one-time-signature leaf index at the start of the hash input that is meant to rule out multi-target attacks. The search can match the final digests, which is the better choice against SHA-256/192, or, after appending a Kelsey-Schneier expandable message, the internal chaining states of long signed messages, which is effective for full SHA-256. For SHA-256 with NIST's bound of $2^{64}$ signatures, which may be spread over any number of keys, the cost in compression-function calls falls from the nominal $2^{256}$ to about $2^{166}$ for messages of up to 4 GiB and to about $2^{156}$ in the formal limit of maximal message length, a loss of 100 bits. For SHA-256/192, digest matching costs about $2^{153}$ for $2^{64}$ signatures of any length, a loss of 39 bits. Because the attack pools signatures across keys, even the first signature of an individual key contributes to a potential overall exposure of an ecosystem. The attacks exploit the chaining state of SHA-256, which is narrower than twice the targeted security level; the SHAKE256 parameter sets are not affected.
papers.authors: Falko Strenzke

papers.title: LINE-Break: Cryptanalysis and Reverse Engineering of Letter Sealing
papers.abstract: We present a security analysis of the messaging service known as LINE, a popular platform used daily by millions of users in East and Southeast Asia – most notably Japan, Taiwan, Thailand, and Indonesia. More specifically, we focus on its underlying custom end-to-end encryption (E2EE) protocol, known as Letter Sealing v2. Our findings show that Letter Sealing allows a TLS Machine-in-the- Middle attacker or malicious server to violate integrity, authenticity, and confidentiality of communications. The stateless design of the protocol allows message replay, reordering, and blocking attacks without the user being notified. The lack of origin authentication facilitates impersonation attacks, in which the authorship of mes- sages in one-to-one or group chats can be forged by malicious users colluding with the adversary. Lastly, stickers and URL previews present a notable leakage of plaintext, which leads to a violation of confidentiality. To verify the correctness of our findings, we mounted a Machine-in-the-Middle attack on an iOS device, yielding the device’s outgoing traffic and the corresponding server responses. Utilizing this setup, we experimentally verified our attacks against the authentic LINE application and an independent implementation. We discuss our findings in comparison to the state-of-the-art E2EE protocols, and conclude that Letter Sealing does not satisfy the requirements expected from a modern E2EE messaging protocol.
papers.authors: Diego F. Aranha, Adam Blatchley Hansen, Thomas Kingo T. Mogensen

papers.title: Isotaxis: Optimal Asynchronous Byzantine Consensus with Ordering Linearizability
papers.abstract: Despite ensuring both consistency and liveness, state machine replication (SMR) protocols remain vulnerable to adversaries that manipulate transaction order, causing, e.g., MEV attacks. To mitigate this, researchers have proposed new variants augmented with order-fairness. However, existing protocols that employ dependency graphs, such as Aequitas (Crypto 2020), Themis (CCS 2023), and SpeedyFair (NDSS 2024), often suffer from suboptimal performance, limited resilience, or weakened security guarantees. Pompē (OSDI 2020) introduced a novel ordering notion called ordering linearizability (OL) that may circumvent those drawbacks. However, its guarantee holds only under favorable network conditions, making the protocol vulnerable to order fairness violations during network delays and susceptible to performance degradation in the presence of Byzantine faults. Also, implementing SMR under OL remains an open challenge in asynchronous settings, as no known protocol achieves this without sacrificing liveness of SMR. In this paper, we present $\mathsf{Isotaxis}$, a state machine replication with ordering linearizability; moreover, our protocol has communication complexity $\mathcal{O}(n\ell+\lambda n^2)$, where $n$ is the number of processes, $\ell$ is the input (transaction) size, and $\lambda$ is the security parameter. This is optimal when $\ell\geq \lambda n$, while previous works have cubic communication. To the best of our knowledge, $\mathsf{Isotaxis}$ is the first protocol to achieve ordering linearizability in the asynchronous setting, especially one with optimal communication complexity and optimal Byzantine resilience. We implemented $\mathsf{Isotaxis}$ and conducted extensive experiments using up to 100 EC2 c6a.2xlarge instances. The experimental results show that our protocol robustly outperforms Pompē across all system scales, ranging from 4 to 100 nodes.
papers.authors: Vincent Gramoli, Zhenliang Lu, Qiang Tang, Pouriya Zarbafian, Xinrui Zhang

papers.title: Iterated-Logarithmic Additive Hardness for Bin Packing
papers.abstract: The question of obtaining a constant-additive approximation for bin packing was highlighted in the third of ten open problems in Williamson and Shmoys' The Design of Approximation Algorithms [SW11, Chapter~17, Problem~3]. We prove that there is an absolute constant $c>0$ such that, unless $\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}$, no deterministic polynomial-time packing using at most $\mathrm{OPT}+c\log^*\mathrm{OPT}$ bins, where $\mathrm{OPT}$ is the minimum number of bins. In particular, no such algorithm has additive error $o(\log^*\mathrm{OPT})$. The best known upper bound, due to Hoberg and Rothvoss [HR17], is $\mathrm{OPT}+O(\log\mathrm{OPT})$, achieved by a randomized algorithm with expected polynomial running time. OpenAI [Ope26] previously showed that, unless $\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}$, no deterministic polynomial-time algorithm guarantees a packing using at most $\mathrm{OPT}+O(1)$ bins. We conjecture that the optimal additive approximation error for bin packing is $\Theta(\log \mathrm{OPT})$.
papers.authors: Zhao Song

papers.title: Extraction meets Distillation - cryptanalytic techniques to recover parameters from a Deep Neural Network
papers.abstract: We study fully connected neural-network reconstruction by combining cryptanalytic weight-direction extraction with learning from predicted labels. We adapt a ReLU extraction implementation to Leaky ReLU, compare sign-search methods, and estimate biases and output layers. We prove conditional bounds for direction recovery with approximate prefixes, preservation of local distance votes, prediction changes from aligned parameter errors, and sign selection with independent scoring data. We also specify exact row restoration and distinguish its guarantee from that of gradient masking. The experiments evaluate assisted extraction, with privileged access to gradients, hidden activations, and victim parameters, followed by label-based reconstruction. Across eight search seeds on the largest synthetic architecture, Leaky ReLU recovers 51--57 neurons in the deepest hidden layer, while ReLU recovers none. This advantage does not hold uniformly across architectures and layers. Removing victim-weight access from the sign walk gives less accurate signs, despite high final prediction agreement. Across 40 seeded runs on the two smallest synthetic victims, agreement on 5,000 inputs excluded from fitting and selection ranges from $0.9890$ to $0.9992$. On two CIFAR-10 victims, the reconstructed models achieve $56.40\%$ and $58.29\%$ agreement and exceed the distillation baseline on three functional metrics. We report label requests separately from privileged access and explain why prediction agreement does not identify network parameters.
papers.authors: Biprarshi Biswas, Arya Anshuman Ojha, Yubaraj Das, Devansh Khosla, Kamran Rais, Saankhya Samanta, Subhamoy Maitra, Pantelimon Stanica
